DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.21277673 Giouli et al. applications across a wide range of tasks. MWEs such as idioms, collocations, and phrasal verbs – among others – often do not adhere to the general rules of the language. Challenges are particularly evident in downstream tasks such as syntactic parsing, where MWEs disrupt grammatical structures, and seman-tic parsing, where their non-compositional meanings are hard to capture. More-over, in certain applications such as machine translation or sentiment analysis, MWEs frequently lead to inaccurate results. To this end, MWE processing is of paramount importance, and it often relies on elaborate language resources, such as annotated corpora and computational lexicons (Constant et al. 2017). This chapter presents and discusses the results of a twofold survey on the use of MWE lexicons in NLP tasks and applications. More precisely, our goal is to identify what types of lexicons and what kind of information contained in them have been employed in NLP tasks. In particular, we show: (i) which tasks/applications MWE lexicons are used for (Sections 5.3.1 and 6.2.1); (ii) what types of information from the MWE lexicons are relevant for the respective tasks (Sections 5.3 and 6.2.2); (iii) what types of information MWE lexicons lack and could be worth including (Section 6.2.3); and (iv) to what extent has the inclusion of the lexical resource at hand impacted the overall performance of the task or of the tool (Section 5.5). In other words, we want to quantify the contribution of MWE lexicons to the tasks and applications at hand, especially in the era of Machine Learning (ML) and Large Language Models (LLMs). The contributions of this chapter are the following: (i) to the best of our knowl-edge, we deliver the first critical assessment of the impact of MWE lexicons on NLP tools and applications; (ii) we provide a thorough literature review on MWE lexicons and their contribution to NLP tasks and applications; (iii) complemen-tarily, we present the results of a questionnaire, devised to gather updated infor-mation on how MWE lexicons are used in research and language technologies; and (iv) we identify characteristics and features that might be useful for future inclusion in MWE lexicons, as well as relevant knowledge that can be used to discover and inform synergies between efforts to build these resources and the development of NLP. The remainder of the chapter is structured as follows: in Section 2, we present the scope and aims of the survey; Section 3 overviews relevant literature while Section 4 elaborates on the methodology adopted; Section 5 presents the find-ings of the critical review of prior work concerning the use of MWE-dedicated or MWE-aware lexicons across a range of NLP tasks; Section 6 reports on the user survey, considering dissemination, respondent profiles, and the data and results obtained; the findings of these surveys and their relevance for further de-velopments of MWE lexicons are discussed in Section 7. Finally, Section 8 offers concluding remarks. 100 3 Using MWE lexicons in NLP tasks 

# 2 Scope and aims of the survey 

Our study aims to explore the use of MWE-related lexical resources in NLP tasks. The intersection of the two, lexical resources and NLP tasks, is the focus of in-terest. Consequently, MWE lexical resources that are not used in NLP tasks fall outside the scope of the current research. In this section, we elaborate on the types of resources that are central to the survey and clarify the intended NLP tasks. We are primarily interested in computational lexicons, that is, structured re-sources – often stored in a database – that catalog lexical entries (single- and/or multiword ones) with their linguistic properties or features at various levels of linguistic analysis (lexis, morphology, syntax, semantics, and pragmatics). The term computational lexicon refers here to a lexical resource in electronic form in which information about words and phrases is encoded. Computational lexi-cons appear in a variety of forms, ranging from simple text documents to more elaborate lexical databases, and are used to facilitate various NLP tasks. We are interested in MWE-dedicated and MWE-aware lexical resources (Losnegaard et al. 2016). While the former treat only MWEs as lexical entries and encode their idiosyncrasies, the latter are more inclusive in scope; they not only account for MWEs explicitly but also focus on lexemes of a language and integrate MWEs alongside single words within the same lexical framework. These lexicons pro-vide representations of both single- and multiword entries, treating the latter as an integral part of the broader lexicon. In the past, computational lexicons of all sorts were primarily designed as static resources tailored to specific applications. Their creation, maintenance, and enrichment relied heavily on manual or semi-automatic input from expert lexicographers to define and categorise MWEs. These lexicons typically encode linguistic information about lemma or canonical form, part-of-speech tags, syn-tactic structures, and even semantic features. However, with the advent of word embeddings and neural models, a shift has occurred towards data-driven ap-proaches. Word embeddings, such as those created by word2vec or BERT, rep-resent words and MWEs as dense vectors in a continuous space. This shift has opened new avenues for capturing the nuances of MWEs, as their meanings can be inferred through contextualized representations learned from large datasets. These models often show improvements in capturing the non-compositional na-ture of MWEs. Recent developments also include the use of MWE-dedicated resources broadly referred to as “compositionality rating datasets”, which quantify how compositional or idiomatic a given MWE is. Compositionality ratings refer to 101 Giouli et al. human evaluations of the degree to which the meaning of a compound word or phrase can be inferred from the meanings of its components (Reddy et al. 2011). There are two main approaches: (a) rating the compositionality of the entire compound, and (b) rating the degree of compositionality of the entire MWE in relation to its constituents. Such ratings are performed by expert annotators or by non-experts (native speakers of the language at hand via crowdsourcing, or a combination of both Reddy et al. 2011, Schulte im Walde et al. 2016, Schulte im Walde 2024). While initial attempts aimed at obtaining binary judgments, ratings are now typically collected using a scale: on one end of the continuum, compounds are judged as “completely opaque”, while on the other end MWEs are rated as “completely transparent”, with various degrees of partial transparency in between. These datasets can be used to train models that more effectively predict whether a MWE should be treated as a single lexical unit, or whether its meaning can be derived from its parts. The focus of this study is placed on computational lexical resources of all sorts: computational lexicons, compositionality datasets, and resources aimed at contextualised representation of MWEs. We are equally interested in lexical resources that are manually constructed or obtained (semi-)automatically, pro-vided they are used in NLP tasks. We also consider any new type of resources that reflect the trends of the new methodologies such as LLMs. We delve into two types of NLP tasks. On the one hand, we are interested in the task of MWE identification; in this sense, the focus is on MWE lexical re-sources used within the task of MWE identification (Constant et al. 2017). On the other hand, the focus is on various NLP tasks that range from downstream ones (e.g., dependency parsing, semantic analysis) to applications such as informa-tion extraction, sentiment analysis, hate speech detection, machine translation, etc. Other uses of MWE lexicons by human users, such as in traditional language teaching and learning, while interesting, fall outside the scope of the current re-search, while usage of MWE lexicons for computer-assisted language learning is retained. Moreover, in the era of Machine Learning, the emphasis is placed on LLMs optimized to represent spans of text and embeddings of all sorts of MWEs, as well as on all kinds of tasks using LLMs related to MWEs and their respective datasets. 

# 3 Related work 

Over the past ten years, surveys on MWEs have primarily focused on two main areas: (i) how MWEs are represented in various types of language resources, par-102 3 Using MWE lexicons in NLP tasks ticularly with respect to language coverage, language diversity, and MWE meta-data descriptions; and (ii) how MWEs are handled in NLP applications, either by analyzing their interaction with downstream tasks or by focusing on tools and techniques specifically designed to process MWEs. In this section, we discuss relevant work aligned with these two areas and highlight how the present survey offers a distinct contribution, providing new insights into MWEs from a different perspective. 

3.1 MWEs in language resources 

Rosen et al. (2015) present a survey on the annotation of MWEs in 17 treebanks in 15 languages with the aim of contributing to the development of common princi-ples and guidelines for the annotation of MWEs in syntactic resources. The sur-vey was conducted by inviting experts familiar with each treebank to complete an online questionnaire. Respondents were asked to describe the annotation of different MWE types – such as nominal, phrasal, prepositional, adjectival, id-iomatic, and other expressions – within the context of their specific language and theoretical framework, including whether the treebank followed a depen-dency or constituency model, and whether it was based on Head-driven Phrase Structure Grammar or Lexical Functional Grammar. For each MWE type, participants reported whether the construction occurred in the language, whether it was annotated in the treebank, and whether it was analyzed compositionally, and were asked to provide example sentences along with analysis descriptions and search expressions. The survey results were analyzed with a comparative focus on key categories of MWEs. Prepositional MWEs were found to be annotated in all surveyed re-sources, although the strategies varied considerably; these expressions were typ-ically represented with internal syntactic structure rather than as words with spaces. Verb-particle constructions, such as phrasal verbs, were annotated in sim-ilar ways across treebanks. However, the main challenge associated with this cat-egory was not annotation strategy, but the difficulty in consistently identifying such constructions. Multiword named entities displayed the greatest variation in annotation, ranging from simple, fixed expressions to complex structures that sometimes embedded other named entities. The study concluded that, while some MWEs are clearly language-specific, others – particularly named entities – are subject to more diverse and inconsis-tent annotation practices. It also highlighted a general lack of standardised anno-tation guidelines and metadata documentation across treebanks. These findings 103 Giouli et al. underscore the need for harmonised annotation principles to improve the compa-rability, interoperability, and reusability of MWE-annotated syntactic resources. Two other surveys focus on language resources for MWEs. The first one, by Losnegaard et al. (2016) reports on a survey conducted within the framework of the IC1207 COST Action PARSEME, which aimed to provide a basic overview of the status of various types of language resources across multiple languages. The ultimate goal was to create a portal granting researchers access to previously unavailable or newly developed MWE(-aware) resources. This survey identi-fied approximately 110 resources, including 13 MWE lists, 48 MWE-dedicated or MWE-aware lexicons, such as semantic dictionaries (e.g., wordnets), and 27 corpora and treebanks with annotated MWEs (monolingual, bilingual, and mul-tilingual). The other 19 identified language resources include MWE extraction tools, corpora with annotated MWEs, lists of MWE resources, datasets contain-ing MWEs, annotated texts, pattern dictionaries of verbs, and domain-specific MWE lists. These resources cover 19 languages, including Arabic, Bulgarian, Croatian, Czech, Dutch, English, Estonian, French, German, Hebrew, Italian, Macedonian, Polish, Portuguese, Russian, Serbian, Slovak, Slovene, and Swedish. English was the most represented language with 12 resources, followed by Italian, which appeared in 7 resources. The survey focused on metadata descriptions of the resources highlighting several challenges, including their availability in large language resource repositories and cataloging issues that hinder efficient discov-ery and reuse by researchers. The discussion and conclusions centered on the standardisation and enhancement of metadata descriptions. However, no defini-tive set of features for describing MWE lexicons was established. The survey ultimately contributed to the development of a metadata schema for language resources containing MWEs; ultimately, the schema is aimed at facilitating the creation of a meta-resource that could be useful to end users. The second survey by Markantonatou et al. (2026) builds upon and extends the scope of the previous one, by updating and expanding the inventory of MWE-related resources from 2016 onward, focusing on computational lexicons. This follow-up effort was carried out within the framework of the UniDive COST Ac-tion (Savary et al. 2024), specifically as part of Working Group 2, which aims to articulate the lexicon-corpus interface (Barbu Mititelu et al. 2024). The new survey identified 66 resources using strict inclusion criteria with special empha-sis on the languages featured in the resources and their level of representation. Thus, the survey is following the UniDive COST Action idea to highlight the extent to which MWE lexicons are developed for less-resourced languages. The survey focuses on key features of computational lexicons that require deeper ex-ploration, aligning with the broader vision of establishing a connected ecosystem 104 3 Using MWE lexicons in NLP tasks of lexicons and corpora where MWEs are systematically encoded and annotated, ultimately enabling more robust and comprehensive NLP applications. A central goal of the survey was to offer a detailed account of the current state of computa-tional MWE lexicons, while also considering recent developments in the context of LLMs. From a different perspective, Hubers et al. (2020) report on interdisciplinary work carried out within the framework of the ISLA project, which focused exclu-sively on idiomatic expressions as a subset of formulaic language. The project aimed to investigate the acquisition and processing of MWEs from the view-points of psycholinguistics and second-language acquisition. To support this multi-faceted research, the project developed a set of tools and language re-sources considered essential. These included (i) a comprehensive database of 374 Dutch idiomatic expressions, annotated with information such as frequency of exposure, familiarity of meaning, usage, transparency, and imageability, along with cross-linguistic data indicating whether similar expressions exist in German and Standard Arabic; (ii) a test instrument designed to evaluate idiom knowledge and to gather data on idiom properties among both native speakers and L2 learn-ers; and (iii) a Computer-Assisted Language Learning (CALL) system, featuring immediate corrective feedback to help second-language learners practice Dutch idioms in a structured environment. The results showed that both native speakers and second-language learners were capable of reliably assessing idiom properties. However, performance var-ied depending on factors such as language distance and second-language profi-ciency. As future work, the researchers indicated exploring improved methods for identifying MWEs that go beyond simple frequency-based approaches, as well as developing standardised procedures for data collection to ensure comparabil-ity across studies. A continuously updated and extensible database of formulaic language resources was also referred as a core outcome of this effort. 

3.2 NLP applications and MWEs 

Considering a direct relation between MWEs and NLP applications, Constant et al. (2017) provide an overview of how MWEs are handled in these, namely, in parsing and machine translation. Rather than treating MWEs as a purely linguis-tic phenomenon, their study focuses on MWE processing, defining it as a task with two main sub-tasks: discovery and identification. The former is concerned with finding new MWEs (types) in text corpora and storing them for future use in a repository such as a lexicon. In contrast, MWE identification is defined as 105 Giouli et al. the process of automatically annotating MWEs in running text and classifying them into predefined categories. The study explores the interactions between MWE processing and parsing and machine translation applications, emphasizing how key MWE properties, such as discontiguity, non-compositionality, ambigu-ity, and variability, present both challenges and opportunities for MWE-aware systems. The language resources considered in this survey include (i) lexical re-sources, i.e., databases containing MWEs, MWE lexicons, and general-purpose dictionaries containing MWEs; (ii) corpora, i.e., corpora annotated with MWE tags and parallel corpora with sentence-level alignments; and (iii) treebanks, that is, special corpora with syntactic relations annotation where MWEs are explicitly marked. The analysis and discussion of these language resources focus primarily on their relevance for parsing and machine translation. The authors conclude that, while MWE processing presents challenges, it also offers opportunities. Discontiguity hinders discovery and identification but sup-ports parsing by linking nonadjacent words. The orchestration of tasks is crit-ical for MWE processing, as identification benefits from prior syntactic analy-sis, while pre-processing is more effective for fixed MWEs like named entities. Additionally, MWE categorisation influences processing strategies, with verbal MWEs requiring different approaches than compounds. Despite these insights, the authors identify several open issues and research questions. These concern evaluation inconsistencies, which, again, hinder dis-covery, identification, and re-use, particularly in machine translation. Improved metrics and annotation standards for MWEs were considered needed. Also, com-parative studies across tasks, processing strategies, and MWE categories are lack-ing, limiting insights into optimal processing approaches. Finally, coverage lim-itations persist, as hand-built MWE dictionaries remain a primary resource but suffer from limited domain and language coverage. Integrating automatic dis-covery methods into downstream applications (e.g., identification, parsing, and machine translation) could enhance coverage and improve extrinsic evaluation methods. Ramisch et al. (2023) conduct a review of experiments for MWE identifica-tion using data from the SEMEVAL DiMSUM (Schneider et al. 2016) and the three editions of the PARSEME Shared Tasks (Savary et al. 2017, Ramisch et al. 2018, 2020). The study analyzes 40 papers on MWE identification, focusing on often-overlooked experimental factors, such as corpus selection, pre- and post-processing, MWE encoding, evaluation metrics, statistical significance, and error analyses. These aspects significantly influence experimental results and conclu-sions, underscoring the need for systematic descriptions of experimental con-ditions to mitigate the risk of misleading findings due to poorly designed se-106 3 Using MWE lexicons in NLP tasks tups. The survey aims to base its discussion on quantitative data extracted from the analysed papers, including details on languages covered in the corpora; data partitioning for training, development, and testing; MWE categories targeted by models; corpus pre- and post-processing strategies; MWE encoding and decoding methods, particularly for classification and tagging models; evaluation metrics used; statistical significance of model comparisons; and error analyses conducted. A key focus of the survey is on how unseen MWEs are handled by identification systems. Findings indicate that corpus characteristics, including the number of languages, application domain, and data partitioning strategies, impact experi-mental outcomes. The authors emphasise that standardised reporting on corpus selection, pre-processing, evaluation metrics, and statistical significance testing is crucial for ensuring the reliability and reproducibility of MWE identification research. Relevant conclusions on open issues include studying automatic evalu-ation techniques, while regarding the role of manual evaluation, particularly in downstream tasks where MWE quality may influence final outcomes, and new evaluation protocols to address questions such as whether certain MWE cate-gories are more significant than others. The survey ultimately advocates for the gradual adoption of methodological standards and best practices in both shared tasks and independent research, promoting more transparent, replicable, and ro-bust experimental frameworks for MWE identification. More recently, Mahajan et al. (2024) present a survey on the approaches, techniques, and features required for MWE identification, presenting language-specific descriptions. The study includes a detailed list of tools used for the extraction and identification of MWEs, such as parsers, semantic analyzers, chunkers, part-of-speech (PoS) taggers, word aligners, and ontology editors. It offers a literature survey on methods and techniques employed for MWE pro-cessing in non-Indian languages, covering seven European languages, three Asian languages, and three African and Middle Eastern languages. The survey also includes a dedicated section that reviews the methods and techniques for MWE identification for seven Indian languages. The work draws attention to recent progress in applying machine learning techniques to Indian languages while also identifying major challenges, including the lack of annotated corpora, the diversity of writing styles, and the complexity of morphological structures. By examining various MWE identification approaches – linguistic, statistical, machine learning, and hybrid – particularly in the context of Indian languages, it underscores the importance of combining methodologies to improve accuracy. Moreover, the study highlights a significant gap in research on MWEs in some In-dian languages, such as Marathi, emphasizing the need for further investigation and for the development of specialized approaches tailored to these languages. 107 Giouli et al. Unlike the surveys discussed in this section, the present chapter focuses on MWE lexical resources, integrating both perspectives: the description and anno-tation of MWEs, and the use and contributions of these resources to NLP tasks and applications. Concentrating on recent developments, we aim at identifying MWE lexical resources through a comprehensive literature survey, further com-plemented by a community-wide questionnaire. The resources examined include lexicons specifically dedicated to MWEs, as well as more general datasets that in-corporate MWE information. We provide a detailed analysis of these lexicons, considering multiple dimen-sions such as lexicon type, categories of expressions included, language cover-age, and the linguistic information encoded. These aspects are also examined in relation to their use and impact on NLP tasks and applications, including their relevance to recent advances in LLMs and emerging directions in this area of research and development. By offering an in-depth analysis of related work, along with a systematic liter-ature review and a dedicated community questionnaire, this study goes beyond the description of MWE representation in language resources and their handling in NLP applications. It aims to assess the broader impact of MWE lexicons on NLP tools and applications, while identifying critical gaps and emerging trends in the field. 

# 4 Methodology 

This section provides a detailed overview of the methodology used in our study, describing the processes for selecting the relevant papers and for developing a questionnaire on the use of MWE lexical resources by the community (including both academic and industrial environments). 

4.1 Paper selection process 

The paper selection process followed a structured approach. It began with an initial search and filtering of papers based on relevance and publication date. This was followed by peer review by team members. Finally, a list of selected articles was compiled, forming the basis for the analysis in this survey. To curate a selection of relevant papers for our survey, we focused on three prominent sources: the ACL Anthology, 1 EUROPHRAS, 2 and arXiv. 3 To identify

In contrast, the EUROPHRAS and arXiv selection process involved the manual extraction of papers. In addition, after the initial search, reference lists of recent papers were reviewed to identify new and rele-vant papers for inclusion. To ensure the inclusion of recent and relevant research, papers published within the last six years (January 2019 to March 2024) were con-sidered. A total of 68 papers were retrieved. After the initial search and filtering, each extracted article was reviewed by two team members to assess its relevance to the survey. In cases where the two reviewers disagreed on the relevance or inclusion of a paper, a third member of the team was brought in to read the paper and make the final decision. All results of this review process were then discussed in regular meetings, allowing consensus to be achieved on the final selection of articles. This approach reduced the risk of omitting important papers or including less relevant ones. The final list of 37 papers was compiled and served as the basis for the analysis presented in the survey (Section 5). 

4.2 Devising the questionnaire for the community 

To gather detailed information about current practices and the use of MWE lexi-cons in various NLP tasks, in addition to the literature review mentioned above, a questionnaire was created for the user community. The primary objectives of the questionnaire are as follows: • to understand the professional demographics and activities of individuals working with MWE lexicons; • to collect detailed information about the use, characteristics, and effective-ness of MWE lexicons in NLP tasks; • to identify specific challenges and requirements associated with the use of MWE lexicons; • to gather information about the supplementary resources and integration guidelines for MWE lexicons (if any) in NLP systems. 109 Giouli et al. The questionnaire design was grounded on several interdisciplinary approaches within the fields of computational linguistics, NLP, and lexicography. Generally, it is focused on the identification of the specialized resources used to improve syntactic parsing, semantic analysis, and machine translation; the techniques for automatic extraction and application of MWEs; and the lexicons’ characteristics such as size, format, update frequency, etc. used for the above-mentioned tasks. The questionnaire was structured to include the following sections: • Participant consent and understanding . This section was developed with the purpose of ensuring the informed and voluntary consent of the partici-pants. The questions confirm that the participants understand the purpose of the survey and agree to the terms, ensuring ethical compliance and data protection. • Professional background . On the one hand, questions on the area of pro-fessional activities, roles or functions, and community representation help identify the demographic and professional distribution, which is important for data segmentation and targeted analysis. On the other hand, these aid in understanding how the professional environment might influence the participants’ experiences and reveal challenges faced during the use of the lexicons. • Experience with MWE lexicons . This section gathers information on par-ticipants’ experience with MWE lexicons over the last five years, focusing on practical applications and specific NLP tasks. Understanding the diver-sity and depth of experience makes it possible to assess the impact of MWE lexicons on different applications. • MWE lexicons characteristics . This section collects specific details about the lexicons’ use, including their title, size, format, type, direction, lan-guage coverage, access, and update frequency. These detailed attributes are important for evaluating different MWE lexicons. • Perception on MWE lexicons use in NLP . This section focuses on ques-tions about specific features, complementarity with other resources, chal-lenges, and evaluation methods, as well as questions about guidelines, community-driven approaches to integrating MWE lexicons in NLP sys-tems, and recommendations help identify common problems and best prac-tices. 110 3 Using MWE lexicons in NLP tasks 

# 5 Critical literature review on MWE lexicons and their contribution to NLP tasks and applications 

In this section, we present the results obtained from the critical literature review focusing exclusively on lexical resources reported to have been used in an NLP downstream task or application. Based on the papers selected, we want to shed light on the following aspects: • papers identified and the venues in which they were presented; • lexicons reported; we elaborate on the features of the lexicons (linguality type, languages covered, types of MWEs treated, and linguistic informa-tion that is encoded for MWEs); • NLP task or application for which the MWE lexicon is used; the focus is on the linguistic information that was used in the task and the overall impact of incorporating/using the MWE resource; • the interplay between LLMs and MWEs. 5.2.3 Types of linguistic information encoded about MWEs 

The lexicons we identified in this survey typically encode MWE-related infor-mation beyond the one used in the task reported. The nature and extent of the linguistic information encoded depend on the type of the lexical resource (whether MWE-aware or MWE-dedicated), its intended purpose, and the over-arching framework (linguistic, task- and application-oriented, etc.). This infor-mation is subsequently utilised in NLP tasks based on the specific requirements 115 Giouli et al. of the task at hand. The diversity of approaches to MWE encoding in lexicons should be noted, as it poses challenges for any systematic analysis. In MWE-aware lexicons, such as wordnets, information about the lemma and part-of-speech is typically encoded. In such resources, MWEs are treated follow-ing the same principles as single-word entries. On the contrary, MWE-dedicated lexical resources primarily encode part-of-speech information and the type of MWE, such as idioms, light verb constructions, verbal collocations, and com-pound nouns (see Section 5.2.2). This classification supports a more nuanced understanding of MWEs and aids in their proper treatment. Various MWE-dedicated lexicons encode syntactic information, often encom-passing internal structure (Baptista 2012), argument structure, and syntactic de-pendencies between their constituents (Espinosa Anke et al. 2019, Müller et al. 2022), or even distributional constraints on argument slots and transformational properties (Baptista 2012). Such information is aimed at modeling the behavior of MWEs in context in a straightforward and explicit manner. In contrast, other resources provide sample sentences that depict the distribution of MWEs in an implicit way (Cook et al. 2008, Haagsma et al. 2018, Tayyar Madabushi et al. 2021, Zhou et al. 2021). As mentioned above, three wordnets were identified in the study, targeting English (Fellbaum 2010), Polish and English (Rudnicka et al. 2015), and German (Henrich & Hinrichs 2011). These resources typically encode semantic infor-mation by structuring both single- and multiword lexemes into synonym sets (synsets), which are accompanied with glosses (definitions). In addition, they capture lexical-semantic relations and establish interlingual correspondences via the Inter-Lingual Index (ILI). Besides glosses, paraphrases are often used to represent the semantics of MWE entries in lexicons or lexical datasets (Tayyar Madabushi et al. 2021, Liu & Hwa 2016, Pershina et al. 2015). More elaborate MWE-dedicated datasets encode sense information for MWEs using fine- or coarse-grained sets of meanings along with usage information (Tayyar Mad-abushi et al. 2021). Moreover, lexical functions, as introduced in the Meaning-Text Theory (Mel’čuk 2007), are also used as a device to capture the semantics of collocations in Espinosa Anke et al. (2019). In semantics-oriented tasks, such as sentiment analysis, the identification and interpretation of MWEs play a crucial role. In the survey, specialised MWE-aware lexicons tailored to meet the needs of such applications were identified; in these lexicons, both single- and multiword entries are labeled for semantic orien-tation and intensity (Moreno-Ortiz et al. 2020). Reflecting the specific demands of sentiment analysis, some of the MWE-dedicated lexicons in our survey are de-signed to encode discrete emotion categories (Prochnow et al. 2024), while others 116 3 Using MWE lexicons in NLP tasks focus on capturing prior and contextual sentiment polarity: positive, negative, or neutral sentiment (Jochim et al. n.d., Moreno-Ortiz et al. 2020). Certain datasets identified in the survey specifically target the so-called pos-sibly idiomatic expressions (PIEs), that is, expressions that can be interpreted either literally or idiomatically depending on context (Haagsma et al. 2018, Zhou et al. 2021, Cook et al. 2008). These datasets provide contextualized examples accompanied by fine-grained annotations, including binary or categorical labels indicating whether each instance is used literally or idiomatically. Similarly, ad-ditional semantic aspects are captured through ratings for idiomaticity, semantic opacity, and familiarity degree (Hubers et al. 2020). The extent to which a lexicon incorporates linguistic information typically reflects the specific requirements of the target task. In addition to core lexical data, some resources encode supplementary – or domain-specific – linguistic information, such as language proficiency levels (Capel 2015, de Jong et al. 2016). Others provide links to external resources (Collard et al. 2023), or offer only minimal lexical detail (Sarwar 2022), indicating a more diverse or limited scope. In summary, the lexicons used in NLP tasks can vary significantly in terms of the type of linguistic information they encode. While some lexicons contain only linguistic features relevant to a specific task (e.g., PoS, syntactic, and semantic information), others incorporate different kinds of information that support a broader range of applications (see Table 2).

5.3 MWE lexicons in NLP tasks and linguistic information used 

We provide an overview of the NLP tasks for which the use of a MWE lexicon has been reported, highlighting the type(s) of information provided by such re-sources that proved relevant or useful for these tasks. 

5.3.1 NLP tasks for which a MWE lexicon is used 

MWE lexicons are used for NLP tasks that vary from MWE detection and ex-traction, bilingual term extraction, lexicon development by extraction, lexicon induction, sentiment labeling, machine translation, neural machine translation to modeling, recognizing, and categorizing MWEs, testing idiomaticity and im-proving language models to capture idiomaticity, natural language parsing, lan-guage generation, and evaluation of LLM performance on MWEs. The tasks also include gender identification, idiom and MWE teaching and learning systems, id-iomatic compound detection and semantic relations for terminology, including synonymy, antonymy, and hypernymy. Generally, a notable subset of papers focuses specifically on idiomatic expres-sions, indicating a significant interest in understanding their complexities. For instance, Lee & Uvaliyev (2023) examine the selection of MWEs for graded vocab-ulary lists, emphasizing the role of phrasal verbs and idioms in language learning, while other articles apply a more general approach to idiomatic expressions. At the same time, some other papers have a general focus on MWEs, analysing their contextual information, structure, and semantic and syntactic idiosyncrasies. The NLP task for which MWE lexicons are most frequently used is MWE identification, with 21 out of 37 papers reporting this use (i.e., 56%). Given that (multiword) terms and named entities can also be treated as MWEs, this number could actually be increased by two more papers (thus accounting for 62% of all the literature reviewed). Idiomaticity is directly addressed in two papers, but if we include literature dealing broadly with the identification of concepts for which a single word does not exist in the target language – and which are instead expressed through multiword combinations – then we arrive at a total of 25 papers (corresponding to 67%) that relate to idiomaticity in a broad sense. Another three papers (8%) report the use of MWE lexicons for sentiment label-ing. Given that MWEs are, more often than not, associated with a connotation, be it positive or negative, this explains the interest in MWEs for this downstream task. Other tasks, each illustrated by one paper in our survey set, are: sentence simplification, sentence generation, author gender identification, understanding 118 3 Using MWE lexicons in NLP tasks how LLMs work and probing them, lexical complexity, validation of lexicon or grammar, and machine translation. 

5.3.2 Linguistic information for MWE processing in NLP tasks 

The type of linguistic information revealed by the studies analysed includes sev-eral crucial elements that contribute to the understanding and processing of MWEs, and includes a diverse range of MWEs such as idioms, phrasal verbs (Lee & Uvaliyev 2023, Zhou et al. 2021 and others), and nominal phrases (Maziarz et al. 2022, Premasiri et al. 2022 and others). Key components encompass an-notated dependency trees, including the representation of syntactic structures, where words are connected to their syntactic heads, showing how each word in a sentence relates to others, part of speech tags used to assign grammatical cat-egories to words, identifying the roles of different words within an expression, and facilitating the analysis of their roles in MWEs (Collard et al. 2023). Surveys on the semantic relations between constituents explore how these expressions interact within contexts (Fisas et al. 2020, Maziarz et al. 2022 and others). Ad-ditionally, lemmatisation, which is the process of reducing words to their base forms, allows for a more consistent analysis across different word forms. The linguistic information used in these studies describes various aspects that are essential for analysing MWEs. This includes a variety of lexical features, such as morphological and syntactic characteristics that are important for un-derstanding how MWEs function within the language. The resources often cap-ture information regarding the meaning and interpretation of the expressions, emphasizing their non-compositionality and context-dependency. Furthermore, the frequency of use (e.g. Hubers et al. 2020) plays a critical role, as it affects how MWEs are processed in different linguistic contexts. A key area of focus is the semantic and syntactic classification of MWEs. For ex-ample, Zhou et al. (2021) focus on the semantic classification of idiomatic expres-sions, specifically examining their compositionality. This classification is crucial for tasks such as paraphrasing and idiomatic sentence generation, as it helps determine how these expressions can be effectively utilized and recognised in various contexts. In another study, Espinosa-Anke et al. (2021) address the classi-fication of collocations, where MWEs are classified based on their compositional or semi-compositional nature. This classification improves the understanding of MWEs in natural language processing tasks such as lexical resource development and language modeling. When addressing sentiment labeling, a mere list of MWEs will prove insuffi-cient; thus, resources containing emotion annotation, polarity, and intensity of MWEs are rather useful. 119 Giouli et al. 

5.3.3 Methodologies employed 

The experiments used in the papers analysed include different tasks and meth-ods, some of which were not directly dependent on the lexicon development, but provided their integration into various NLP tasks. One of the main goals of these tasks is the identification and extraction of MWE, such as idiomatic expressions, collocations, and phrasal verbs from text (Tanner & Hoffman 2023), and for this purpose, the lexicons serve as structured resources for recognizing MWEs in cor-pora. As a result, various techniques are applied, including rule-based systems, which rely on predefined linguistic rules to identify MWEs based on patterns in the text (Maziarz et al. 2022), machine learning methods, where models are trained on annotated data to learn how to identify MWEs (Kanclerz & Piasecki 2022), and statistical processing used to find or identify MWEs in large datasets. For example, some techniques focused on identifying MWEs through predefined patterns, which aid in the recognition of nonliteral expressions, and for this pur-pose, the PARSEME corpora were applied (Müller et al. 2022). Furthermore, researchers generally address three MWE-related tasks, espe-cially, evaluating and improving automatically generated MWE resources (Lee & Uvaliyev 2023), curating lexicons for Machine Translation (MT) systems to cover idioms and other MWEs (Zhou et al. 2021) and detecting idiomaticity in context, often in zero- or one-shot settings (Jakhotiya et al. n.d.). Studies use a range of techniques and methods like transformer fine-tuning, where models such as eBERT-multilingual-uncased, DistilBERT-multilingual-uncased, XLM-RoBERTa-large, and XLM-Net are trained to classify tokens as idiomatic (Jakhotiya et al. n.d.); AMR-driven chain-of-thought method that prompts Abstract Meaning Rep-resentations (AMRs) to guide LLMs in detection of idioms (Jin et al. 2024); gath-ering synsets to improve MWE recognition accuracy (Maziarz et al. 2022). In any case, the resulting systems are evaluated by fine-tuning and testing on zero- and one-shot settings to evaluate how well transformer models can detect idiomatic expressions or classify MWEs (Jakhotiya et al. n.d.). Such evaluations help refine the models and ensure that the MWE lexicons are contributing meaningfully to the task. In addition, the lexicons that include sentiment-related annotations, such as polarity and intensity, are used to improve the accuracy of sentiment analysis models. As a result, two main tasks are revealed, especially those focused on sen-timent evaluation (Hwang & Hidey 2019), in which MWE-aware resources help models to label expressions and, those dedicated to the acquisition and learning of idioms (Hubers et al. 2020), where a combination of linguistic, educational, and other perspectives guide models how idiomatic meaning is created. 120 3 Using MWE lexicons in NLP tasks In general, the methodologies involved demonstrate the diverse strategies for MWE detection, classification, and integration into NLP applications. And different experiments demonstrate that MWE lexicons play an important role in various NLP tasks, both as basic resources for rule-based and statistical ap-proaches and as components for training and evaluating machine learning and transformer-based models. 

5.4 MWEs and LLMs 

In general, the integration of MWEs into the pre-training or fine-tuning stages of LLMs still remains limited. Despite the recognized importance of MWEs for various NLP tasks, there are relatively few efforts that systematically incorpo-rate MWE lexicons into LLM pipelines. This suggests a gap in current practices, where the potential of MWE-aware or MWE-dedicated lexical resources remains largely unexplored. In the next sections, we focus on the impact of MWE lexicons on the pre-training and fine-tuning of LLMs, and on the mutual impact between MWE datasets and LLMs. 

5.4.1 Computing multiwords for LLMs 

Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) tokenisation, as introduced by Sennrich et al. (2016), is an adaptation of the original BPE data compression algorithm (Gage 1994) for subword segmentation in NLP. This method has since been developed into BPE variants tailored for MWEs, such as those incorporating pointwise mutual infor-mation to guide merge operations (Kumar & Thawani 2022). Another approach, which represents statistically determined MWEs as individual tokens, is used to compress the text input of LLMs (Gee et al. 2023). The Principle of Least Effort, where the tokeniser independently learns an integrated vocabulary of subwords, words and MWEs, has also been introduced (Yang 2024). Kumar & Thawani (2022) investigate the incorporation of MWE-based tokeni-sation into transformer-based neural machine translation systems. At the same time, the architectures and techniques they examine can be directly applied to LLMs, which typically employ BPE or similar subword tokenisers. In contrast, Yang (2024) explicitly targets tokeniser design for LLMs by introducing the Less-is-Better (LiB) model, a cognitively inspired tokeniser that learns a joint vocab-ulary of subwords, words and MWEs. The LiB model aims to minimise both the number of tokens and vocabulary size. MWE-based tokenisation is not widely used in LLMs, mainly due to the chal-lenges of integrating fixed multiword units into dynamic subword-based models 121 Giouli et al. and the lack of large-scale, high-quality MWE resources suitable for training. It has only been experimentally investigated to a limited extent (mainly for ma-chine translation). Such approaches recognise the value of MWEs as language units, although their main goal is to reduce computational costs. Alternative recent approaches build on the idea for multitokens being directly included in the algorithms for pre-training the LLMs. In Multitoken Prediction (MTP), LLMs are equipped with some additional parameters to predict multiple tokens simultaneously and in parallel using independent output heads (Gloeckle et al. 2024). DeepSeek V3 (DeepSeek-AI et al. 2025) has modified the MTP so that additional tokens are predicted sequentially, and the full causal chain is preserved at each prediction depth. However, MTP still remains experimental and has not yet become widely adopted in mainstream LLM architectures. 

5.4.2 Fine-tuning of LLMs for the recognition of MWEs 

Several experiments have investigated how LLMs can be fine-tuned to improve their performance in MWE classification. Fine-tuning of pre-trained models re-quires annotated data suitable for a classification task. In the broadest sense, datasets containing annotated MWEs can be exploited as lexicons, as the anno-tated multiword units can be easily extracted from the datasets and classified based on the annotated attributes and their values. The following language models were mainly used for the fine-tuning experi-ments: BERT (base and large, uncased) (Devlin et al. 2019), RoBERTa (base and large) (Liu et al. 2019), DistilBERT (Sanh et al. 2019), ALBERT (Lan et al. 2020), XLNet (base and large) (Yang et al. 2019), and XLM-RoBERTa (Conneau et al. 2020). For example, BERT, DistilBERT, XLM-RoBERTa, and XL-NET are the models used in an experiment to recognise idiomatic expressions using binary classi-fication in two different settings: zero-shot and one-shot (Jakhotiya et al. n.d.). The training and development dataset (Tayyar Madabushi et al. 2021) consists of samples containing one target sentence, one MWE (with or without idiomatic meaning), and two context sentences. The results show that the one-shot setting performs better than the zero-shot setting. In many cases, fine-tuning of LLMs is conducted for a single language. For example, using the Romanian annotation in the multilingual PARSEME corpus for several types of VMWEs (Ramisch et al. 2020), significant improvements were achieved in the identification of unseen Romanian MWEs (Avram et al. 2023) by using a lateral inhibition layer and adversarial training for multilingual LLMs such as XLM-RoBERTa. 122 3 Using MWE lexicons in NLP tasks The impact of Pattern Exploit Training (Schick & Schütze 2021), a few-shot method of classification, and BERTRAM (Schick & Schütze 2020), a method of creating contextual embeddings, is evaluated on the task of idiomaticity detec-tion. In evaluating the models, SemEval 2022 Task 2: Multilingual Idiomaticity Detection and Sentence Embedding (Tayyar Madabushi et al. 2022) was used. The dataset consists of three languages: English, Portuguese, and Galician. The results suggest that few-shot learning methods are effective on the task of id-iomaticity detection despite the lower accuracy on Portuguese and Galician. Sim-ilarly, the results support the conclusion that improved MWE representations does have an impact on improved detection. Three experiments are carried out for French (Bui & Savary 2024): (i) fine-tuning the models on Sequoia (Candito et al. 2020), a French corpus annotated for all MWE types; (ii) treating verbal (PARSEME dataset for French) and non-verbal MWEs as separate tasks (union approach), training the models on the respective datasets and then merging the predictions; (iii) a multi-task approach in which the models are trained jointly on both types (verbal and non-verbal). The results show that the combination of independent models (union approach) performs better than single-task and multi-task models, especially when using monolin-gual transformer models: CamemBERT (Martin et al. 2020) and FlauBERT (Le et al. 2020). The conclusion was that the union approach effectively utilises the complementary strengths of the models trained on different datasets and pro-vides a robust solution for MWE identification. To summarise, various fine-tuning methods are used in BERT-based transform-ers to identify MWEs. Fine-tuning requires annotated MWE datasets instead of lexicons. However, as discussed above, these annotated datasets can be consid-ered some sort of lexicons because they encode structured linguistic information relevant to MWE processing. 

5.4.3 Evaluation of LLMs for the recognition of MWEs 

Studies on encoder-only models have shown that pre-trained language models do not adequately capture and represent the meanings of idiomatic expressions (Garcia et al. 2021). A set of probing measures and a dataset for English and Por-tuguese are proposed to investigate how accurately idiomaticity in MWEs, espe-cially in noun compounds, is captured in vector space models, focusing on some widely used representations such as BERTRAM, BERT, SBERT, DistilB, ELMo (Peters et al. 2018), and GloVe (Pennington et al. 2014). The probing tasks have shown that contextualised models may not recognise idiomatic noun compounds 123 Giouli et al. that have a lower degree of substitutability of the individual components com-pared to more compositional noun compounds. It was shown that all transformer models outperform the Long Short‑Term Memory (LSTM)-based method in recognising MWEs, and it was concluded that transformer models can overcome the challenges posed by MWEs in local do-mains such as plant names and flower names better than previous neural meth-ods such as LSTM (Premasiri et al. 2023). Furthermore, generative models such as GPT-2 perform poorly when process-ing figurative language without the use of mitigation strategies (Jhamtani et al. 2021). A survey of recent work on MWE semantics has shown that, while transformer-based language models with an encoder-only architecture (BERT, mBERT, XLM-RoBERTa, RoBERTa, ALBERT, DistilBERT, SBERT, DeBERTa) and GPT capture some aspects of MWE meaning, this ability is neither comprehen-sive nor consistent (Miletić & Schulte im Walde 2024). The conclusion was that improvement with optimisation strategies such as fine-tuning and knowledge ex-pansion would yield very different gains. This can be explained by the fact that MWE representations rely on memorized information rather than sophisticated meaning processing, which is reflected in the suboptimal generalisation ability. Previous research has shown that encoder-only pretrained language models can effectively represent MWEs when fine-tuned with appropriate data (Tayyar Mad-abushi et al. 2022). Experiments were conducted on an English language dataset to evaluate the ability of LLMs such as the 7‑billion‑parameter (7B) versions of Llama 2, Vicuna, and Mistral to detect idiomatic expressions in a zero-shot setting (De Luca Forna-ciari et al. 2024). The results of the study show that when it comes to recognising the meaning of an ambiguous sentence, LLMs struggle to distinguish between literal and idiomatic language use. Further experiments on the recognition of MWEs were carried out in English, Portuguese, and Galician with different gen-erative models from the GPT family, the Gemini family, the Llama 2 family, the Flan-T5 family, Phi-2, and Mistral (Phelps et al. 2024). The results showed that generative language models deliver competitive results, but do not reach the per-formance of fine-tuned, pre-trained language models. Further experiments were conducted with open-source and proprietary LLMs (from the GPT family and the Lamma 3 family) to investigate how these mod-els handle MWEs in different languages and contexts, using a dataset with ex-amples in three language pairs – Galician-Spanish, English-Spanish, and Portu-guese-Spanish (De Leon et al. 2025). The ability of LLMs to recognise whether MWEs are used as idioms or literally, the extent to which LLMs effectively cap-ture the non-compositional meanings of MWEs, the ability of LLMs to acquire 124 3 Using MWE lexicons in NLP tasks information from the prompt, and the relationship between LLM size and per-formance on texts containing MWEs with non-compositional meanings were investigated. The experiments show that LLMs, despite their abilities in many other tasks, continue to have difficulties processing MWEs. The conclusion was that this gap highlights the limitations of these models compared to fine-tuned language models such as XLM-RoBERTa, which are much smaller models and contain far fewer parameters. While some results show that the processing of MWEs with non-compositional meanings in English is comparable to fine-tuned pre-trained language models, the same cannot be said for other languages. 

5.5 Impact of using MWE lexicons 

The current survey reveals that many NLP tasks are idiom-related. MWE lexicons are used to extract idioms (Maziarz et al. 2022) from corpora, to detect (the degree of) idiomaticity (Jakhotiya et al. n.d.), and enhance idiom learning approaches (Krotova et al. 2020). Lu (2022) uses a lexical resource to improve the handling of MWEs in ML, specifically for classifying idiomatic expressions. In the work of Liu & Lareau (2024), the model correctly guesses the masked token around 60% of the time for tokens within idioms, compared to only 25% for simple lexemes. There is no significant difference between the three types of idioms: 62% for weak idioms, 58% for semi-idioms and 62% for strong idioms. This reveals again the model’s higher capacity in predicting tokens within idioms than simple lexemes. The impact of incorporating MWE resources into linguistic tasks is significant, particularly in improving the performance of applications such as translation, vocabulary extraction, and language generation. For example, Lee & Uvaliyev (2023) report that corpus-based evaluations of automatically generated vocabu-lary lists benefited from using MWEs. Especially, the use of MWEs allowed for an evaluation of semantic compositionality, which led to more accurate vocabu-lary extraction. Kumar & Thawani (2022) discuss the impact of MWEs on neural machine translation, particularly between English and Hindi. Their findings in-dicate that applying naive extensions of BPE to MWEs resulted in suboptimal performance, as the method often split MWEs incorrectly, distorting their mean-ings. The research highlights the need for more sophisticated methods that ac-count for the specific properties of MWEs in translation tasks. These and other findings demonstrate that the proper integration of MWE resources can greatly enhance both the accuracy and contextual relevance of linguistic tasks. The study by Haviv et al. (n.d.) shows that idioms help us understand how transformer models make accurate predictions. The authors state that idioms are useful for studying memorisation. MWE lexicons are also used for idiomatic 125 Giouli et al. sentence generation and paraphrasing (Zhou et al. 2021). There are also experi-ments on sentence similarity identification carried out by Knietaite et al. (2024) that explore the impact of using the local context and glosses for MWE compo-nent words, revealing that it is beneficial for the sentence similarity task. The authors observe an increase in performance as the dataset size increases and the impact of using glosses. However, the authors identify that it does not improve the models’ representation of idioms. There is an impactful part of research effort focusing on MWE lexicons and datasets related to general MWE identification and extraction by working on training and testing the datasets (Premasiri et al. 2022, Maziarz et al. 2022). Mohamed et al. (2024) advocate that lexicons even with minimal morphosyn-tactic information, i.e., PoS information and verbal MWE types, can amplify current MWE-annotated datasets and refine identification strategies. Müller et al. (2024) demonstrate that lexicons containing broader lexical coverage, i.e., more detailed syntactic description, particularly about distinguishing between sentence-internal and sentence-external modifiers, facilitate accurate parsing of MWEs. Such resources can also amplify current MWE-annotated datasets, as well as improve identification strategies. NLP tasks also involve lexicons for enhancing sentiment analysis. For example, Negi et al. (n.d.) show that using MWE resources enhances the model’s ability to accurately extract and classify aspect terms, provide more context-aware sen-timent analysis, and improve performance in domain-specific scenarios where MWEs play a significant role. The integration of MWEs into Aspect-Based Sen-timent Analysis pipelines ensures a more sophisticated analysis. The use of lexi-cons also improves alignment and translation quality in NLP applications (Adjali et al. n.d.). The use of a MWE lexicon enhances automatic author gender identification as noted by Sarwar (2022). The author notes that in experiments using only sin-gle words as features, only MWEs as features, and MWEs plus single words as features, the last option seems to perform better for most classifiers (i.e., Sup-port Verctor Machine (SVM) performs best) and pre-trained models (Multilin-gual BERT, DistilBERT, XML-RoBERTa, Multilingual DeBERTa). However, the experiments in Structural Topic Modelling (STM) reveal a twofold insight (Kokki-nakis et al. 2023). The results suggest that the STM models perform only slightly better without MWEs than with MWEs. One reason could be that the vocabu-lary is larger without MWEs included, so the number of topics captures more words. Still, there is some indication that MWE identification leads to better in-terpretability of the STM, as calculated by the semantic coherence, which was 126 3 Using MWE lexicons in NLP tasks higher for the dataset with MWEs. Therefore, it can be concluded that the identi-fication of MWEs can slightly enhance the explainability of the generated topics and themes, which could lead to a more appropriate labeling of the topic itself during the qualitative interpretation of the generated topics, i.e., incorporating MWEs into the models creates slightly more informative resulting topics.

6.2 Data and results 

This subsection is organized according to the topics addressed by the survey questions, namely the use and applications of MWE lexicons, their performance and effectiveness in NLP tasks, insights and comments on improving and fur-ther using MWE lexicons, and information regarding the resources used by the respondents. 

6.2.1 Use and applications of MWE lexicons 

After the demographic questions concerning their professional background, re-spondents were asked if they had worked with MWE lexicons or vocabularies for NLP tasks in the past five years and, if so, to provide examples of the specific NLP tasks where these lexicons had been used. The responses revealed a rich variety of NLP tasks in which MWE lexicons have been applied over the past five years. Among the most frequently mentioned were parsing, followed closely by Ma-chine Translation and Named Entity Recognition. Figure 7 presents the diversity and distribution of the NLP tasks reported. These tasks were applied in various contexts, as shown in Table 3. Other tasks not necessarily related to NLP in which MWE lexicons were used include coreference resolution, idiomaticity representation in language models, metaphor extraction, quality monitoring, terminological checking, cor-pus revision, post-editing, encoding and standardisation, and language teach-ing/learning. 

6.2.2 Evaluation of MWE lexicons 

When asked to rate the effectiveness of the lexicons in enhancing the perfor-mance of the NLP tasks, most respondents did not provide an answer (42.9%). The reasons for this evaluation may be linked to the specific features that the respondents considered relevant for the usefulness of MWE lexicons in NLP tasks, as well as the difficulties and challenges they encountered when using the lexicons. 6.2.3 Improving MWE lexicons and suggestions for further use 

According to the respondents, existing resources could be improved to enhance their usefulness in NLP tasks in three key areas: (i) Coverage : expanding MWE lexicons to include language varieties and di-alects, specialized domains, and language registers (e.g., slangs), as well as implementing regular and dynamic updating processes. (ii) Information richness : providing more detailed and finer-grained syntactic and semantic annotation of MWEs, along with adding more and better examples, including links to annotated corpora. (iii) Interoperability and access : adopting a universal canonical form for MWEs and standardised representations, defining and adopting a univer-sal MWE typology (e.g., as aimed for in the PARSEME project), ensuring licensing, broad distribution and compatible or convertible formats, and enabling cross-linguistic applications and search capabilities. 132 3 Using MWE lexicons in NLP tasks Finally, in response to the open suggestions and comments question, it was noted that MWE lexicons could be further utilized for domain adaptation, as part of lexicon customisation for specific domains, and to create benchmarks for testing LLMs on their ability to understand and process idiomaticity. 

6.2.4 Details on MWE lexicons 

In a dedicated section of the survey, respondents were asked to provide details on the lexical resources they used in NLP tasks in the past five years. Responses provided details on 24 electronic resources, ranging from encyclopedias to cor-pora. The units used to describe the resources varied significantly (e.g., MWE, lemma, collocation, file, MB, term, among others), which made it challenging to obtain comparable sizes. Among the four resources described using MWE as a unit, sizes ranged from 1,500 MWEs to 11,000 MWEs. The majority of the re-sources are monolingual (18 out of 24), while three are bilingual and another three are multilingual. # 7 Discussion 

The surveys conducted allowed us to gather information to address the four main research questions that set the framework for this chapter, briefly repeated here: (i) which tasks and applications MWE resources are used for; (ii) what types of information in the MWE resources are relevant for the respective tasks; (iii) what types of information MWE resources are lacking and should be included; and (iv) to what extent the use of these resources impacts the overall performance or tool. This section presents the analysis of the combined results from both surveys, highlighting areas of consensus and/or validation from users’ responses and the literature, cases where the information is complementary, and instances of noticeable divergence. 

7.1 Tasks and applications in which MWE resources are used 

The NLP tasks in which MWEs were utilized largely overlap across the conducted surveys. Both surveys refer to tasks such as parsing, semantic annotation (e.g., sentiment labeling), MWE identification (including detection and extraction, but also modelling, recognition, and categorisation of MWEs), lexical resource build-ing (through extraction or induction), grammar development (e.g., in the context of language generation), language variety identification (e.g., testing idiomatic-ity and improving language models to capture idiomaticity), foreign language education (e.g., systems for teaching and learning idioms and MWEs), machine translation (including neural machine translation and machine translation eval-uation), LLM quality analysis (e.g., evaluation of LLM performance on MWEs), idiom mining (including idiomatic compound detection), and term extraction (in-cluding bilingual extraction). Additionally, results from the users’ survey include the following tasks: shallow processing and chunking, coreference resolution, named entity recognition, false friends extraction, collocation extraction, topic modelling, keyword identification, information extraction and retrieval, seman-tic search, sentiment analysis, hate speech detection, readability and text com-plexity prediction, and machine learning and interpretation of transformers. The literature survey also included semantic relation extraction for terminology, and gender identification. The comprehensive list attests to the significance of MWEs and MWE resources in NLP tasks in general. 

7.2 Relevant information in MWE resources 

Both surveys report similar properties of the MWE resources in terms of (i) types of resources (including dictionaries, lexicons, wordnets, framenets, encyclopae-134 3 Using MWE lexicons in NLP tasks dias, corpora, and various types of MWE datasets); (ii) number of languages cov-ered by the resources (see Table 4); (iii) MWEs covered (nominal, verbal, adver-bial, collocations, idioms, terms); and (iv) linguistic information provided in the resources (morphological, syntactic and semantic properties of the MWE com-ponents and/or the expressions; compositionality and context-dependency; fre-quency). The broad features relevant to the use of MWEs in these tasks are accessibil-ity, format, coverage, and manual validation. The contrast between the responses obtained from the users’ survey and the information gathered in the literature review indicates that, in addition to basic and comprehensive information re-garding MWE canonical forms and entries, and morpho-syntactic and syntactic information (PoS, syntactic structure, lemma, or inflectional variation), there is a focus on more sophisticated information. This includes linking to corpora for frequency and collocational data, examples in context, as well as information on compositionality, sense/meaning descriptions, and semantic relations.

7.3 Information to be included in MWE resources 

An analysis of the two surveys shows that they are complementary in terms of the information to be included in MWE resources. Although this information can be directly related to the purposes and tasks for which the resources are used, there is a consensus that detailed and fine-grained syntactic and semantic annotations of MWEs should be provided. This includes information about the meaning and interpretation of MWEs, as well as their semantic classification of MWEs concerning compositionality or syntax/semantic classification of MWEs based on collocational properties. Furthermore, responses from the users’ survey highlight additional avenues for future developing, such as expanding MWE lexicons to encompass special-ized domains, language varieties, and dialects, which can mean new informa-tion encoded in the resources. Suggestions also include linking MWEs to authen-tic/corpus data, through corpus annotation or concordances extraction, and cre-ating or reusing existing resources to establish benchmarks for testing LLMs. 135 Giouli et al. This could involve compiling specific corpora or utilizing declarative prompting to create a direct connection between MWEs and their meanings and usage re-strictions. All collected suggestions point to the need for and value of standards and ref-erences, whether related to MWE representations, whether in terms of univer-sal/compatible typologies and formats, or whether concerning available training data. Interestingly, all suggestions appear to be language-independent and can be applied to various languages or even to multilingual contexts. 

7.4 Assessing the impact of using MWE resources on the overall performance or tool 

The users’ survey was informative in what concerns the direct link between the resources used and their impact on the task at hand. Several cases and references were provided that illustrate the positive impact of MWE resources on parsing (e.g., Gonçalves et al. 2021, Müller et al. 2024), particularly concerning support-verb constructions (Baptista & Mamede 2020, Baptista et al. 2022), the treatment of the syntax of auxiliary verbs in Portuguese and Spanish (Baptista & Crismán 2021), and other verbal idioms (Galvão et al. 2019). The use of MWE resources in the identification of MWEs in corpora or texts is also described as highly beneficial (Savary et al. 2019, Reis et al. 2021, Kroon & Odijk 2024). Other tasks in which the positive impact of MWE resources has been highlighted include language teaching (Eryiğit et al. 2022), particularly in applications such as controlling vocabulary associated with specific proficiency levels and readability assessment for educational placement (Da Corte & Baptista 2024). As presented in Section 5, the literature survey addressed the impact of the use of MWE resources on specific tasks, with these being evaluated in the contexts of the studies reviewed. The tasks in which the positive impact of the use of MWE resources was reported included the identification of MWEs in corpora, but also translation and neural machine translation, vocabulary extraction, and language generation. Regarding the assessment of the use and respective impact of MWE resources, the surveys are complementary. 

7.5 LLMs and the need for MWE lexicons 

Although MWEs play an important role in NLP, their integration into pre-training and fine-tuning of LLMs is still limited. Approaches such as n-gram frequency analysis, BPE enhanced with Pointwise Mutual Information (Kumar 136 3 Using MWE lexicons in NLP tasks & Thawani 2022), and input compression by treating MWEs as single tokens (Gee et al. 2023) have been explored, but these methods are still experimental and primarily aim to improve efficiency. Multitoken prediction models (Gloeckle et al. 2024, DeepSeek-AI et al. 2025), which enable the prediction of multiple to-kens at once or sequentially, are only used to a limited extent. LLMs have been fine-tuned on annotated datasets to improve MWE classifi-cation, with models such as BERT, RoBERTa, DistilBERT, ALBERT and XLM-RoBERTa showing encouraging results. LLMs such as LLaMA 2, Mistral, and Phi-2 continue to have difficulties in distinguishing between literal and idiomatic meanings in zero-shot scenarios, especially in different languages (De Luca For-naciari et al. 2024, De Leon et al. 2025). In contrast, smaller, fine-tuned models such as XLM-RoBERTa are still superior to these larger language models in MWE-related tasks. Currently, the role of MWE lexicons can be seen in two ways: (i) for evaluating predictions from LLMs about whether a particular part of a sentence is complex and idiomatic; (ii) for annotating data with MWEs to fine-tune different types of LLMs. While their use with LLMs is still limited, the rapid advances in language modelling indicate a growing potential for the more effective incorporation of MWEs as they play a significant role in language complexity. 

# 8 Conclusion 

This survey underlines the importance of MWE lexicons in a wide range of NLP tasks. Based on a literature review and feedback from the community, it becomes clear that MWE resources are already being integrated into key tasks and ap-plications such as syntactic parsing, machine translation, named entity recog-nition, and sentiment analysis - among others. And from this perspective, the users’ perception survey aligns with previous surveys regarding the usefulness of MWE lexicons in different NLP tasks (Constant et al. 2017), while also extend-ing their applicability to other tasks, such as named entity recognition, author gender identification, as well as understanding how LLMs work. In any case, the highest value of MWE lexicons resides in the linguistic richness they provide. These include morpho-syntactic and semantic annotations, usage examples, fre-quency data, and multilingual mappings. Lexicons that are manually validated and cover a wide range of languages are especially important. But despite that, evaluation of MWE lexicons in the context of NLP task implementation remains a challenge for the community, as evidenced by diverse user perceptions. This underscores the importance of developing standardised evaluation protocols and 137 Giouli et al. methodological frameworks, including manual evaluation (Ramisch et al. 2023). Consistency and standardisation issues were also highlighted in the users’ sur-vey, particularly regarding the encoding of information, definitions, and annota-tion of MWEs, and other metadata types. Beyond the general call for enhance-ment of metadata descriptions (Losnegaard et al. 2016), users identified specific areas for improvement, including the coverage, richness of information, inter-operability, and accessibility of MWE lexicons. These findings emphasize the need for continued advances in the development and evaluation of MWE lexi-cons to meet user and application demands more effectively. Finally, given that the papers analyzed primarily focused on improving the performance of specific NLP tasks, the impact of using dedicated and/or aware MWE resources was men-tioned only when it positively affected the task. As expected, instances of neg-ative or null impact were not reported. This selective reporting highlights the need for dedicated and comprehensive research on the broader impact of MWE integration in NLP tasks, which remains both necessary and highly relevant.

This chapter introduces VIDiom-PT, a corpus of European Portuguese annotated for verbal idioms (e.g. O Rui bateu a bota ”Rui hit the boot” ”Rui died”). This lin-guistic resource is intended to support the development of Natural Language Pro-cessing systems capable of identifying and handling such constructions in this lan-guage variety. Two custom tools were developed to facilitate the annotation pro-cess: one for detecting potential instances of verbal idioms in texts, and another of-fering a graphical interface for manual annotation. The annotation effort resulted in a corpus comprising 5,178 instances of 747 distinct verbal idioms, drawn from a dataset of over 200,000 sentences. Annotation reliability was assessed using Krip-pendorff’s alpha for nominal data, achieving a high agreement score of 0.869 based on 5% of the data independently annotated by three experts. A portion of the anno-tated corpus has been made publicly available. We perform a series of experiments with a Large Language Model to assess its ability to identify instances of idiomatic expressions. We explore prompts with varying degrees of information, as well as different approaches to example selection. Overall, the results show that providing several examples that are tailored to the expression being analyzed has a positive impact on the performance of the LLM in this task. 

# 1 Introduction 

This chapter addresses verbal idioms (or verbal idiomatic expressions ), with a fo-cus on European Portuguese (PT). These are a special type of multiword expres-sion (MWE) where the main verb and one or more of its arguments are frozen

Furthermore, the overall meaning of these expressions often cannot be derived from the meaning that each element presents when used separately; in other words, the meaning of these constructions is non-compositional (Constant et al. 2017, Galvão et al. 2019). The example Ana atirou o projeto às urtigas lit. ‘Ana threw the project into the nettles’, ‘Ana abandoned the project’ showcases how the conventionalized meaning conveyed by these expressions cannot be directly deduced from their constituents. Several aspects make analyzing and automatically processing these expres-sions a challenging task, notably: the non-compositionality of these expressions and the unpredictability of distributional constraints; the limited and often un-predictable inflection of frozen complements; and the syntactic structure they often exhibit, allowing for insertions and permutations of constituents, among other general syntactic transformations. In addition, their frequency in texts is usually very low, making them hard to model. Given the low frequency of MWEs in written text, it might be assumed that one could disregard their unique characteristics during text analysis. However, the estimated number of verbal idioms in a native speaker’s lexicon is surprisingly high, and the mastery of such expressions is relevant for language proficiency. Estimates range from being of the same order of magnitude as the number of single-word verbs (Jackendoff 1997) to several times the number of simple, distri-butional verbs: for example, Gross (1996) presents a French Lexicon-Grammar 1

of 20,340 verbal idioms (called “frozen sentences”), which contrasts with that of 14,215 simple, distributionally free, verbal constructions, covering the bulk of French verbal predicates. Considering all of this, it is clear that to achieve good performance in the syntactic and semantic analysis of natural language texts, one cannot overlook the existence of these constructions, as they contain essential information for understanding the content of a given text. Moreover, studies have shown that proper identification of MWEs can lead to better parser performance (Hogan et al. 2007, Constant et al. 2017) by reducing parsing errors. A great amount of work has been performed to integrate the analysis of verbal idioms into Natural Language Processing (NLP) systems (de Uzeda Garrão & Dias 2001, Salton et al. 2014, Peng & Feldman 2017, Zeng & Bhat 2021). As posited by Savary et al. (2019b), several NLP systems address MWEs by resorting to a lexicon.
