156 4 Verbal idioms of European Portuguese: An annotated corpus This is the case for the system used in this paper, which also adopts a lexicon-based approach (a lexicon of verbal idioms). In this system, this lexicon takes the form of a Lexicon-Grammar , that is, a matrix database, where lines correspond to the lexical entries (the verbal idioms) and columns encode their structural, distributional, semantic, and transformational properties. At the time of writing, the Lexicon-Grammar of verbal idioms of European Portuguese contains 2,714 lexical entries and 106 columns describing their individual properties. The system identifies instances of verbal idioms based on this Lexicon-Grammar and the linguistic constraints described therein, through the extraction of a relation called FIXED. This 𝑛 -ary relation links the frozen elements of the ver-bal idiom, e.g., meter a mão na massa lit. ‘to put the hand in the dough’ ‘to work ac-tively on something’, which is represented by FIXED_C1P2(meter,mão,na,massa). Assessing the ability of systems to identify occurrences of verbal idioms re-quires access to annotated corpora. Focusing on the role of MWEs in parsing, the PARSEME project (Savary et al. 2017) 2 produced a multilingual 5-million-word annotated corpus that served as a benchmark for a Shared Task on the identifi-cation of verbal MWEs (Ramisch et al. 2018). In its second edition (Ramisch et al. 2018), approximately 20% of the annotated verbal MWEs (1,130 out of 5,536) are classified as verbal idioms (tagged as ‘VID’). It is important to note that, although PARSEME included a Brazilian Por-tuguese section, no equivalent corpus for the European variety was included in any of its editions. While the two varieties are largely similar and mutually intel-ligible, a previous comparative experiment (Baptista 2008) has shown that they share only a limited number of equivalent verbal idioms (approximately 10%). It was therefore essential to create a new corpus for European Portuguese, as, to the best of our knowledge, no such resource has been made publicly available to date. Finally, recent work has shown that Large Language Models (LLMs) perform reasonably well in idiomaticity detection, despite being inferior to fine-tuned task-specific models (Phelps et al. 2024). In this study, we also leverage these models for detecting idiomaticity in the context of building the European Por-tuguese corpus. First, we evaluate the LLMs’ intrinsic ability to perform this task in a zero-shot setting using different prompts. Then, we explore how their per-formance can be improved through few-shot learning and analyze the impact of different example selection strategies. # 2 Related work 

Research on multiword expressions (MWEs), and in particular verbal idioms, has produced a wide range of lexical resources, corpora, and processing strate-gies across languages. The complexity of representing MWEs in computational systems, given their non-compositional semantics and syntactic variability, has been extensively surveyed (Constant et al. 2017, Savary et al. 2019b). A recent edited volume by Giouli & Barbu Mititelu (2024) provides an updated overview of the state of the art in the integration of MWEs into lexical resources, high-lighting both methodological advances and ongoing challenges for multilingual representation. This broader landscape contextualizes more specific efforts de-voted to idiom annotation, corpus construction, and evaluation, to which our work on European Portuguese contributes. The annotation of idioms in English corpora has seen a significant amount of work. One can find important resources like the ‘ High Fixed Corpus ’ and ‘ Low Fixed Corpus ’ presented by Salton et al. (2014). This project aimed to advance the machine translation of verbal idioms by employing a substitution method and using 3 dictionaries: a dictionary of idioms in the source language; a dictionary of idioms in the target language; and a bilingual dictionary with a correspondence between idioms of the two languages. To test their system, they chose to translate between English and Brazilian-Portuguese and built two test corpora: the ‘ High Fixed Corpus ’ and ‘ Low Fixed Corpus ’. The first corpus features 17 different idioms of the type Verb + Noun , while the second one features 11 different idioms of the same type. These corpora contain 10 sentences featuring each different idiom, which were extracted from the web. Recently, Haagsma et al. (2020) focused on the automatic identification of po-tential idiomatic expressions, based on existing dictionaries of idioms. Potential instances of such constructions were extracted from the British National Corpus 

(BNC) through a parsing-based method that considers lemmas and dependency relations among tokens. They were then manually annotated using graphical in-terfaces built for that purpose. The meaning of these idioms was classified mainly as being literal or non-literal. Haagsma et al. (2020) culminated in the MAGPIE 

158 4 Verbal idioms of European Portuguese: An annotated corpus corpus, which features 56,622 annotated phrases with 1,756 different idiom types annotated as being used literally or not. Adewumi et al. (2022) performed a similar task with two main differences: (i) the extraction of potential idiomatic expressions was performed manually, which reduces the likelihood of both false-positives and false-negatives, but mas-sively increases the amount of time and effort required for this task; and (ii) the annotation of idioms considered a broader set of senses, such as ‘irony’ and ‘eu-phemism’. This project produced a corpus with 1,197 cases of idioms totaling over 20,100 samples/sentences. When it comes to other languages, Hashimoto & Kawahara (2008) provide a good example of a similar approach to verbal idiom annotation. Firstly, they used a dependency parser for Japanese and a dictionary of Japanese idioms to detect examples of these expressions in a Japanese Web corpus (Kawahara & Kurohashi 2006). Then, human annotators classified the expressions as idiomatic or literal, which resulted in a corpus spanning 146 idioms across 102,846 sentences. Recently, for German, Ehren et al. (2024) presented another effort towards the annotation of verbal idioms. Based on an electronic dictionary of German idioms (featuring roughly 30,000 verbal idioms), candidate instances of relevant expressions were fetched from the Parallel Meaning Bank (PMB), using the same extraction method described by Haagsma et al. (2020). Potential idiomatic ex-pressions were marked as belonging to one of 5 categories: idiomatic, probably idiomatic, probably literal, literal, or both. This strategy constitutes an interest-ing variation from the rest of the works discussed here, as it addresses the lack of context that is made available to the annotator. The resulting collection features 1,945 annotated verbal idioms across 5,821 sampled sentences. For European Portuguese, the target language of this article, the amount of work addressing verbal idioms is scarce. However, the research topic of MWEs in general has seen the construction of resources, namely, a lexical database of MWEs of Portuguese in the scope of the project COMBINA-PT (Antunes et al. 2006, Mendes et al. 2006). The expressions were automatically extracted through the analysis of a balanced 50 million word written corpus sampled from the Ref-erence Corpus of Contemporary Portuguese (in Portuguese, Corpus de Referência do Português Contemporâneo ). This information was then statistically interpreted with lexical association measures and validated by hand. The phenomena were broadly classified as 5 types of MWEs: (i) groups forming a lexical category, (ii) groups forming a phrase (e.g., nominal or adverbial phrase), (iii) groups that con-stitute a verbal phrase (the group which verbal idioms are a part of), (iv) groups that specify named entities, and (v) cases that require further attention as they are doubtful (these expressions include some verbal idioms). 159 David Antunes, Eugénio Ribeiro, Jorge Baptista & Nuno Mamede Lastly, one can find works like LIDIOMS (Moussallem et al. 2018), which con-sists of a multilingual dataset of idioms (in general) containing five languages: English, German, Italian, Portuguese, and Russian. The data was crawled and in-tegrated from 4 online data sources. The idioms had to be manually filtered by experts, so that only the non-compositional constructions were considered, cor-responding to roughly half of the crawled expressions. Moreover, all idioms were evaluated by two native speakers and one linguist (per language) to ensure the quality of the data. The LIDIOMS dataset provides linking between idioms across languages by using English as a pivot language, since all the target translations are in English. This means multilingual translation makes use of inference and multiple bilingual patterns, where English definitions are used as a bridge. This dataset presents a total of 13,889 annotated samples, which model 815 different concepts with 488 translations, of which 115 are indirect translations. LLMs have been successful in a wide variety of NLP tasks. However, these models are still struggling when it comes to capturing the meaning of MWEs, since this requires understanding the context in which idioms occur, as well as language-intrinsic features (Mi et al. n.d.). Still, recent research on MWEs (Hakkarainen & Engelbrecht 2024, Phelps et al. 2024) appears to be increasingly aligned with broader NLP trends, favoring the exploitation of LLMs. Hakkarainen & Engelbrecht (2024) compared the performance of GPT-4, Gem-ini Pro, and recurrent neural networks in detecting non-literal sentences, includ-ing, but not limited to, verbal idioms. The variables examined in the LLM ex-periments included the strategic manipulation of textual prompts–specifically, the wording of instructions and the information provided–as well as the use of guiding examples in the system prompt. Results showed that, while Bidirec-tional Long Short-Term Memory models (BiLSTM) consistently outperformed both LLMs and unidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (LSTMs), the LLMs pos-sess robust baseline capabilities—with Gemini Pro achieving up to 95% precision and 95% recall in separate evaluations. Interestingly, both LLMs performed bet-ter in a zero-shot setting, when no example is provided in the prompt, than in a one-shot setting. Finally, Phelps et al. (2024) evaluated the performance of a large variety of LLMs on the detection of idiomatic expressions across different datasets, includ-ing SemEval 2022 (Tayyar Madabushi et al. 2022), FLUTE (Chakrabarty et al. 2022), and MAGPIE (Haagsma et al. 2020), which span multiple languages. The authors found that although LLMs may be competitive, they generally under-perform when compared to smaller, fine-tuned encoder-only models tailored for the task. However, LLM performance improves with model scale and benefits 160 4 Verbal idioms of European Portuguese: An annotated corpus from prompt engineering. These findings highlight the potential of LLMs for id-iomaticity detection. 

# 3 The corpus 

3.1 Corpus description 

For this study, a corpus comprising 178 text documents was compiled from two sources. The first source includes 127 transcriptions of sessions from the Por-tuguese Parliament, covering two distinct periods: May 2004 to March 2005 and March 2018 to September 2018. The second source consists of 51 documents ex-tracted from CETEMPúblico (Santos & Rocha 2001). 3 This is a publicly available resource containing approximately 180 million words of European Portuguese newspaper text from the daily newspaper Público, spanning 1991 to 1998. This corpus was developed to support research and development in Portuguese lan-guage processing. The selection of the Portuguese Parliament transcriptions and the CETEM-Público corpus for this study on verbal idioms is strategically motivated by the distinct linguistic characteristics and communicative contexts they repre-sent. The Portuguese Parliament Transcriptions offer a rich source of formal spoken language, capturing spontaneous speech patterns within structured de-bates. Such settings are conducive to the use of verbal idioms, as speakers often employ idiomatic expressions to emphasize points, convey nuanced meanings, or engage listeners. The dynamic nature of parliamentary discourse provides valuable insights into how idioms function in formal spoken Portuguese. In con-trast, the CETEMPúblico corpus comprises written journalistic texts from the newspaper Público, reflecting formal written language use. This corpus allows for the examination of idiom usage in edited, published materials, offering a perspective on how idioms are employed in written communication and how they may differ from spoken usage. By analyzing both corpora, the study can explore the variability and stability of verbal idioms across different modes of communication—spoken and written—and contexts—parliamentary discourse and journalism. This dual approach facilitates a comprehensive understanding of idiomatic expressions in European Portuguese, shedding light on their syn-tactic flexibility, frequency, and pragmatic functions in diverse communicative settings. 3.2 Corpus annotation 

The partition of the annotated corpus corresponding to the texts of CETEM-Público is publicly available. 4 However, due to licensing restrictions, we are unable to release the documents from the Portuguese Parliament at this time. The resource is in the format of a set of .txt files, with one file for each source document—these documents are also made available. Each file contains pairs of consecutive lines corresponding to annotated in-stances of verbal idioms. The first line presents the FIXED dependency that iden-tifies the idiomatic expression, 5 while the second line provides the sentence in which the expression occurs. Notably, the fixed elements of the construction are not explicitly marked within the original sentence. For example, consider the an-notation for the verbal idiom bater na mesma tecla lit. “to hit the same key” “to dwell on a subject or to harp on the same point”: 

Verbal Idiom: FIXED_CP1(bater,em,tecla) Is present in sentence: Mas tem carácter obrigatório : a oposição também está a bater na mesma tecla. 

3.2.1 Annotation tools 

To minimize the human resources and time required for annotating verbal idioms in the corpus, two programs were developed. The first is a script which automati-cally detects potential instances of idiomatic expressions. The second consists of

Detection of potential verbal idioms 

This script scans the textual content to identify potential instances of verbal id-ioms within each sentence and compiles its findings into a well-structured file. A sentence is considered to contain a potential verbal idiom if all (lemmatized) lex-ical elements that define an idiomatic expression (the main verb and frozen com-plements) are present. Furthermore, applying a heuristic inspired by Manning & Schütze (1999: p. 159), the maximum allowable distance between consecutive elements of an idiomatic expression within a sentence is limited to five tokens. For instance, regarding the previously mentioned verbal idiom meter a mão na massa lit. “to put the hand in the dough” “to actively engage in work”, the tool retrieves sentences where the inflected forms corresponding to the lemmas me-ter ‘put’, mão ‘hand’, and massa ‘dough’ appear, in any order, with no more than five tokens separating each element. This tool utilizes the Lexicon-Grammar of European Portuguese verbal idioms integrated into the NLP pipeline (Baptista et al. 2004, 2014, Galvão 2019, Galvão et al. 2019, Antunes 2024, Antunes et al. 2025a,b) as its source of information. It identifies relevant expressions by focusing on their fixed components, thereby ex-clusively searching for verbal idioms documented within the Lexicon-Grammar. Although this resource does not encompass all idiomatic constructions in the language, it includes a comprehensive and systematically described set of 2,714 verbal idioms, covering the most frequently used expressions.

3.2.2 Annotation process 

The annotation of the corpus documents was carried out by three annotators with expertise in European Portuguese verbal idioms. They utilized the annota-tion tools described in Section 3.2.1 and adhered to the guidelines outlined in the Appendix (Section A). First, a subset of the corpus, comprising seven randomly selected documents and representing approximately 5% of the potential verbal idioms detected, was annotated by all three annotators. This step aimed to measure inter-annotator agreement and assess the effectiveness of the annotation guidelines. Given the nature of the task, Krippendorff’s alpha for nominal data (Krippendorff 2008) was employed as the agreement metric. The resulting K-alpha value of 0.869 indicates a high level of reliability among the annotators. Upon completing this initial annotation phase, the annotators collaboratively resolved any discrepancies to establish a consensus annotation, thereby creating a gold-standard collection. Table 2 presents the precision and recall metrics for each annotator, bench-marked against the consensus annotation, along with the overall inter-annotator agreement. As illustrated, all annotators demonstrate comparable performance relative to the gold-standard dataset. The discussion among the three annotators to reach a consensual annotation underscored the complexity of verbal idioms, particularly the difficulty in deter-mining idiomaticity when contextual information is limited. Despite this, most discrepancies were attributed to annotator oversight rather than genuine dis-agreement. Limitations of the annotation process 

Two main issues were identified. Firstly, several verbal idioms have not yet been incorporated into the Lexicon-Grammar matrix. Although these idioms share lex-ical components with existing entries, they convey distinct meanings. As a result, such expressions are incorrectly flagged as potential idioms already present in the lexicon. For example, the idiom falar com língua bífide lit. “to speak with a forked tongue” “to speak deceptively”, which had not yet been included in the ma-trix, was mistakenly identified as an instance of the already defined idiom falar a língua de alguém lit. “to talk someone’s language” “to agree with someone”. This occurred in the sentence: um dia viria a falar com língua bífide, afirmando no discurso científico o que negava no poético. “one day, he would come to speak deceptively, affirming in scientific discourse what he denied in poetic language”. Secondly, many other verbal idioms remain absent from the Lexicon-Grammar. Consequently, these expressions are not detected by the system and thus cannot be annotated, limiting the scope of the annotation process. 165 David Antunes, Eugénio Ribeiro, Jorge Baptista & Nuno Mamede 

Compromises in the annotation guidelines 

Several pragmatic solutions were devised to address the issues outlined above. First, expressions not yet described in the Lexicon-Grammar but identified as potential verbal idioms—due to shared fixed elements with existing idiomatic expressions—were provisionally annotated as instances of those already defined. Subsequently, these expressions were incorporated into the Lexicon-Grammar, and their annotations were refined to reflect the appropriate verbal idioms. Second, when multiple idioms already defined in the Lexicon-Grammar and sharing key components are detected as potential matches in the same sentence, all are initially considered to be present in that instance. After the full annotation of the document, the annotator revisits these cases to determine which idiom is most contextually appropriate, ensuring only one is retained. For example, the expressions (1) bater à porta de alguém lit. “to knock on someone’s door” “to approach someone (for help)” or “for some problem to affect someone”, (2) bater à porta errada lit. “to knock on the wrong door” “to seek help, information, or support from the wrong person or source”, and (3) bater à porta certa lit. “to knock on the right door” “to seek help, information, or support from the right person or source’ were all detected as potential idiomatic expressions in the sentence: odesencanto e o insucesso, que batem à porta de milhares de jovens e adolescentes “the disenchantment and failure that affect thousands of young people and teenagers”. Initially, all three idioms were considered, but upon review, the sentence was annotated solely as an instance of the first idiom. Third, when the annotator is unable to determine whether an expression is used idiomatically or literally due to insufficient context, the sentence is marked as non-idiomatic. For instance, in the sentence Vai integralmente ao fundo! lit. “It goes completely to the bottom!”, the potential expression ir ao fundo lit. “to go to the bottom” “to go under” could have either an idiomatic interpretation (e.g., if the subject is projeto ‘project’) or a literal one (e.g., if the subject is barco ‘boat’). With an inter-annotator agreement score of 0.869—exceeding the commonly accepted threshold of 0.8 for satisfactory reliability (Krippendorff 2008)—it was reasonable to assume consistent performance among annotators in the annota-tion task. This high level of agreement facilitated an optimized workflow for the remaining 171 documents, which were evenly and randomly distributed among the annotators, with each document assigned to a single annotator.

# 4 LLMs: Experimental setup 

The construction of this corpus motivated a series of experiments aimed at eval-uating the capacity of LLMs to identify idiomatic expressions in European Por-tuguese texts. Since only a portion of the corpus—the documents from CETEM-Público —is publicly available, we opted to restrict the experiments to this subset. This decision ensures that the experiments are fully replicable and that future research can rely on a consistent and accessible baseline. The task simulates the role of a human annotator who contributed to the original corpus annotation. Specifically, the model is provided with potential id-iomatic expressions automatically identified by our tool in the documents under analysis. Based on the sentence context and the set of words comprising a possi-ble instance of a verbal idiom, the model must determine whether the instance constitutes a valid idiomatic expression. Due to the substantial computational resources required to run locally large open-weight models, their evaluation is deferred to future work. Instead, this study focuses on exploring different prompting strategies and assessing their relative effectiveness. All experiments were conducted using the GPT-4o mini model, accessed via the OpenAI API. Given the non-deterministic nature of both the model’s responses and certain example selection methods, each experiment was repeated three times to account for variability. 4.1 Prompting strategies 

The performance of prompt-based LLMs is significantly impacted by the quality of the prompts or instructions (Mishra et al. 2022, Giray 2023). Our experiments include variations in both the system and the user prompt, as we aim to draw insights about the type of prompt that is more efficient for this task based on the data. 

4.1.1 System prompt 

The system prompt contains a clear description of the task to be performed by the model, in particular, the information that will be available and what is ex-pected as a reply. Expert impersonation is motivated by prior research showing that prompting LLMs to adopt the role of domain experts can enhance their per-formance (Salewski et al. 2023). In this study, we focus on two types of system prompts, namely generic and descriptive ones. We will elaborate further in the next paragraphs. 

Generic 

The generic prompt directly targets the concept of verbal idioms in an attempt to leverage any intrinsic knowledge the LLM may possess regarding the task. 

> PT: És um perito em expressões idiomáticas de núcleo verbal características do português europeu. Vais receber uma frase e uma combinação de palavras (verbo e seus argumentos) contida nessa frase. Terás de indicar se essa combinação de palavras é usada como uma expressão idiomática de núcleo verbal. Responde apenas com Sim ou Não. EN: You’re an expert in verb-nucleus idiomatic expressions characteristic of Euro-pean Portuguese. You will receive a sentence and a combination of words (a verb and its arguments) contained in that sentence. You must indicate whether this combination of words is used as a verb-nucleus idiomatic expression. Respond only with Yes or No.

Descriptive 

The descriptive prompt follows the same structure as the previous one, but includes a detailed explanation of what constitutes an idiomatic expression. This addition is intended to provide the model with further guidance, thereby ap-proximating the conditions under which the original corpus annotation was per-formed. 170 4 Verbal idioms of European Portuguese: An annotated corpus 

PT: És um perito em expressões idiomáticas de núcleo verbal características do português europeu. Sabes que expressões idiomáticas de núcleo verbal são expressões com um significado não-composicional em que o verbo principal é distribucionalmente fixo com um ou mais dos seus argumentos. Vais receber uma frase e uma combinação de palavras (verbo e seus argumentos) contida nessa frase. Terás de indicar se essa combinação de palavras é usada como uma ex-pressão idiomática de núcleo verbal. Responde apenas com Sim ou Não. EN: You’re an expert in verb-nucleus idiomatic expressions characteristic of Euro-pean Portuguese. You know that verb-nucleus idiomatic expressions are expres-sions with a non-compositional meaning in which the main verb is distribution-ally fixed with one or more of its arguments. You will receive a sentence and a combination of words (a verb and its arguments) contained in that sentence. You must indicate whether this combination of words is used as a verb-nucleus id-iomatic expression. Respond only with Yes or No. 

4.1.2 User prompt 

The user prompt contains the sentence to be considered as well as the set of words that comprise the potential idiomatic expression detected therein. The format is as follows: PT: Frase: [TEXTO] Combinação de Palavras: [LISTA DE PALAVRAS] Idiomático: EN: Sentence: [TEXT] Word Combination: [WORD LIST] Idiomatic: Optionally, this prompt may also include a set of examples of valid instances of verbal idioms annotated in the corpus. If any set of examples is included, the following sentence is added to the system prompt: PT: Em conjunto com esta informação, vais receber alguns exemplos para ajudar a decidir a tua resposta. EN: Along with this information, you will receive some examples to help you decide your answer. 171 David Antunes, Eugénio Ribeiro, Jorge Baptista & Nuno Mamede We experiment with user prompts containing a varying number of examples, namely: no example (zero-shot); one example (one-shot); two examples (two-shot); and three examples (three-shot). The examples are provided sequentially at the beginning of the user prompt. Each example follows the format: PT: Exemplo: Frase: [TEXTO] Combinação de Palavras: [LISTA DE PALAVRAS] Idiomático: Sim EN: Example: Sentence: [TEXT] Word Combination: [WORD LIST] Idiomatic: Yes Furthermore, we experiment with two strategies of example selection: 

Random 

The example(s) included in the user prompt consist of randomly selected in-stances of potential idiomatic expressions that have been annotated as valid ver-bal idioms in the corpus. While studies have shown that random selection of ex-amples yields high variance and worse average performance (Chang & Jia 2022), we expect that, for the task at hand, these examples will have a positive impact by complementing the knowledge of the model, given the limited amount of Por-tuguese verbal idioms that LLMs are exposed to during training. 

Targeted 

The example(s) included in the user prompt are annotated instances of the specific construction under analysis. This means that the set of words comprising the idiomatic expression(s) in the example(s) must exactly match the set of words in the potential idiomatic expression being presented to the model. Some constructions are detected as potential verbal idioms but have no anno-tated instances confirming their idiomatic status. This means there are no valid examples to use. Thus, potential verbal idioms of these constructions cannot be included in the few-shot targeted example experiments. As a result, the one-shot experiment with targeted examples includes only those constructions with at least one annotated instance; the two-shot experi-ment considers only constructions with at least two annotated instances; and the three-shot experiment includes only those with at least three. 172 4 Verbal idioms of European Portuguese: An annotated corpus Table 6 presents the number of potential expressions for which there are a certain number of examples. It also presents the number of these expressions that are annotated as idiomatic, and the total number of different constructions. To ensure a fair comparison between random and targeted example selection strategies, both must be applied to the same set of potential verbal idioms. For each experiment using n targeted examples (where n = One, Two, or Three), we created a corresponding configuration using n random examples, restricted to the same set of idioms. These are referred to as “ n-Shot Random (limited)” settings. This design isolates the effect of the example selection strategy, ensuring that any observed differences in performance are not due to variation.

# 5 Evaluation 

5.1 Evaluation metrics 

We adopt two of the most widely used evaluation metrics in prior studies on auto-matic idiomaticity detection, namely accuracy and the macro F1 score. Accuracy measures the overall proportion of correctly classified instances, providing an indicator of the model’s ability to precisely identify the idiomatic status of each expression. However, given the imbalance in the distribution of idiomatic and non-idiomatic instances across the set of potential verbal idioms, the macro F1 score is also employed to better capture model performance across both classes and to reveal potential biases. For both metrics, the manual annotations of verbal idioms in the corpus are treated as ground truth, while the LLM’s responses are regarded as predictions. 173 David Antunes, Eugénio Ribeiro, Jorge Baptista & Nuno Mamede

5.2.1 Zero-shot 

The zero-shot setting serves as the baseline against which the impact of increas-ing prompt specificity is evaluated. As shown in Table 7, providing a definition of a verbal idiom leads to a noticeable decline in performance compared to the generic prompt, suggesting that the LLM possesses an intrinsic capacity to iden-tify verbal idioms without additional guidance. This observation motivated the exclusive use of the generic system prompt in the subsequent few-shot experi-ments. It is also noteworthy that performance variability across runs is greater when using the generic prompt.

The few-shot experiments were designed to evaluate how the presence and the nature of examples included in the prompt influence model performance. # 6 Conclusion 

This paper introduced VIDiom-PT, a publicly available corpus of European Por-tuguese annotated for verbal idioms. We described the criteria for source text selection, the Lexicon-Grammar framework adopted for the linguistic descrip-tion of verbal idioms, the annotation process—including detailed guidelines—and the development of two annotation tools, culminating in a fully annotated and structured dataset. Several challenges encountered during the annotation process were discussed, with particular emphasis on the difficulty of distinguishing idiomatic (i.e., non-compositional) from literal meanings—a core issue in idiom annotation. The re-sulting corpus comprises 5,178 annotated instances covering 747 distinct verbal idioms. The reliability of the annotation process was assessed through an inter-annotator agreement study, yielding a Krippendorff’s alpha of 0.869 based on independent annotations of 5% of the data by three experts. A gold standard was established through consensus annotation of this subset. We conducted a series of experiments in which the GPT-4o mini model was tasked with identifying valid instances of verbal idioms from a set of potential ex-pressions detected by one of the annotation tools. The experiments varied along three dimensions: prompt type, number of examples provided, and example se-lection strategy. The results indicate that the LLM possesses intrinsic knowledge about the concept of verbal idioms; that random example selection does not lead to improved performance; and that targeted examples substantially enhance per-formance, with larger numbers of examples yielding better results. We expect VIDiom-PT to be a valuable resource for advancing research in a range of NLP tasks involving verbal idioms in European Portuguese, including idiom identification, sense disambiguation, and machine translation.

# Appendix A Annotation guidelines 

Annotation Process 

The annotation tool will display a sentence, highlighting words that potentially form a verbal idiom. The targeted words can be separated by up to 5 tokens (words or punctuation). This chapter describes the acquisition and applications of multiwords in the SPE-CIALIST Lexicon and Lexical Tools. The SPECIALIST Lexicon is a large morpho-syntactic lexicon of biomedical and general English, which provides the lexical in-formation needed for the Unified Medical Language System Natural Language Pro-cessing systems. Various applications utilizing the Lexicon and Lexical Tools are reviewed to illustrate their improved performance due to multiwords.

2.1 LexRecords and the Lexicon 

The Lexicon consists of a set of lexical entries, with one entry for each spelling or set of spelling variants in a particular part of speech (POS). These lexical entries are called lexRecords. Each lexRecord utilizes a frame structure consisting of slots and fillers to record syntactic, morphological, and orthographic information needed by NLP Systems (Browne et al. 2018, Lu et al. 2020b). Figure 1 shows lexRecords of tear for both the noun and verb POS. In this example, the base form 5 of the entry (e.g., tear ) is encoded in the base = slot. Each lexRecord has an entry unique identifier (EUI) as encoded in the entry = slot. The grammatical category (i.e. POS) is encoded in the cat = slot. Morphological information is encoded as reg and irreg in the variant = slot for regular and irregular inflections. 6

Verb complementation patterns are also encoded in the lexRecord of E0060022, such as intran (intransitive), tran (transitive), and cplxtran (complex-transitive), in this example. Verb-particle constructions are encoded as part() attached to the complementation codes. Lexical information associated with a base form is encoded in one lexRecord if they are the same. Semantic information is not taken into account. For example, tear|verb has different semantic meanings, such as 

rupture , pluck , charge , and fill with tears . However, it has only one lexRecord in the Lexicon. 

2.2 Definition and scope of multiword terms in the Lexicon 

Multiword Expressions (MWEs) are idiosyncratic interpretations that cross word boundaries (or spaces). They include various types of linguistic units and expres-sions, such as idioms, fixed phrases, noun compounds, phrasal verbs, light verbs and other habitual collocations, etc. (Sag et al. 2002, Rayson et al. 2010). Multi-words in the Lexicon are defined differently from MWEs, as described below. The base form of a lexRecord must meet three requirements: a POS, corre-sponding inflectional morphology, and meaning (McCray et al. 1993, Browne et al. 2018, McCreedy et al. 2019). Linguists in the Lexical Systems Group (LSG) look at the usage of candidates in various sources (such as MEDLINE, Google Scholar, dictionaries, etc.) to add lexical entries into the Lexicon if the above three re-quirements are met. Base forms and inflectional variants may be single words or multiwords - words that contain space(s), such as ice cream or tear break up time .

In general, most single words are valid lexical entries in the Lexicon because they meet the three requirements. Foreign words or sub-words that have entered the language as part of MWEs and are not used as standalone lexical items, are thus considered invalid lexical entries. For example, versa , blanche , and habilis 

are invalid lexical entries as they only occur in the valid lexical entries vice versa, carte blanche and Homo habilis , respectively. Multiwords and single words have the same requirements for being valid lex-ical entries in the Lexicon. They must have a POS, inflectional morphology, and meaning. One key feature of UMLS is to map text to its intended mean-ing for bioinformatic NLP applications. The UMLS Metathesaurus (hereafter, the Metathesaurus) facilitates the mapping between concepts and terms. In the Metathesaurus, a concept is a meaning. 7 Therefore a Metathesaurus concept is taken as evidence that a multiword meets the meaning criterion for being added to the Lexicon. Multiwords in lexRecords are multiword terms that meet the three requirements. In practice, two guidelines are used to allow linguists to make their best judgement on validating the requirement of meaning for multiword terms:

188 5 Effective multiword acquisition • A multiword term must have a specific meaning. For example, in house has a specific meaning of internally and is a valid lexical entry. On the other hand, in the house has no distinct meaning apart from its generic compo-sitional meaning and thus it is not a multiword term. The Lexicon does not include all MWEs with generic compositional meanings as multiword terms because there are too many, and they won’t improve performance for UMLS concept mapping. • A multiword term must lexicalize a specific concept that is used consis-tently, even if its meaning is the same or similar to the compositional meaning. For example, pregnant woman is a multiword term because it has a specific concept in the biomedical domain even though its meaning is compositional. A MWE with compositional meaning might evolve to a multiword term if the concept becomes consistent and results in higher fre-quent use. For instance, community spread did not have a specific concept in the Metathesaurus and was not a multiword term before Covid-19. It ap-pears 10 times more frequently in MEDLINE after the Covid-19 pandemic began. Two concepts, community transmission (C5392207) and community spread transmission pattern (C5400769) were added to the Metathesaurus in 2020. Accordingly, community spread was added to the Lexicon during the pandemic. In addition, frequency alone is not sufficient to determine if a MWE is a multi-word term. For example, undergoing cardiac surgery occurs frequently (6,367 hits in 5,051 documents) in the 2022 MEDLINE N-gram Set (MNS), but it is not con-sidered a multiword term because it is a phrase composed of more than one POS (verb + noun). On the other hand, this phrase contains the term cardiac surgery ,which also occurs frequently (59,115 hits in 34,212 documents) in the 2022 MNS. 

Cardiac surgery is considered a multiword term because it has a single POS (noun) as well as inflectional morphology. Moreover, verb-particle constructions are not multiword terms. They are attached to verb complementation types in lexRecords to coordinate lexical meaning with syntactic characteristics of the verb (Browne et al. 2018). For example, tear something down can be constructed from the lexRecord of tear 

(E0060022). tear is encoded as a transitive verb with a verb-particle construction of down in the Lexicon, as shown in Figure 1. Similarly, light verb construc-tions that are covered within lexRecords, such as make love and give birth , are encoded as tran=np|love| and ditran=np|birth|,pphr(to,np) in the lexRecords of 189 Chris J. Lu, Amanda Payne & James G. Mork 

make (E0038623) and give (E0029785), respectively. 8 The information on these types of MWEs is stored inside the lexRecords and they are not considered multiword terms (not a base form or inflectional variants of a lexical entry). However, they can be retrieved and identified by a parser (LexCheck). 9 Finally, non-decomposable idioms, such as kick the bucket and shoot the breeze , are not considered lexical terms because semantic interpretation is beyond the scope of the Lexicon. In short, multiword terms in the Lexicon are a subset of MWEs due to the three requirements. The Lexicon including multiword terms com-monly seen in the biomedical domain allows the Lexicon to more completely characterize biomedical English. 

2.3 Development background, objective and motivation 

The main source for the Lexicon is MEDLINE. 10 An element word model was ap-plied to acquire multiword terms from MEDLINE (Lu et al. 2014). The model takes into account lowercase single words without punctuation that are not stopwords. High frequency single words from titles and abstracts of MEDLINE that are not in the Lexicon are considered. The Essie search engine (Ide et al. 2007) provides features to find the surrounding context of these words in MEDLINE. LSG lin-guists utilize the Essie search engine to find multiword term candidates to build the Lexicon. The usage and lexical information of candidates are reviewed and added to the Lexicon through a centralized web-based tool, LexBuild 11 , if they meet the three requirements for lexRecords. LSG staff completed adding element words with high frequency (word count ≥ 1,500) to the Lexicon in 2015. Several issues showed up in the element word approach. First, this approach is very time consuming due to the interactive processes with the Essie search en-gine. In addition, new multiword terms associated with processed element words are missed; for instance, social distance would not be added during the Covid-19 pandemic because social and distance were previously processed element words. Finally, multiwords associated with high frequency element words do not nec-essarily have high frequency. LSG conducted a study on the growth of lexical entries, distribution, and coverage of words (single words and multiwords) in MEDLINE in 2016 (Lu et al. 2016b). The results showed that single words had in-creased 2.6 times from 180,468 in 2002 to 468,655 in 2016. The Lexicon has a very

As for multiwords, we observed continuous growth in the Lexicon from 88,324 in 2002 to 446,928 in 2016. These observations on both the high coverage of existing single words and the trend of increasing growth of multiwords in the Lexicon lead to our position that multiword acquisition is the key for building a comprehensive Lexicon. Our objective for multiword acquisition is to develop a generic methodology to retrieve high precision multiword term candidates to effectively build a com-prehensive Lexicon. Research on MWEs has been growing since the late 1990s. State of the art methods including statistical association measures (Da Silva & Lopes 1999, Fazly et al. 2009, Pecina 2010), web queries (Takahashi & Morimoto 2013), machine learning (Boukobza & Rappoport 2009, Tsvetkov & Wintner 2011, Green et al. 2011), syntactic patterns (Seretan & Wehrli 2009, Kim & Baldwin 2010, Green et al. 2013), semantic analysis (Pearce 2001, Baldwin et al. 2003), and a com-bination of the above methods (Calzolari et al. 2002, Bejček et al. 2013, Sangati & van Cranenburgh 2015) are used in research for MWE acquisition, identification, interpretation, disambiguation and other applications. Despite a great deal of re-search on MWEs, there is no approach that fits perfectly for building multiword terms in the Lexicon due to the three qualifying requirements. Thus, a new approach using an n-gram model was developed to resolve the above issues. The n-gram model is a more effective system in providing higher precision multiword term candidates. The generated candidates can be used di-rectly without the aid of the Essie search engine for faster Lexicon building. Sev-eral models using an n-gram approach were developed to provide an average pre-cision of 82.60 for effective multiword acquisition. These models are described in detail in Section 3.1. In addition, a novel approach of using the semantic network WordNet is presented in Section 3.2.

The corpus approach involves acquiring multiword terms from a target corpus. The n-gram sets, fil-ters and matchers are generic and suitable for both single words and multiword terms. Multiword term acquisition focuses on those n-grams where n ≥ 2. Sec-tion 3.1.4 describes the processes for evaluating multiword terms. This approach was developed, practiced and published beginning in 2015 (Lu et al. 2015, 2016b, 2017b). 3.1.1 The MEDLINE N-gram Set (MNS) 

In practice, several requirements must be defined to reduce the size of n-grams and make the generation of an n-gram set feasible from a large scale corpus. Re-quirements used in the MNS include the range of n, maximum length of n-gram, and frequency information (Lu et al. 2015). LSG conducts an analysis on these requirements annually, and the results confirm that the requirements are appro-priate. First, a MNS with n = 1 to 5 is used to retrieve 99.34% of lexRecords. Sec-ond, an n-gram with a maximum length of 50 characters is used to cover 99.42% of lexRecords. In addition, accurate frequencies of n-grams, such as document count (DC) and word count (WC), are needed in the MEDLINE N-gram Set. The 2022 MEDLINE has over 33 million documents. Titles and abstracts from MEDLINE documents are collected and then tokenized to 224 M sentences and 4,680 M single words (tokens). Due to the large-scale size, the actual frequency associated with n-grams (for n ≥ 3) takes too long even for powerful computers to retrieve. Due to this, most research projects derive n-grams from bigrams and get an approximate frequency of n-grams (for n ≥ 3) based on bigrams (Seretan et al. 2003, Pedersen et al. 2011). LSG developed a sophisticated algorithm (SGFCS – split, group, filter, combine and sort) to generate the MNS with actual DC and WC for n-grams that have word count ≥ 30 (Lu et al. 2015). N-grams with smaller word counts ( < 30) are ignored because they are either spelling errors or irrelevant in downstream NLP applications.

A set of exclusive filters (hereafter, filters), based on empirical models with heuris-tic rules, was developed to filter out invalid lexical entries from the n-gram set (Lu et al. 2017b). 3.1.3 Inclusive matchers 

Four inclusive matchers based on empirical patterns were developed and applied to the MNS and DMNS to retrieve high precision multiword term candidates. The design objective of matchers is to achieve higher precision for multiword term candidates instead of aiming at the overall recall rate. They are described as follows. 197 Chris J. Lu, Amanda Payne & James G. Mork 

3.1.3.4 Acronym Expansion Pattern (AEP) matcher 

Expansions of acronyms are usually multiword terms. For example, the acronym expansion in the n-gram zinc finger proteins (ZFPs) is a multiword term. First, all n-grams that match the PAP are retrieved by the PAP filter. A sophisticated algorithm was developed to find acronym expansions from these retrieved n-grams. These expansions are used as multiword term candidates for the Lexicon building. 

3.1.3.5 Spelling variant pattern (SVP) matcher 

As we observed, an n-gram (n ≥ 2) is a good multiword candidate if it has spVars existing in the same corpus. A sophisticated computer algorithm was developed to identify all n-grams that are potential spVars. Spelling variant pattern, spelling variant normalization (Lu et al. 2017b), Metaphone (Philips 1990), edit distance (Damerau 1964), and sorted distance (Lu et al. 2017b) are used in the SVP matcher. 

3.1.3.6 Concept mapping pattern (CMP) matcher 

A multiword term in the Lexicon must have meaning(s). We use the Metathe-saurus 16 to validate if n-grams have a meaning because it is one of the most com-prehensive and commonly used ontology databases in the biomedical domain (Humphreys et al. 2020). The 2022AA release of the Metathesaurus 17 provides a database for the mapping between 2.5M terms to 900K concepts. Sub-Term Map-ping Tools (STMT) (Lu & Browne 2012) were utilized in the CMP matcher to find mapped concept(s) in the Metathesaurus for text. N-grams that have Metathe-saurus concept(s) are retrieved with the CMP matcher. 

3.1.3.7 End-word pattern (EWP) matcher 

In the biomedical domain, multiwords often end with certain words (end-words), such as syndrome , disease , virus , etc. For example, contiguous gene syndrome , rib syndrome , and purple glove syndrome are multiword terms that have the same end-word of syndrome . This model utilizes the top 80 most frequent end-words in the Lexicon with a sophisticated algorithm and heuristic rules.

3.1.4 Evaluation processes on multiword term candidates 

The retrieved multiword term candidates are evaluated by the following pro-cesses. First, linguists in the LSG review the usage of candidates in various sources, including MEDLINE, Google Scholar, dictionaries, etc., to add lexical entries through LexBuild if the three requirements are met. LexBuild provides features to modify, reject, and approve submitted lexRecords. The precision (Pre) of a candidate list is calculated as TP/(TP+FP), where T is true, F is false, and P is positive, by computer program after the list is completed. Candidates that are added in the Lexicon are TP while candidates that are not added in the Lexicon are FP. In addition to these candidates, more multiword terms associated with these candidates could be found during the review processes and added to the Lexicon in practice. For example, ten lexRecords were added to the Lexicon from the single candidate acute myeloid leukemic .18 These associated multiword terms are not considered in the precision score because they are not retrieved directly from our models.

The MNS includes n-grams (n = 1–5) from MEDLINE. They are a useful resource for UMLS NLP and Medical Language Processing (MLP). 3.2 Semantic network approach – WordNet 

In addition to acquiring multiword terms from a corpus, we also developed a sys-tematic approach to acquire multiword terms from a semantic network. Word-Net® (Miller 1995, Fellbaum 1998) was chosen because it is a large lexical database of English and popularly used in NLP systems. This semantic network approach is described in the following sections. 

3.2.1 General exclusive filtering processes 

Different NLP projects may have different requirements and result in different definitions of valid lexical entries. Filtering processes are applied systematically 203 Chris J. Lu, Amanda Payne & James G. Mork to exclude entries that are valid in WordNet, yet invalid in the Lexicon. These excluded entries are categorized into twelve groups, as shown in Table 7. For example, tear down in group 1, a verb-particle construction, is not a multiword term because it is recorded as a verb-particle construction in the complement type code in the lexRecord of tear instead, as shown in Figure 1. For the same reason, light verb constructions (group 2) are not multiword terms, as described in Section 2.2. Similarly, words in groups 3 to 11 do not meet the requirements of a valid lexical entry. Group 12 comprises words without a specific concept. Words that have concept(s) are retrieved by the CMP matcher for candidates with higher precision. The CMP matcher is discussed in Section 3.2.3.

Entries in WordNet and the Lexicon are linked via derivations, synonyms and antonyms. 3.2.3 Domain specific matchers – concept mapping pattern (CMP) and MEDLINE matchers 

Biomedical NLP applications often require finding the meaning of a target text. A multiword term with a specific meaning in the biomedical domain usually has mapped concept(s) in the Metathesaurus. The 2022AA release of the Metathe-saurus and STMT are used to find mapping concept(s) of multiwords in Word-Net for the CMP matcher. The example of young lady in group 12 in Table 7 is not a multiword term because its meaning is compositional from each individual word, without a specific meaning otherwise, and it has no mapped concept in the Metathesaurus. In addition, MEDLINE is the main corpus for biomedical NLP applications and source to build the Lexicon. A MEDLINE matcher using the 2022 release of the MNS was developed to identify multiwords from WordNet that are in the biomedical domain.

Despite the different size and domains of word collection, WordNet and the Lexicon can be used to enrich and validate each other. However, the difference between WordNet and the Lexicon must be analyzed before using them to enrich word collections and relationships among words. 4.1 Concept mapping – Sub-Term Mapping Tools (STMT) 

Concept mapping is an important core operation in most biomedical NLP ap-plications. Identifying phrasal units (hereafter units) and concept mapping on identified units is the key to finding the correct meaning for input sentences. In practice, we observed the longest multiwords in a sentence often lead to the best meaning match (Lu et al. 2020b). Based on this assumption, our multiword approach is to identify the longest known multiword terms as units in a sen-tence. The unidentified words can be processed in a window shifting concept lookup algorithm (discussed later in this section). Finally, stopwords are ignored if they are not part of the multiword terms. Identified units are used for further processes, such as POS tagging, Name Entity Recognition (NER), and concept mapping (Lu & Browne 2012). This novel multiword approach of identifying the longest known multiword term as a unit in a sentence improves the performance of computation time, precision and recall. The LexItem Sub-term Finder (LSF) and Synonym Mapping Tool (SMT) in the STMT tool package provide underly-ing NLP components for Metathesaurus concept mapping using the multiword approach (Lu & Browne 2012). 24 

The LSF is used to identify phrasal units in a sentence. All multiword terms for an input text are retrieved by LSF. LSF preloads all words and multiword terms in the Lexicon in a reversed TRIE (Aho et al. 1983) mechanism for multiword retrieval. TRIE is a tree used for fast search and retrieval. For example, LSF finds all seven sub-units of tear break up time that are in the Lexicon, which are break, break up, break up time, tear break up time, tear, time and up . For illustration pur-poses, a partial TRIE that is associated with this example is shown in Figure 3. The TRIE is composed of nodes and starts with the node Root. Each node repre-sents a sub-unit (single word) of a multiword term. Each multiword term starts with the node Root, contains node(s) of sub-units, and ends with a node of $. LSF traverses the TRIE by going through each token of the input text starting from the root node. It identifies a sub-unit as a lexRecord if a node of $ is reached. The traversed paths with found lexRecords in the TRIE are highlighted in Figure 3.

4.2 Spelling error detection and correction - CSpell 

Natural Language Understanding of free text might be hindered by misspellings. For example, health-related questions asked by consumers often contain many orthographic errors. These errors include non-word errors, i.e. words not in the dictionary, and real-word errors (errors that are valid words, but not intended). In most NLP systems, white spaces are used as word boundaries. Word boundary infractions caused by misplaced whitespaces are treated as special cases in both non-word and real-word errors. The word boundary problems include aggluti-nation (missing spaces between two or more words) and split errors (splitting a single word) (Kukich 1992). Agglutination and split errors can be corrected by split and merge corrections, respectively (Kilicoglu et al. 2015). Finally, multiple corrections are needed to accommodate combined errors. To detect and correct various types of spelling errors, LSG developed a distributable spell-checking tool, CSpell, that handles non-word errors, real-word errors, word boundary in-fractions and combinations of the above (Lu et al. 2019). 26 

A test set was collected from consumer health questions submitted to the NLM customer services. It consists of 471 consumer health questions with 24,837 to-kens, 1,008 annotation tags and 964 instances of real-word corrections. The er-rors were manually annotated by 2 annotators independently. CSpell applies a multiword approach to check if the split candidates are known multiword terms directly. Thus, the algorithm of generating and val-idating split candidates is enhanced to use candidates that are multiword terms first, then the traditional approach. The traditional approach is used only if no multiword term is found in the candidates. This approach improves performance of speed and F1. For instance, in Table 12 cases 1–4, versa , planus , blanche , and ha-bilis are invalid single words in English and thus the split correction can only be performed in the multiword approach. Multiwords are often integrated directly into English from other languages without the individual sub-words. For exam-ple, carte blanche is an English multiword, but not blanche on its own. Cases 1 and 2 are borrowed from Latin and case 3 is borrowed from French. In addition, taxonomic terms, including genus and species terms, often have sub-units that are not valid single words, such as case 4. In these cases, tokens in the split can-didate are not valid single words, yet the whole split candidate is a multiword term. Corrections in cases 5–7 can be achieved by either a multiword approach or traditional approach because all tokens are valid single words. CSpell applies the multiword approach on cases 5 and 6 for better speed and performance and applies the traditional approach on case 7 because i love ice cream is not a multi-word term. CSpell splits case 5 to tear breakup time because it is a spelling variant of tear break up time and has fewer tokens (3 instead of 4).

# 5 Conclusions 

We have developed two systematic approaches to effectively build multiword terms in the Lexicon from corpora and semantic networks with a high precision value of 81.39. We have also developed exclusive filters based on empirical models with heuristic rules to filter out invalid multiword terms. These filters were tested on the Lexicon resulting in a high recall rate of 99.96. As a result of this work, the Lexicon, a large collection of multiword terms, provides a rich multiword resource for many biomedical NLP research applications. We have illustrated two applications (STMT and CSpell) to show the improvement in performance found by utilizing lexical multiwords and we included a novel multiword approach to demonstrate the significance of multiwords. Multiword acquisition processing has been applied on annual releases of MED-LINE due to the rapid annual growth of MEDLINE (> 1 million articles/year). 29 

For each annual release of MEDLINE, the processing includes generating the MNS and the DMNS followed by applying our filters and matchers to the MNS and DMNS sets. The multiword acquisition process for WordNet was only done once since WordNet is static. As a result, both approaches cumulatively con-tribute multiword terms to the Lexicon with 32,108 lexRecords, 45,069 base forms and 71,978 unique spelling forms from the time since they were implemented up

This chapter describes interdisciplinary research at the crossroads of Natural Lan-guage Processing and Foreign Language Teaching/Learning (FLT/L). We propose an approach in which developing lexical competence through reading is supported by a fully interpretable rule-based MWE identifier which relies on MWE entries from the French Wiktionary. The tool is integrated into Linguse, a reading applica-tion for language learners. This chapter discusses the FLT/L aspects of this work. We apply the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages (CEFR) as the didactic framework. We explain how it accounts for reading as a leisure activ-ity and how it integrates MWEs into the lexical competence of language learners. We perform user experiments with a group of Polish students learning French as a foreign language. The experiments show that the developed functionality for identifying and annotat-ing MWEs within the reading platform was appreciated by learners, as it allowed them to focus on reading rather than on explaining unknown MWEs. Although the functionality makes some identification and/or annotation errors, they were not perceived as problematic by the learners. Moreover, they can be relatively eas-ily corrected since the whole process is fully controlled. In this work, the domains of FLT/L and NLP mutually inform each other and we report on findings stem-ming from this interdisciplinary effect. In particular, this work sheds new light on the constraints that must be met in MWEs identification, to make it applicable in end-user applications in FLT/L.

# 1 Introduction 

Identification and annotation of multiword expressions (MWEs) have been con-sidered important issues in Natural Language Processing (NLP), as shown no-tably by Constant et al. (2017). Much progress has been achieved on this topic and current mainstream methods, including those using Large Language Models (LLMs), often can efficiently handle MWEs while processing and generating text (Miletić & Schulte im Walde 2024, Hashiloni et al. 2025). It is, however, less clear how well such achievements can benefit end user applications, in which specific requirements should be met. One field in which NLP meets end users is Foreign Language Teaching/ Learning (FLT/L). In fact, this domain poses specific challenges. For instance, when NLP support is used to develop lexical competence, there is a need to cover most MWEs present in text, also the infrequent ones. However, the state of the art in MWE identification shows poor generalization: MWEs unseen in training corpora are not adequately accounted for (Ramisch et al. 2020). Such unseen MWEs correspond to the majority of existing MWEs, since manually annotated training corpora are relatively small. Therefore, it is recommendable to support MWE identification with lexical resources (Savary et al. 2019a). An-other constraint from FLT/L is the quality and richness of NLP support. Current LLMs struggle to get comparable performances to supervised MWE identifiers (Arslan et al. 2025), and their objective evaluation is not easy due to possible contamination of pre-trained models with evaluation data (Dong et al. 2024). Moreover, if MWE identification is used for the development of lexical compe-tence in learners, identified MWEs should be accompanied with high-quality definitions, possibly manually crafted or validated by experts. Moreover, feed-back from both learners and teachers should ideally enrich the NLP tool, for instance for a better control of the studied vocabulary. Finally, when an NLP outcome contains errors, it should be possible to explain their origins, so as to maintain the users’ engagement. For all these reasons, in Überrück-Fries et al. (2024) we proposed an approach in which learning/teaching French is supported by a fully interpretable, lexicon-based and rule-based MWE identifier. It is integrated into Linguse, a reading application for language learners. While the previous publication thoroughly addressed the NLP component, this chapter discusses the FLT/L aspects of this work, including user experiments with a group of Polish students learning French. The chapter is organized as follows. We discuss the state of the art in NLP support for FLT/L and we define the objectives of the study (§2). We describe 226 6 Identification and annotation for French as a foreign language reading as a leisure activity (§3), the approaches to teaching/learning vocabu-lary (§4), and the role of MWEs in FLT/L in comparison to NLP (§5). We briefly introduce Linguse (§6) and summarize its MWE identification and annotation module (§7). Then, we describe user experiments and their results (§8), and we offer a discussion of emerging issues and trends (§9). Finally, we conclude and propose perspectives for future work (§10). 

# 2 State of the art and the objectives of the study 

Multiword expressions (MWEs), referred to as fixed expressions in Foreign Lan-guage Teaching/Learning (FLT/L), constitute an essential component of any language and represent a crucial communicative component (Sułkowska 2013, Tigani 2024). Consequently, they should occupy an appropriate place in FLT/L, particularly in the development of lexical competence, as recognized in the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages (CEFR) (Council of Europe 2001). These expressions function in the mind of a native speaker as fully-fledged units, with the meaning regarded as autonomous and global (Mejri 2004, González-Rey 2005). Consequently, fixed expressions are “used and learnt as wholes” (Council of Europe 2001: 110). However, due to the complex-ity of their linguistic characteristics, grosso modo their semantic opacity (Gross 1996, Cavalla 2016), syntactic and lexical unpredictability (Gross 1982, Tutin & Grossmann 2013) and non-modifiability (Tigani 2024), they raise significant challenges within FLT/L, both in reception and production activities. In reading comprehension, which is the focus of this study, two main difficulties should be considered: identifying a “suspected” sequence of words, whose compositional meaning does not fit the meaning of the complete sentence, and then assigning the correct meaning. To address these obstacles, didactics can turn to Natural Language Processing (NLP) technologies and tools, leveraging their potential to analyze, classify, and support teaching MWEs. By integrating these advanced computational methods, the process of teaching/learning fixed expressions need not be daunting or, as some might say, mission impossible . NLP tools, as will be illustrated by the example of the reading platform Linguse, 1 can provide learners with structured, context-aware approaches to mastering MWEs, enhancing the development of linguistic competences. E-books and reading devices are widely embraced by foreign language learn-ers, particularly, at least partially, for leisure purposes. However, their pedagog-ical applications have received limited attention in academic research. Specif-

# 3 Reading as a leisure activity in Foreign Language Teaching/Learning 

Reading comprehension, as presented in Council of Europe (2020), belongs to reception activities (cf. Figure 1). It is divided into six different types concerning different domains of language use (public, educational, occupational, and per-sonal), among them reading as a leisure activity. The last activity covers a broad spectrum of materials, ranging from fiction and non-fiction to creative texts and various forms of literature, tailored to individual interests (Council of Europe 2020: 58). Although reading as a leisure activity is a new activity added in 2018, it is rooted in its predecessor – reading for pleasure , developed within the personal domain of language use (Council of Europe 2001: 45). Far from being an innate or pre-existing skill, according to Médioni (2010), pleasure in this respect is not a prerequisite but a construction. Learners do not commence the educational process with this capacity fully developed, but they have to gradually acquire it. Reading as a leisure activity and for pleasure, are both closely intertwined with the development of language autonomy and the ability to construct mean-ing. Meaning construction is understood as “a dynamic system” (Venant 2007) integrating semantic and discursive dimensions. As for the semantic dimension, the construction of meaning involves the search of meaning at the lexical level, taking into account polysemous characteristics of words, but also going beyond this level, to the complexity of semantic opacity of MWEs. Indeed, lexical limita-tions are indicated as the first obstacle in reading comprehension in a foreign lan-guage (Güngör 2015). Furthermore, the learners examined in the same research mentioned idiomatic expressions as problematic in understanding a text. activity 5 dealing with B1 level learners. Despite its potential to enhance linguistic competence and foster learners’ engagement, reading autonomously in a foreign language raises some challenges. The learners’ lexical repertoire at B1 level is still very limited, especially when the content of the text is broader than everyday top-ics (Council of Europe 2020). In consequence, they may need lexical assistance in their reading comprehension in order to make reading a genuine leisure ac-tivity. On the one hand, this activity differs from reading as a typical classroom activity for linguistic purposes. However, Cornea (2010) talks about synthetical reading , typical of foreign language teaching, which focuses primarily on the formal part of the text, particularly on its lexical and grammatical structures, yet it still leads to a global understanding of the text. She also admits that even in this kind of reading, learners’ interest in the text is essential, otherwise teach-ing risks becoming ineffective. It suggests that reading in general, whatever its purpose, is an activity that engages learners mainly cognitively and emotionally. Therefore, language assistance is necessary to overcome linguistic obstacles for reading comprehension. Consequently, in terms of text selection for the reading application tested in our study, the inclusion of MWE-rich material was intended to meet both peda-gogical and engagement criteria. Such texts should both introduce new expres-sions and reinforce previously learned ones, thus optimizing vocabulary acquisi-tion. Reading applications could integrate features to guide learners through this synthetical reading process, annotating MWEs in context to enhance their com-prehension, while at the same time maintaining learners’ interest and motivation to continue reading. 

# 4 Two main approaches to teaching/learning vocabulary 

In the realm of language acquisition, two primary approaches to teaching and learning lexicon are often highlighted: explicit and incidental (Dryjańska 2024). Explicit teaching and learning involve a structured progression where learners systematically explore metalexical concepts, such as semantic fields, polysemy, synonyms, antonyms, and related elements (Grossmann 2011). This method is deliberate and aims to deepen the learners’ metalinguistic awareness by focusing on targeted vocabulary strategies.

This approach focuses on contextual lexical expla-nations that naturally arise within these tasks (Huckin & Coady 1999, Grossmann 2011). In our study, we adopted the incidental teaching/learning approach, integrat-ing lexical and metalinguistic explanation into a reading activity. This method aligns with the objective of fostering vocabulary acquisition in an authentic and contextually relevant manner. 

# 5 Multiword expressions in FLT/L and in NLP 

The importance of MWEs in FLT/L stems from their presence in everyday com-munication and their contribution to fluency and precision of expression. How-ever, their prototypical characteristics raise significant challenges, manifested in their linguistic description, as well as in application within FLT/L and NLP (Überrück-Fries et al. 2024). The concept of MWEs in computational linguistics and in FLT/L serves com-plementary but distinct purposes. In the former tradition, Baldwin & Kim (2010) define MWEs as lexical items that can be decomposed into multiple lexemes and exhibit idiomatic behavior, while Ramisch (2015) extends this by stipulating that MWEs must also be treated as a single unit in computational processes. These definitions primarily aim to solve the inherent challenges of processing MWEs. As a result, they give rise to a particularly broad category that captures a diverse array of phenomena, from semantic and syntactic to pragmatic idiosyncrasies, all with the goal of refining automated language understanding and generation. From a syntactic standpoint, MWEs are often subject to constraints that hinder their straightforward usage. The term fixed expressions stresses this syntactic feature of MWEs. On the one hand, its importance can be confirmed by the fact that tests used to identify the idiomaticity of an expression, such as blocking transformational properties, non-modifiability of the order of constituents and of their grammatical categories, are based on this feature (Cavalla 2016). On the other hand, the fixedness of an expression has a gradual nature which means that different expressions, or their parts, accept different syntactic constraints. Another characteristic of MWEs is discontinuity, meaning that the elements of an expression may be separated by other words or phrases, making their recognition and processing more complex both for learners and NLP specialists. From a semantic perspective, MWEs are described in terms of non-compositio-nality and opacity. While non-compositionality refers to the inability to deduce 232 6 Identification and annotation for French as a foreign language the meaning of an expression from its individual constituents (encoding phase), opacity pertains to difficulty, perceived by the receiver (decoding phase), in dis-cerning the expression’s metaphorical or figurative meaning. These semantic di-mensions also exhibit gradation, as highlighted by Cavalla (2016), which further complicates their linguistic analysis and the teaching/learning process. In conclusion, while both NLP and FLT/L approaches share an interest in and a pragmatic approach to idiomatic expressions, the operational approaches in the two disciplines are different. In language teaching and learning, the focus is on phrases that should be treated as non-decomposable units of meaning be-cause they function as such in communication. Detailed linguistic properties of these units are rarely discussed. In NLP, conversely, MWEs are seen as combina-tions of words with idiosyncratic properties which have to be accounted for in processing. 

# 6 Linguse – a reading application for language learners 

Linguse 6 is a web-based application for synthetic reading, offering a range of features, including the ability to upload text files in different formats, and receive contextual assistance on unfamiliar vocabulary through the identification and annotation of single word forms. It also allows users to track and save vocabulary items during the reading process. For the purpose of this study, the Linguse interface was extended to incor-porate functionalities for MWEs, as shown in the left screenshot in Figure 2. When the user clicks on any part of an identified MWE, the application auto-matically highlights the entire expression. It then displays relevant glosses from Wiktionary and offers a contextualized machine translation of the expression to the language previously chosen by the user. Additionally, if the user opts to add the expression to their learning vocabulary, then the present and all further oc-currences are visually marked, until the user moves it to their known vocabulary list. To facilitate the user experiments, two additional web pages were created within the Linguse environment. The first served as a central hub for guiding participants through the various phases of the study. The second was devoted to administering a pre- and postquiz, shown in the right screenshot in Figure 2, designed to gauge the participants’ knowledge and understanding of MWEs.

# 7 Automatic identification and annotation of MWEs 

Automatic identification of MWEs (henceforth MWEI) is a task in which, given an input text (raw or containing linguistic annotations such as lemmas, parts-of-speech, or syntactic dependencies), it should be returned with automatically highlighted occurrences of MWEs. Constant et al. (2017) mention three cate-gories of MWEI methods. Firstly, rule-based methods rely most often on lexi-cons in which MWEs are explicitly encoded and various kinds of grammar rules (whether local grammars or full-fledged formal grammars) encode their morpho-syntactic variation. Secondly, word-sense disambiguation methods pre-identify potential MWE occurrences and classify them into idiomatic occurrences on the one hand (as in: You owe me 100 euro by the way ) and literal or coincidental co-occurrences of the same sets of lemmas on the other hand (as in: I recognized her by the way she walked ). Thirdly, sequence tagging methods encode a sen-tence as a sequence of B, I or O tags: B for a word beginning an MWE, I for a word inside an MWE, and O for a word outside any MWE. Sequence taggers are trained in a supervised manner on manually annotated corpora. A fourth cate-gory of methods – unsupervised MWEI – emerged with the advent of distribu-tional semantics-based language models. MWEs can be identified, e.g., by train-ing deep neural networks which aggregate contextual and non-contextual vector representations of the components of an MWE, so as to compare their idiomatic and literal uses (Zeng & Bhat 2021). MWEs can also be identified by generative models via prompting (Hashiloni et al. 2025). 7 Most of the above-mentioned ef-forts were dedicated to only a single language or a small number of languages. As far as multilingual MWEI is concerned, the PARSEME network organized a series of evaluation campaigns dedicated to automatic identification of verbal MWEs in up to 19 languages along unified principles (Savary et al. 2017, Ramisch et al. 2018, 2020). A majority of the performing systems was based on supervised machine learning methods such as naive Bayes, conditional random fields, bi-directional long-short-term memory networks, recurrent neural networks, and fine-tuned transformers. Interestingly, also a relatively simple rule-based system Seen2Seen (Pasquer et al. 2020), focusing on the MWEs seen in the training cor-pus, proved competitive and achieved the second best global F-score. One of the main findings from these campaigns was the critical hardness of MWEs unseen in the training corpus, whatever the underlying machinery. On this basis, it was recommended to rely on large MWE lexicons in order to extend the repository
