8.1 Quantitative evaluation 

To assess the impact of the reading task on lexical acquisition, various scor-ing methodologies evaluating vocabulary proficiency may be employed (Leńko-Szymańska 2019: 56–64). One of the most straightforward approaches is the Eu-rocentres Vocabulary Size Test, which uses a yes/no response format across ten-item samples derived from consecutive frequency bands (Meara & Jones 1989). For the purposes of this study, the Vocabulary Knowledge Scale Test (Paribakht & Wesche 1993 as cited by Leńko-Szymańska 2019) was selected. This test offers pedagogical advantages by adopting a non-binary perspective of lexical knowl-edge, contrasting with the binary format of the Eurocentres Vocabulary Size Test. Participants evaluate their comprehension of MWEs using a five-level scale. Whereas the first two levels rely solely on the learners’ self-assessment, the sub-sequent levels require participants to substantiate their knowledge by providing evidence such as synonyms, translations, or example sentences. This combined approach, integrating self-reporting with evidence-based evaluation, enables a more comprehensive measurement of both the breadth and the depth of partici-pants’ MWE knowledge. The quizzes contained the following options, here translated into English: 10 

I I don’t remember seeing this expression before. II I’ve seen this expression before, but I don’t know what it means. III I’ve seen this expression and I think it means… IV I know this expression. It means… V I can use this expression in a sentence that shows I understand it well. For example… Option I indicates the expression is not known. The attribution of 1 point for this option was chosen to reward the students’ participation in the quiz and their reflection. As for option II, the expression is familiar but its meaning is not known, and it is rewarded by 2 points. If learners select option III, they can get 3 points if they are able to give a correct explanation (via a synonym or a translation). If not, they obtain 2 points, as in option II. If option IV is selected and a correct explanation is given, 4 points are attributed to the learner, meaning

# 9 Discussion 

This interdisciplinary research revealed interesting benefits and issues from both didactic and computational points of view. Involving undergraduate students in the project made them encounter the principles of research methodology: formulating scientific hypotheses, design-ing and implementing an experimental scenario, performing quantitative and qualitative evaluation. Our experiment also showed the potential to enhance students’ awareness that lexical knowledge cannot be accurately represented through binary measures. Through the design of the quizzes, students gain an understanding that vocab-ulary acquisition is a multifaceted process. This process involves engaging in diverse activities rather than solely relying on memorization techniques, such as studying “word lists”. It emphasizes the progression from an initial encounter 243 Agnieszka Dryjańska, Till Überrück-Fries & Agata Savary with a word to the eventual ability to use it accurately and appropriately within a given context. The user experiments suggest that extensive MWE coverage in terms of their identification and annotation is highly valued by language learners. Such breadth seems fundamental in satisfying the diverse needs of learners, especially if var-ious proficiency levels are concerned. Furthermore, the user experiments high-light that second-language learners exhibit a tolerance for noisy assistance, pro-vided they are supported by a rich array of contextual resources. However, this issue needs further consideration. More particularly, there is a need to explore what types of “minor annotation errors” can be identified and tolerated by learn-ers compared to “real errors”, which are typically recognized by teachers or other qualified annotators. Understanding learners’ tolerance for such minor inaccura-cies could inform the design of more learner-centered annotation systems, im-proving user experience without compromising the educational value of the ap-plication. The above issue reveals a broader challenge: the necessity to establish a bench-mark for key metrics such as F-score, precision, and recall, in order to evaluate the level of identification and annotation of MWEs appropriate for FLT/L pur-poses. To the best of our knowledge, no such benchmarks exist currently. This lack of reliable standards made it challenging to evaluate the quality of the find-ings of this study, highlighting the clear need for further research in this field. In particular, it is needed to establish an optimal balance between recall and pre-cision in the context of Foreign Language Teaching, especially for applications focused on reading as a leisure activity (independent reading), which can possibly be different than the benchmarks imposed in other fields (e.g., in NLP, optimal F-measure is valued most of the time). Achieving this balance could enhance the effectiveness of such tools and address the unique needs of learners engaged in self-directed reading practices. A new research question that has emerged from this study is: Do false positives have a more detrimental effect than false negatives in the context of language teach-ing applications? This question underscores a fundamental tension between tradi-tional didactic perspectives concerning didactic materials and student-centered approaches. On the one hand, development of quality materials for FLT/L is a very complex endeavor (Tomlinson 2011) involving various criteria, e.g., linguis-tic, pedagogical and cultural ones (Tomlinson 2011, Pasquale 2022, Littlejohn 2022). Their linguistic accuracy is hardly explicitly discussed as materials that “emerge from specialist team” (Littlejohn 2022) are assumed to be accurate by default. As far as authentic materials, used vastly in FLT/L (Pasquale 2022), are concerned, the question of language correctness should be raised. When it comes 244 6 Identification and annotation for French as a foreign language to the application of open-source resources like Wiktionary, or tools like Wikt-Seen (§7), for didactic purposes, this concern becomes even more relevant. The assumption of their linguistic accuracy cannot be taken for granted, as can be seen in the following issues, drawn from the reading experiments described in Section 8. Firstly, no distinction is made between adverbial locution and adverb, as illus-trated in Figure 2 by the MWE useless. Detailed differentiation of parts of speech may seem less important when teaching a language in a school context; in Ro-mance philology, however, it is an important skill. Secondly, some inconsistencies can be observed. MWEs, like to acknowled-geor to have access, are well identified but neither definitions nor synonyms are provided. As for be supported, first, each element is identified separately, then, within the sentence, these elements are highlighted as an expression. Conversely, the MWE ad hoc is not identified as an expression within a sentence, but ad is incorrectly annotated as an adverb when treated separately. The MWE really!is correctly annotated as an interjection, but oh should also be annotated as an in-terjection, whereas it is annotated as a verb. These errors probably stem from spurious automatic part-of-speech tagging. Some MWEs are illustrated by examples which are not appropriate because they do not demonstrate the particularity of the MWE. For instance, the speci-ficity of the MWE to welcomeis that the noun welcome is used without an article. This MWE is illustrated by example (5), where an indefinite article a accompa-nies welcome. The example is correct, as the noun welcome is followed by an adjective, which often requires the use of an indefinite article. But this example does not illustrate the idiosyncrasy of skipping out the article in the absence of an adjective. (5) Il It est is important important de of

warm chaleureux to.the aux invited. invités. ’It is important to give the guests a warm welcome.’ It appears that students, Internet users accustomed to not fully correct or sys-tematically designed content, consider “minor annotation errors”, such as those presented above, acceptable, as these do not significantly impede their learning experience. However, as mentioned above, the concept of “minor annotation er-rors” needs to be clarified through further research. Particularly, it should be compared to the evaluation of specialists what kinds of errors are acceptable. As for the functionality of highlighting all the results of the identification pro-cess, its range should also be discussed with pedagogical issues in mind. Indeed, 245 Agnieszka Dryjańska, Till Überrück-Fries & Agata Savary highlighting even the most basic expressions might be counterproductive, dis-tracting, or exhausting for the learners. Moreover, customization of this function-ality should take into account the learner’s level of language proficiency and/or their individual needs, which raises new technical issues, rarely analyzed in the treatment of MWEs in NLP. Other new insights for NLP can be seen notably in confronting a well-studied NLP task (MWE identification) with a concrete application and real users. As a result, it is necessary to re-consider the attention paid to various challenges posed by this task. Firstly, correct identification of unseen MWEs is often con-sidered a major challenge in NLP. In language learning, conversely, the benefit from MWEs seen in lexicons is more straightforward, since they can be asso-ciated with definitions. If language learners are to acquire unseen MWEs with equal benefit, MWE identification has to be studied jointly with automatic gen-eration of definitions of such MWEs (Mickus et al. 2020). High effectiveness of both processes must be achieved jointly if their application to language learning is to be considered. Another shift in challenges concerns literal readings of MWEs. Past NLP re-search (Savary et al. 2019b) showed that literal occurrences of verbal MWEs are rare in texts and, therefore, pose only minor challenges in MWE identification, contrary to what many past papers had claimed. In the current project, how-ever, where MWEs of all syntactic types are studied, we observed that non-verbal MWEs (nominal, adjectival, adverbial, and functional) may display opposite ten-dencies, as discussed with respect to example (4). This brings the literal vs. id-iomatic disambiguation problem back to the front of the MWE processing land-scape. Concerning the methodological aspects of MWE identification, our experi-ment demonstrated the usefulness of (computationally light and fully interpre-table) rule-based methods, as opposed to the mainstream NLP, currently largely dedicated to computationally heavy and non-interpretable pre-trained language models. In particular, to optimally meet the needs of language learners, MWE identification should be parameterized by the precise vocabulary whose learn-ing we want to achieve. For instance, systematic identification of frequent and easy expressions, such as t]it needsit is necessary to, might hinder the pleasure of reading and diminish learning outcomes. Finally, as discussed above, this work also sheds new light on evaluation prac-tices. An optimal F-measure might not be the right quality criterion. Weighing precision vs. recall, depending on the learners vs. teachers perspectives, might be considered instead. Additionally, novel evaluation measures such as diversity 246 6 Identification and annotation for French as a foreign language (Lion-Bouton et al. 2022) could be more useful than standard performance mea-sures. Namely, it might be more important to identify many different MWEs, even if some of their occurrences are skipped, than all occurrences of only a few most frequent MWEs. 

# 10 Conclusions and perspectives 

This research operates at the crossroads of FLT/L and NLP in French. Within the CEFR didactic framework, we target reception activities – and more precisely reading as a leisure activity – via incidental teaching and learning. We use Lin-guse, a reading application for language learners, which we enhance with Wik-tSeen, an MWE identification tool based on MWE entries, definitions, and ex-ample sentences from French Wiktionary. We perform user experiments with a class of Polish learners of French as a foreign language. Via a reading exercise, ac-companied with a pre- and a postquiz, we measure possible impact of the tool on MWE-related lexical competence. Whereas our experimental results have only an indicative value due to the low number of participants, the evaluation scenario seems insightful and applicable on a larger scale. This interdisciplinary research also brings user-driven insights to language learning on the one hand and to the broader field of MWE research on the other hand. Perspectives for future work include the extension of the experiments to larger numbers of learners, at various learning levels, so as to obtain more conclusive results. Other languages than French are already covered by Linguse, but MWE identification is not yet implemented for them. WiktSeen should be adaptable to at least those languages for which the corresponding Wiktionary modules are rich enough in MWE entries and examples. More feedback gathered from extended experiments might usefully feed the methodological discussions such as those from Section 9.

Proper handling of multiword expressions (MWEs) is a key aspect of developing linguistically sound natural language processing applications. Nevertheless, Large Language Models (LLMs) are not built specifically considering MWEs from the first layers. However, due to their presence in training data, higher layers of LLMs may develop features useful for MWE identification and analysis. This chapter explores the usefulness of LLMs when dealing with MWEs. Theoretical considerations are presented, starting with the tokenization mechanism. Then experimental results, specifically involving MWEs, are given. The main contribution of this work is in its empirical investigation of how LLMs treat MWEs (MWE identification) using zero-shot and Chain-of-Thought prompting. We provide a contrastive analysis of open-source LLMs and their performance in the task of MWE identification. 

# 1 Introduction 

Natural language processing (NLP) applications split texts into tokens to facili-tate processing. Tokens are commonly associated with words and punctuation marks, while deeper, sub-word tokenization techniques are employed in Large Language Models (LLMs). For languages using spaces to separate words, the prob-lem of splitting a text into word-level tokens seems trivial, being reduced to iden-tifying space characters. However, the problem of what constitutes a word is sur-prisingly complex, as noted by Baldwin & Kim (2010), Haspelmath (2023). Mul-tiword expressions (MWEs) have specific properties which are not predictable from the properties of their component words. Sag et al. (2002) further define

Jackendoff (1997) estimates that the number of MWEs in a speaker’s lexicon is of the same order of magnitude as the number of single words. While this estima-tion may vary with the size of the speaker’s lexicon, depending on the speaker’s age and background, the large number of MWEs commonly used in our day-to-day interactions makes the proper identification and analysis of MWEs an important problem to consider when developing NLP applications. Generative pretrained models, such as ChatGPT, Llama, or Gemini, have be-come a standard building block for large-scale NLP applications for both indus-try and research organizations. Common approaches include task-specific fine-tuning, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and prompt engineering. The large number of artificial neural network (ANN) layers, translated into billions of parameters, gives LLMs the capacity to learn complex features associated with text in a self-supervised way. Thus, the capabilities of NLP applications making use of current state-of-the-art (SOTA) models surpass those of previous-generation applications (such as the ones employing static word embedding rep-resentations or contextualized BERT-like embeddings). However, this comes at the cost of requiring a lot of computational power (in terms of CPUs and espe-cially GPUs). The deep neural network approach combined with the large number of train-ing tokens (for example, over 15T tokens used for Llama 3 training) makes LLMs very good at generating text (the commonly known task of next word prediction). Both the input text (“prompt”) and the generated text (“output”) may include MWEs, thus indicating that specific features may have been learned during the training process. The rest of the paper is structured as follows: Section 2 presents related work; Section 3 describes the process of tokenization in LLMs; Section 4 presents the datasets used for the experiments; Section 5 outlines the methodology employed; Section 6 provides details about the prompts used in identifying MWEs; Section 7 explores the results obtained through the chain-of-thought prompting approach; and finally, we conclude in Section 8. More details about the LLMs employed are given in Appendix A. 

# 2 Related work 

The organization of the PARSEME series of shared tasks (Ramisch et al. 2020) on the identification of verbal multiword expressions (VMWEs) led to the devel-opment of different systems able to detect such expressions. According to the 256 7 Prompting Large Language Models for Multiword Expression recognition shared task paper, the best result (an F1 score of 38.5%) for detecting unseen VMWEs was achieved by a system employing a fine-tuned BERT model (Taslim-ipoor et al. 2020). De Luca Fornaciari et al. (2024) experiment with three smaller LLMs (Llama-2-7b-chat, Mistral-7b-Instruct, and Vicuna-7b) using a purpose-built dataset designed for the idiom detection task. Their findings suggest that Llama-2 provides the best recall, Mistral the best precision, and Vicuna the best accuracy. Phelps et al. (2024) investigate the performance of LLMs for idiomatic-ity detection on three datasets (SemEval 2022 Task 2a, FLUTE, and MAGPIE). They find that large LLMs give competitive performance on the tested datasets, but the results are still below those obtained from much smaller fine-tuned encoder-only models. Their research focuses on both API-only models (GPT-3.5, GPT-5, Gemini) and openly available models, including Llama 2 and Mistral. Martínez et al. (2024) investigate the potential of LLMs to provide accurate es-timates of concreteness, valence, and arousal for MWEs, showing that ChatGPT-4o is able to provide good results. Jin et al. (2024) focus on Abstract Meaning Representations (AMRs) and their use for Chain-of-Thought prompting (CoT) in different NLP tasks. Their findings suggest that bad results in AMR-CoT are due in part to the inability of AMR to capture MWEs. Overall, the recent shift from rule-based and fine-tuned neural models to LLMs reflects ongoing changes in the methods used for the detection and analysis of multiword expressions. Further research is required to address the remaining challenges in this area.

Even though all the analyzed LLMs are trained on large volumes of text and employ statistical tokenizers, there are differences in how the test sentence is to-kenized. Some differences may be due to design choices, such as the inclusion or omission of spaces inside tokens. The Grok 2 tokenizer removes spaces, leading sometimes to empty tokens which are kept, while the other tokenizers include the surrounding spaces in the tokens, with preference for including spaces pre-ceding the tokens. Other differences are likely due to the different training data used. For example, Mistral splits the word “surrendered” into three tokens. This is probably because its training places less emphasis on English data and more on other European languages. The other tested models are trained on larger vol-umes of English text (significantly larger compared to other languages) and this resulted in keeping the English words present in the test sentence intact, without sub-word tokens. Nevertheless, for other tokens, sub-word tokenization is still used, such as the year “1945” which is split into two tokens (“194” and “5”) or 4 tokens (“1”,“9”,“4”, and “5”).

Each of the tested models split the MWE into three tokens, one for each of the compo-nent words. Based on the model’s training strategy, the tokens may be preceded by the space character. Thus, we see two tokenization forms “out | of | office” and “_out | _of | _office” (similar to the examples, “_” denotes a space character included in the token). The second test sentence contains the MWE “awoken to”. This consists of two words and in this case the first word (“awoken”) is a less fre-quently used word in the English language. In this case, five out of the six tested LLMs split the word “awoken”. Overall, for the tested LLMs there are three tok-enization variants for this MWE: “awoken | to”, and “_aw | oken | _to”, “_a | wo | ken | _to”. None of the models treated the MWE as a single unit. Furthermore, in the second example, the word “awoken” was split by most of the models into sub-word tokens. This indicates that LLMs are not handling MWEs at tokenization stage and any features relevant for MWEs are learned in higher-level layers. Ku-mar (2024) acknowledges that phrase-level tokenization (treating sequences of words as single tokens) proves advantageous, especially when particular phrases carry substantial semantic or contextual relevance within the given task. Thus, we consider that future inclusion of MWEs as single tokens (or smaller groups of tokens) may allow the models to better process MWEs. In this case, higher lay-ers could focus more on relations between MWEs and their surrounding context. Even though this process is not explored in the rest of the paper, we hypothesize that tokenization unaffected by MWEs may be part of the reason why zero-shot approaches provide only limited results, as detailed in the following sections. Ad-ditional theoretical insights into LLM tokenization are given by Rajaraman et al. (2025). 

# 4 Datasets 

Work on multiword expressions produced a number of datasets with manually annotated MWEs. These include both monolingual and multilingual resources. All of them contain reference text with MWEs clearly identified in different for-mats. This section is not intended as a survey of such resources (the reader is referred to surveys such as Constant et al. (2017)). Instead, in this section, only the datasets used for the purposes of this work are briefly described. Wiki50 (Vincze et al. 2011) is constructed based on 50 random articles from English Wikipedia. Selection was performed in order to ensure at least 1000 260 7 Prompting Large Language Models for Multiword Expression recognition words, without lists, tables or other structured texts. There is a total of 3180 unique MWEs, with 3861 occurrences. The inter-annotator agreement Kappa rate is 0.6938 (as reported by the authors). This indicates fairly good agreement, while still assuming a number of errors are present in the corpus. The dataset also con-tains named entity annotations, but these are not used for this work. CoAM (Ide et al. 2024) is a collection of texts from the following sources: news text written by professionals from EMM NewsBrief (Glavaš & Štajner 2013), com-mentaries on news from the WMT23 shared task (Kocmi et al. 2023), transcrip-tions from the NAIST-NTT TED talk treebank (Neubig et al. 2014), transcriptions from a subset of the IWSLT 2017 shared task (Cettolo et al. 2017), and single sentences from the Universal Dependencies treebanks (Zeman et al. 2018). The resulting corpus contains 874 MWEs in 1301 sentences. The datasets were chosen because they contain different types of MWEs. The CoAM dataset contains MWEs marked as: Noun (noun MWEs or compounds), Verb (Verbal MWEs), Mod/Conn (Adjectival, adverbial, or connective MWEs), Clause (MWEs containing (1) a verb or auxiliary verb and (2) its nominal subject), and Other (MWEs whose head is not contained in them or whose PoS is none of the PoS above). The Wiki50 dataset contains MWEs marked as: Noun com-pounds, Adjectival compounds, VPC (verb-particle constructions), LVC (Light verb constructions), Idiom, and Other. Our interest was not in a particular MWE type or annotation scheme. Instead we were interested in datasets containing as many MWEs as possible to account for different interpretations of MWEs pos-sibly present in the LLMs. Furthermore, experiments involving LLM fine-tuning are available in scientific publications. Even though this chapter focuses on prob-ing LLMs (by means of prompt-based evaluations) for MWEs without performing fine-tuning, and thus the focus is not on finding new SOTA architectures, still it may be interesting for the reader to be able to compare the different approaches. Finally, Wiki50 is an older dataset that was likely seen during LLM training (in-cluding the annotations), while CoAM is a recent one. While the texts in CoAM may have been seen during LLM training, the annotations are new and were not seen by the LLMs used in the following sections.

# 6 Prompting LLMs for MWEs 

Prompting an LLM involves sending a query to the model and retrieving an an-swer. The model processes the received query and uses its text generation capa-bilities to produce relevant output. Figure 1 shows a generic prompting interac-tion with an LLM. The request part actually contains two texts: a system prompt and a user prompt. The prompting framework typically involves two key components that work together to shape the model’s behavior: System prompts serve as meta-instructions that guide how the model ap-proaches the task. While optional, these prompts have proven crucial for perfor-mance optimization. Recent studies by Zheng et al. (2024), Wu et al. (2024), Xu et al. (2024), Giray (2023) show that system prompts can significantly improve results by establishing the right context for the task, constraining what types of outputs the model considers appropriate, and activating the most relevant knowledge areas within the model’s training. User prompts contain the actual task instructions and input data. These need structuring to achieve optimal performance. Key considerations include clearly defining what we want the model to do (in this case, MWE identification), for-matting the input data in ways the model can easily process, specifying exactly how we want the output formatted so we can parse it reliably, and including in-structions for handling edge cases like sentences with no multiword expressions. 

> Figure 1: LLM prompting

The prompt provided by the user specifies the problem to be addressed by the LLM. It must contain the request, such as identification of MWEs, and the in-vestigated data, such as the sentence or text fragment from which the LLM is requested to extract MWEs. In addition, the user prompt may contain informa-tion about the expected format and indications of what should be generated if no MWE is found. Most of the prompt is constant (the problem, format indications) 263 Vasile Păiș & Maria Mitrofan and only the analyzed text varies between LLM invocations. Thus, prompts are organized as templates which get filled with the actual text to be analyzed prior to making an LLM call.

> You are alinguist that identifies multiword expressions.

# 7 Chain-of-Thought prompting 

The basic prompting mechanism described in Section 6 involved a system prompt, one user prompt and one corresponding response. The Chain-of-Thought approach uses a single system prompt (which may be the same as the one used in the basic prompting mechanism or may be different) and mul-tiple user prompts with associated responses. The final response is the one that is considered to be the end result of the Chain-of-Thought prompting approach. This mechanism is very similar to having a conversation with the LLM. The user starts with a problem and through multiple questions directs the model to focus on a specific aspect of interest to the user. Figure 6 gives a typical example of Chain-of-Thought prompting for a LLM. The final response is obtained after the model has been presented with the entire conversation history (the system prompt, user prompts 1..n, and responses 1..n-1). This interaction, depending on the questions asked to the model, may become a kind of Socratic argumentative method, where the model is guided through different questions (“prompts”) to the correct answer. Responses prior to the final response can be either generated by the model or inserted by the user to further guide the LLM in the generation of the final response. 270 7 Prompting Large Language Models for Multiword Expression recognition 

> Figure 6: Chain-of-Thought prompting for LLMs

For the purposes of this work, the responses obtained in Section 6 were refined with a new series of prompts, one for each of the identified MWEs. The template used is given in Listing 7.4. In this case, the template contains two replacement strings (noted with “%s”). The first one gets replaced with the sentence, while the second gets replaced with one of the previously identified MWEs. Thus, the template is used a number of times equal to the previously identified MWEs. If no MWEs is previously identified, then the template is not used.

# 8 Conclusion and future work 

LLMs have been used to improve the results of many NLP tasks. The large num-ber of parameters used in an LLM allows it to easily adapt to different tasks even in zero-shot scenarios. The task is described by means of a prompt and the 275 Vasile Păiș & Maria Mitrofan model provides the results. In this work we assessed the applicability of different LLMs for the task of identifying multiword expressions in English text. Based on this identification, we also considered the identification of sentences containing MWEs. Our approach was focused on two datasets: an older dataset, Wiki-50, and a newer dataset, CoAM. The choice was justified by our desire to explore LLM behavior on data previously unseen during the training process. Since CoAM is newer then all the LLMs tested, we can safely assume the LLMs have not seen this annotated data during their training. We explored two approaches: simple prompting (see Section 6) and chain prompting (see Section 7). In both cases we explored the impact of a basic prompt (telling the model what to do and assum-ing the model has knowledge of the simple wording used) and a more detailed prompt (explaining the task better to the model). Results were discussed in each section, following the tables with data, while in this section we draw conclusions from all the experiments. Considering only the Mistral family of models, our experiments confirm the intuition that larger models (with more parameters) are better than smaller mod-els. Mistral Large (123 billion parameters) behaves better in all cases compared with other Mistral variants. This is usually also confirmed across model families, with larger models performing better than smaller models, although individual differences do exist due to the way the models were trained and the dataset used for training. Llama 3.3 performance on the Wiki50 dataset is different from the CoAM dataset and from the other models. A likely cause for this is that Wiki50 is an older dataset, which was likely used during the training phase of the Llama model. Thus new implementations should take into account the likelihood of a model having seen the dataset during training. Of course, datasets created after the model was pre-trained are likely new to the model. Prompt engineering techniques refer to the way a model is interrogated by means of different input text. In this work we explored basic versus detailed prompts and Chain-of-Thought prompting. Our experiments suggest that de-tailed prompts work better with larger models. This is likely due to the ability of a larger model to better interpret the description and requirements in a larger text prompt. Furthermore, using a conversation-style approach, by means of a chain of prompts, seems to produce better results. Especially on new datasets (such as CoAM), a combination of detailed prompting and chain prompting yields the best results for larger language models for both identification of MWEs and sentences containing MWEs. Considering the overall performance, Vincze et al. (2011) report an F1 score of 0.6342 for MWE identification on the Wiki50 dataset using a Conditional Ran-276 7 Prompting Large Language Models for Multiword Expression recognition dom Field (CRF)-based system. Our best score on the same dataset is 0.3006 using detailed prompting and the Llama 3.3 model (and 0.2870 using chain prompt-ing with the basic prompt and the Llama 3.3 model). This shows that zero-shot approaches using LLMs are not yet on par with SOTA approaches. Looking at individual precision and recall scores, we notice that Vincze et al. (2011) report precision of 0.6986 and recall of 0.5807, while our approach achieves precision of 0.2191 and recall of 0.4789. Thus, it seems the major difference stems from pre-cision, as our approach tends to identify other text spans which are not actual MWEs. This seems to justify the chain approach, in which for each identified candidate MWE we try to ascertain if it really is a MWE. However, in this par-ticular case the result is still poor (precision of 0.2223 and recall of 0.4049). Thus, even though there is a certain increase in precision, there is also a decrease in recall. Ramisch et al. (2023) provide a survey of different experiments for the identifi-cation of MWEs. Our approach may be used as a starting point to identify the best LLMs in a zero-shot approach. However, to compete with SOTA results, it is nec-essary to further fine-tune the language model or employ additional techniques. Moreover, MWE datasets were developed for other languages, such as Romanian Barbu Mititelu et al. (2022), Barbu Mititelu & Mitrofan (2019), Irimia et al. (2019), Leseva et al. (2020). In this paper, we focus on English and corresponding LLMs, while in the future we will consider other languages, including Romanian. The current SOTA results for Romanian are presented by Avram et al. (2023). The study focuses on improving the detection of verbal MWEs in Romanian by us-ing multilingual language models, particularly XLM-RoBERTa. Ongoing efforts continue to refine the detection of MWEs in Romanian. Here, we mention two relevant initiatives: (1) OpenLLM-Ro (Masala et al. 2024) focuses on the develop-ment of Romanian-specific LLMs, such as RoLlama2-7b, with the aim of improv-ing various NLP tasks, including MWE detection, and (2) RoQLlama-7b (Dima et al. n.d.), a lightweight Romanian-adapted LLM that has shown promising results in several downstream tasks. Although not explicitly focused on MWE detection, its architecture could be fine-tuned for such purposes. Another important initia-tive to improve MWE detection is the Sem-Eval shared task 4 that focused on multimodal idiomaticity representation.

# Limitations 

Our work focused on a limited number of LLMs. While they are commonly used in NLP applications and their architecture forms the basis for numerous other models, we acknowledge that not all the LLMs follow the same principles. Fur-thermore, we investigated the zero-shot scenarios, and models fine-tuned specif-ically for the MWE detection task may behave differently. Our experiments were concerned only with the English language, as a language that is very well rep-resented in the tested LLMs. MWE detection in other languages, especially low-resourced ones, is likely to produce different results.

# Claire Bonial a, Julia Bonn b & Harish Tayyar Madabushi c

aU.S. Army Combat Capabilities Development Command Army Research Laboratory bUniversity of Colorado Boulder cUniversity of Bath 

In this chapter, we argue for the benefits of understanding multiword expressions from the perspective of usage-based, construction grammar approaches. We begin with a historical overview of how construction grammar was developed in order to account for idiomatic expressions using the same grammatical machinery as the non-idiomatic structures of language. We cover a comprehensive description of constructions, which are pairings of meaning with form of any size (morpheme, word, phrase), as well as how constructional approaches treat the acquisition and generalization of constructions. We describe a successful case study leveraging con-structional templates for representing multiword expressions in English PropBank. Because constructions can be at any level or unit of form, we then illustrate the ben-efit of a constructional representation of multi-meaningful morphosyntactic unit constructions in Arapaho, a highly polysynthetic and agglutinating language. We include a second case study leveraging constructional templates for representing these multi-morphemic expressions in Uniform Meaning Representation. Finally, we demonstrate the similarities and differences between a usage-based explana-tion of a speaker learning a novel multiword expression, such as “dancing with deer,” and that of a Large Language Model. We present experiments showing that both models and speakers can generalize the meaning of novel multiword expres-sions based on a single exposure of usage. However, only speakers can reason over the combination of two such expressions, as this requires comparison of the novel forms to a speaker’s lifetime of stored constructional exemplars, which are rich with cross-modal details.

# 1 Introduction 

At its inception, Construction Grammar (CxG) approaches have stood apart from other theoretical approaches to language because of their explanatory power when it comes to multiword expressions (MWEs). CxG is able to provide the ma-chinery for elegantly modeling MWEs for two primary reasons. First: in CxG, the basic unit of language is the ‘construction’ (Cxn), which is a pairing of meaning with a form, where the forms can vary across every level of language – thus there are morphological forms, lexical forms, and phrasal forms. As a result, CxG pro-vides a unified theory for accounting for meaning in multi-morphemic structures in precisely the same fashion as MWEs or transitive phrasal structures. Second: as a usage-based theory, CxG research demonstrates how frequency plays a role in facilitating extension but also preventing overgeneralization of flexible, par-tially productive Cxns. Thus, CxG can account for the seemingly idiosyncratic flexibility and productivity of MWEs, which has historically presented a chal-lenge to the simplest Natural Language Processing (NLP) techniques of treating MWEs like “words with spaces” (Sag et al. 2002). To elaborate upon these strengths in a CxG account of MWEs, this chapter begins by detailing the tenets of CxG approaches, with special focus on the no-tion of a Cxn and the role of frequency in the storage and generalization of Cxns (Section 2). We then turn to a description of how constructional templates have been used in modeling English MWEs in the PropBank project (Palmer et al. 2005), enabling theoretical advances in our understanding of the characteristics of MWEs, as well as computational advances in their detection and semantic in-terpretation (Section 3). In this way, we show the benefit of having one unified treatment of both lexical and phrasal structures. Next, we turn to a description of multi-morphemic expressions in Arapaho, including efforts to develop Uniform Meaning Representation (Bonn et al. 2023) for Arapaho. This requires eschewing traditional notions of wordhood in favor of Cxns, whose forms do not require any clear delineation between morphemes and words (as there are no morphological, input/output rules in CxG) (Section 4). Thus, we show the benefit of one theoret-ical approach to account for meaning in multi-morphemic and lexical structures. Finally, we describe the parallels between a speaker’s usage-based acquisition of grammar and the way that Large Language Models (LLMs) process text in order to acquire an impressive amount of linguistic competency (Section 5). We also present two exploratory experiments on both novel and nascent English MWEs that demonstrate that although frequency effects in a speaker’s grammar mimic priors in an LLM’s pre-training, this does not result in fully functional linguistic competence (Section 5.2.1, 5.2.2). This, too, is expected under CxG: whereas an 290 8 Dancing with Deer LLM’s ‘usage’ is all through the processing of text, a person’s usage is enriched by cross-modal association, resulting in vastly different meaning features paired up with a given form. We close with recommendations for future work in devel-oping constructional resources that will help to bridge the gap between human linguistic competency and that of our NLP systems (Section 6). 

# 2 Accounting for MWEs in CxG 

In this section, we begin with the importance of idiomatic expressions, one sub-set of MWEs, in the historical development of CxG. We then turn to a detailed description of what Cxns are, as well as what features of Cxns are posited to be stored in the mental lexicon, or ‘constructicon’. We then turn to a discussion of the importance of frequency of use and the factors that both facilitate and con-strain the extension or generalization of Cxn types to novel instantiations. Such extension leads to Cxns of varying level of abstractness, or ‘schematicity,’ dis-cussed next. We close this section with a description of constructional templates, facilitating the representation of both fixed and flexible constructional slots. 

2.1 CxG: a theory for ‘peripheral’ language phenomena 

Croft and Cruse write, “[i]t is not an exaggeration to say that Cxn grammar grew out of a concern to find a place for idiomatic expressions in the speaker’s knowl-edge of a language” (2004: 205). A place for idiomatic expressions had not been satisfactorily found in the Generative linguistic tradition, e.g. Chomsky (1957), in which idiomatic expressions had been relegated to the ‘peripheral’ language phenomena, which seemingly neither cooperated with nor merited an elegant rule-based explanation of properties. We define idioms as a class of MWEs that exhibit characteristics of lexical idiosyncrasy and syntactic creativity. Idioms are lexically idiosyncratic in that they are tied to certain words with different de-grees of fixedness. They exhibit syntactic creativity in that their behavior may not be accounted for by existing syntactic rules. These characteristics are espe-cially problematic when viewed from a Generative perspective, which posits the autonomy of syntax and semantics – semantic features are stored in the lexicon, while syntax dictates the combinatoric potential of lexical items. The Generative solution to the problem of idiomatic expressions was largely to posit that their non-conventional meaning requires speakers to store them as frozen, inflexible chunks in their mental lexicon. However, the majority of idioms are not frozen, showing some syntactic flexibility, such as the ability to be marked for the past 291 Claire Bonial, Julia Bonn & Harish Tayyar Madabushi tense or passivized: The beans that Nathan spilled... Others are more fixed, resist-ing passivization: *The bucket that Grandpa kicked... .1 If idioms are to be stored in the lexicon, this would reasonably lead one to conclude that some syntactic information is also stored in the lexicon, with respect to what syntactic rules are permissible for which idioms. Thus, to accommodate idioms, the lexicon either had to include such syntactic information, or conversely, one could conclude that syntactic rules exhibit idiosyncratic lexical behavior – sometimes being choosy as to which lexical items can fill certain slots, but according to semantic crite-ria (the idiomatic meaning of the words) as opposed to morphosyntactic criteria. This makes strict separation of syntax and semantics quite difficult to maintain. As a result of their special characteristics making them uncooperative with the Generative view of syntax and semantics, idiomatic expressions were relegated to the peripheral, minor aspects of language. But are such expressions periph-eral? Although definitions of idiomaticity vary, making corpus counts inexact, studies suggest that MWEs, where multiple words function as a single mean-ing unit, make up anywhere from 30 to 50% of an English speaker’s vocabulary (Sag et al. 2002). What’s more, idiomatic expressions interact in important ways with the rest of the grammar, demonstrating a continuum of compositionality in language from lexically fixed, ‘substantive’ idioms on the one hand, and more lexically flexible, ‘schematic’ expressions on the other hand. Fillmore et al. (1988) advocate for “the view that the realm of idiomaticity in a language includes a great deal that is productive, highly structured, and wor-thy of serious grammatical investigation” (1988: 501). The authors go on to argue that an explanatory model of grammar should be able to account for “syntactic configurations larger and more complex than those definable by means of sin-gle phrase structure rules” (idem), and delve into the expression let alone as a case study. The authors summarize their definition of idiomatic expressions as, “something a language user could fail to know while knowing everything else in a language”, where everything else is thought of as the grammar and vocabulary of the language, which does not enable computation of the special meaning of idiomatic expressions. We refer the reader to this article for a detailed catalogue of idiomatic expressions, organized according to syntactic and semantic proper-ties, such as “unfamiliar pieces unfamiliarly arranged,” a category including the Comparative-correlative: The more carefully you do your work, the easier it will get. Notice that this expression is syntactically idiosyncratic in that there is no clear constituent category for each of the juxtaposed “the...” phrases, yet there are some constraints on the parallel nature of the phrases, preventing, for

F<X A Y let alone B> I doubt you could get Fred to eat squid, let alone Louise b. F<X A let alone B Y> I doubt you could get Fred, let alone Louise, to eat squid In this syntactic schemata, each variable is assigned certain semantic prop-erties as well. A and B are the two compared elements, above Fred and Louise .X, representing you could get , in combination with Y, representing to eat squid 

above, sets up a scale. The two juxtaposed structures before and after let alone are points on that scale. Finally, F above, corresponding with I doubt carries a prag-matic meaning, indicating the speaker’s strength of illocutionary force, where the strength of their belief in the first element (doubting that Fred would eat squid) is not as strong as their belief in the second element (doubting all the more that Louise would eat squid). In detailing the syntactic schemata for let alone , the authors demonstrate one kind of formalism for capturing the syntactic slots of a Cxn, their properties, as well as the semantics associated with those slots. Significantly, the authors lay out the ways in which the formalisms of CxG are able to provide the explanatory mechanisms for idiomatic expressions, such as let alone , as well as purely com-positional expressions abiding by the more typical combinatoric rules of phrase structure. Indeed, Fillmore et al. (1988) conclude “the machinery needed for de-scribing the so-called minor or peripheral constructions [...] will have to be pow-erful enough to be generalized to more familiar structures.” (1988: 534). Thus, CxG was developed precisely to have such machinery, enabling a uniform account of all parts of language. 

2.2 Cxns: Form and meaning 

In this section, we provide greater detail into what linguistic information char-acterizes Cxns. They are form-meaning pairings; thus, in many ways, Cxns are quite similar to the Saussurean sign, which is a pairing of a concept and what 293 Claire Bonial, Julia Bonn & Harish Tayyar Madabushi is termed a ‘sound image,’ where these items in turn can be thought of as the signified (e.g., a tree) and the signifier (e.g., tree ), respectively (de Saussure 1916). As a usage-based and cognitively plausible grammatical theory, CxG posits that our linguistic abilities are explained by domain-general cognitive processes, and that many aspects of language rely on our capacity for symbolic thinking, that is, our ability to store arbitrary pairings of form and meaning. Cxns reflect these pairings and are characterized by what is often called a ‘form-pole’ and a ‘meaning-pole.’ The form-pole is characterized by any phono-logically fixed elements as well as the relative locations of more flexible construc-tional slots (i.e. basic ordering or syntactic characteristics). The meaning pole in CxG is merely a shorthand for a complex concept, the details of which vary from speaker to speaker, given that each speaker will have different contextual asso-ciations with that concept and when it is referred to by that particular signifier. Thus, we define a Cxn as an arbitrary pairing of (phonological/syntactic) form and meaning that is stored in a speaker’s mental lexicon, or, as it is sometimes called in CxG, a speaker’s ‘constructicon’. Hereafter, we will refer to the fixed elements as ‘substantive,’ and the flexible elements as ‘schematic’, following the terminology of Hoffmann (2022). Although there are a variety of different schools of CxG (Hoffmann & Trous-dale 2013), all agree that the Cxn, as defined above, is the basic unit of lan-guage. As such, Cxns are found at every level of language – morphemes are Cxns, words are Cxns, phrases are Cxns. For example, unfair is an instance of the un-adjective Cxn, where un is the substantive element and the adjective is the schematic element. The category of the English adjective is itself a distinct schematic Cxn with no fixed phonology, and fair is a fully substantive, lexical Cxn. Similarly, below the belt is both an English prepositional phrase Cxn (with a literal meaning when constituted by lower-level Cxns denoting a spatial relation and an item of clothing), but also a unique, idiomatic phrasal Cxn that also has a meaning pole akin to unfair .Whether an English speaker computes the meaning literally according to in-dividual component Cxns or the idiomatic meaning of the phrasal Cxn depends upon context. The importance of context is, of course, not new or special to CxG. Indeed, if any linguistic generalization has been borne out by the trajectory of successful language modeling – where we see increasing linguistic sophistica-tion as increasing amounts of context are taken into account, up to the point of the web-scale pre-training data of LLMs – it is that context is critical in inter-preting meaning. However, what does set CxG apart, and usage-based theories more generally, is the emphasis on the importance of context that goes beyond 294 8 Dancing with Deer linguistic and beyond the current context of a particular usage. Usage-based the-ories emphasize that each token of linguistic experience updates and enriches a speaker’s stored representation of a Cxn with a variety of cross-modal associa-tions (Bybee 2006). For example, an English speaker stores details about where they were, what was going on, how comfortable they was physically, who else was there, and other details of the full sensory experience when they have heard 

below the belt used idiomatically. 

2.3 Constructional templates for MWEs 

Constructional templates, which represent both the fixed, substantive elements of Cxns as well as the flexible, schematic elements, provide a powerful tool for modeling partially productive MWEs. Such MWEs present a challenge for both modeling and detection because, as partially productive Cxns, their words are not fully fixed (as would be the case in an unproductive Cxn, such as kicked the bucket ); thus, one cannot simply use a ‘words with spaces’ approach to entering them into a computational lexicon and then associating a special meaning with the detection of that fixed form (Sag et al. 2002). On the other hand, their for-mulation is not highly productive (as would be the case, arguably, for English referential Cxns, wherein the pattern of a or the + noun is compatible with a wide variety of nouns). Thus, one cannot posit a clear rule for accounting for all possible cases. However, as the productivity continues to allow for novel variants to enter the language, one can never hope to list all of the different variants in a static computational lexicon. Furthermore, attempting to list all variants leads to overproliferation of the lexicon and ignores generalizations that can be made across all of the related expressions. Positing Cxns within the computational lexicon (or constructicon) models the fixed and flexible characteristics of a Cxn or MWE. 296 8 Dancing with Deer The Proposition Bank (PropBank) uses syntactic parses as a scaffolding for the much more difficult problem of parsing meaning. The underlying idea was that English verbs exhibit patterns in the way they structure their participants both syntactically and semantically, and so by tagging syntactic arguments of a verb with semantic role labels, a system could be trained to understand fundamental propositional semantics (i.e. who did what to whom, when and how?) using syntactic cues. PropBank’s main innovation was in creating a large-scale inventory of rolesets (sense-disambiguated predicate-argument structures) for English verbs, and then having expert human annotators apply them to syntactic parse trees from the Penn TreeBank (Taylor et al. 2003). The PropBank roleset lexicon consists of verb lemmas organized into frame files. Each frame file contains one or more rolesets representing the different semantic senses associated with the verb, with each roleset providing a predicate label, a written sense definition, and a list of roles corresponding to the semantically essential participants of the event. PropBank roles are numbered and given short written descriptions rather than more traditional thematic role labels as a way of splitting the difference between semantic and syntactic primacy of the argument. For example, Arg0s correspond to proto-agents (Dowty 1991), which also tend to occur as syntactic subjects on verbs, and Arg1s generally correspond to proto-patients, which often occur as syntactic objects. Consider the following roleset for the verb catch (2): (2) catch-01: come into possession of 

arg0-agent: catcher 

arg1-theme: thing caught 

arg2-source: giver ‘Liu caught the pitch from Cooper’ Annotation consists of two tasks: roleset or sense selection, followed by assign-ing numbered arguments to denote certain participant roles. For every instance of a verbal relation in a corpus sentence, annotators would first select a roleset and then tag the nodes in the parse tree governed by the verb with either a) a numbered argument from the roleset, or b) one of a small inventory of general se-mantic modifier args (ArgMs, e.g., ArgM-LOC (location), ArgM-DIS (discourse markers), ArgM-MNR (manners and instruments)) (Bonial et al. 2010). One of PropBank’s greatest successes was that, across a wide range of corpora and domains, human annotators were able to make these judgments easily and consistently. Inter-annotator agreement (IAA) was consistently high for Prop-Bank – Bonial et al. (2017) report ‘exact match’ (all constituents and arguments 297 Claire Bonial, Julia Bonn & Harish Tayyar Madabushi match precisely) IAA for English verbal relations at 84.8%, and ‘core-arg match’ (numbered arguments match and ArgMs match, but the specific ArgM, such as Temporal or Locative, need not match) of 88.3%. Propbank 1.0 annotated only verbal relations. During this time, in cases of dis-tinct senses aligning with prepositional verbs (e.g., depend on ) and verb particle Cxns (e.g., catch up ), distinct rolesets were added to the PropBank lexicon to enable accurate annotation of these cases of MWEs. For example (3): (3) catch_up-04: come even with, to catch up

arg2-goal: goal ‘The U.S. paper industry needs to catch up with the European industry.’ Thus, in order to accommodate certain kinds of MWEs, such multi-word re-lations were stored in the PropBank lexicon. Notably, this required significant manual effort as the PropBank lexicon of rolesets was driven by annotation. Thus, in coming upon catch up for the first time, a PropBank annotator would peruse existing rolesets, and, finding nothing appropriate, would note the instance for a set of PropBank lexicographers to create the new roleset, complete with expected argument numbers and a set of examples to guide future annotation. Such manual effort becomes untenable with more productive instances of MWEs. The clearest early case of this issue was with light verb constructions (LVCs). LVCs, when abstracted to the level of, for example, take + deverbal noun, are very productive, but not fully productive. Thus, while many cases of the afore-mentioned pattern are likely to be instances of LVCs, there are also false positives such as take a strip of paper and fold it . Furthermore, because the purpose of PropBank is to model the association of semantic roles with particular syntactic patterns, failing to include the MWE roleset precludes assigning the unique roles of the MWE to its unique constituents. As a result, PropBank 1.0 reflected Gen-erative assumptions that there is a single head, specifically a lexical verb, that assigns thematic roles. Thus, the LVC take a walk , for example, had previously been annotated with a sense of take denoting ‘acquiring something, bringing it with you somewhere.’ Walk was then annotated as the Arg1: ‘thing taken’. As a result, walk would be lumped in with concrete objects such as book , and any semantic roles licensed by the walk relation would also be mis-tagged as some semantic role of take .To avoid such mistakes and to preclude the necessity of attempting to list pro-ductive MWEs in a relatively static lexicon of rolesets, PropBank shifted for the first time to the inclusion of constructional rolesets for LVCs, one type of par-tially productive MWE. In these constructional rolesets, the fixed, substantive 298 8 Dancing with Deer light verb would be tagged with a special ‘LV’ marker, indicating that it pro-vided syntactic scaffolding, but did not contribute a semantic role. Thereafter, the annotators would then leverage the roleset for the event corresponding to the eventive noun, (e.g., walk ), marking that as the relation contributing seman-tic roles to the surrounding arguments, such as Destinations and Manners. The resulting PropBank annotations of LVCs facilitated modeling the properties of LVCs (Bonial 2014), which in turn provided adequate amounts of high-quality training data to develop the state-of-the-art (at its time) system for detecting LVCs and distinguishing them from identical, non-LVC collocations (Chen et al. 2015). The successful modeling of LVCs with a constructional approach was followed by efforts to develop rolesets for other MWEs characterized by fixed and flexible slots. This work coincided with an effort to reorganize the PropBank rolesets according to events with shared semantics and argument structures, as opposed to lexical relations (O’Gorman et al. 2018). For example, there was a single roleset reflecting events expressed as the noun or verb fear , the adjective afraid , and the LVC have fear ; all instantiations of this event would thus be annotated with the same roleset. The ‘unified’ PropBank lexicon of rolesets was adopted by both the Abstract Meaning Representation (AMR) (Banarescu et al. 2013) and the related Uniform Meaning Representation (UMR) projects (Van Gysel et al. 2021). In the AMR project, the notion was to abstract away from syntactic idiosyncracies in order to annotate a more abstract level of meaning. UMR shares this goal, but aims to provide such meaning representations across a wide variety of languages. In both of these cases, it is critical to model meaning consistently, despite the array of differences that arise in the Cxns or forms giving rise to that meaning. # 4 Accounting for MWEs in morphologically complex languages 

Croft says: “Morphosyntax is the analysis of the internal structure of utterances, both above the word level and below it. Why combine morphology and syntax? Because grammatical constructions involve both” (2022: 3). In this section, we look at how a CxG approach that redefines the ‘word’ in ‘multiword expression’ as a meaningful morphosyntactic unit (MMU) (rather than purely syntactic unit) can help make sense of MWE phenomena, including idioms, in polysynthetic lan-guages. We use Arapaho, a highly polysynthetic and agglutinating Algonquian language of the North American plains, as an illustration. 301 Claire Bonial, Julia Bonn & Harish Tayyar Madabushi 

4.1 MWEs and the notion of ‘wordhood’ 

Section 2.1 noted that “the machinery needed for describing the so-called minor or peripheral constructions will have to be powerful enough to be generalized to more familiar structures.” Approaching MWEs in morphologically complex languages as multi-MMU Cxns allows us to do two important things: a) to in-clude polysynthetic languages in discussions of MWEs, and b) to place MWE phenomena in the context of the more general diachronic phenomena of word-building, lexicalization, and development of the mental constructicon. Far from being ‘peripheral’, MWEs are in fact illustrative of the very heart of language development. The process of MWE formation is very much like the process of lexicalization in general. Lexicalization proceeds as follows: through usage over time, conceptu-ally independent meaning units (e.g., words or other MMUs) that were previously instantiated in a variety of higher-order Cxns (e.g., morphemes being combined into words in the case of morphological Cxns, or words being combined into phrases in the case of lexical Cxns) begin to be used at a high frequency in one particular instantiation, which entrenches the forms within that higher-order Cxn. As a result, what was previously readily analyzed as consisting of several sub-Cxns begins to merge into a single coherent semantic concept that is some-how more than the sum of the parts. As this occurs, that new concept takes its place as a new entry in the mental constructicon. This occurs not only at the level of an individual’s mental constructicon, but also in the common constructicon shared by the community of speakers. While word-building through inflectional and derivational processes is not generally thought of as lexicalization, the two are closely related. Borin (2021) says that derived forms frequently end up becom-ing associated with a narrower semantic interpretation than their source forms. In his example from Finnish, the denominal/deadjectival nominalizing suffix -sto/-stö functions productively and compositionally to mean ‘a collection of X’. However, it is not uncommon for the derived forms to take on much more specific meanings, such as kirjasto (‘a collection of books’) coming to refer to a ‘library’ (2021: 225). The compositional usage is derivation, and the semantically shifted usage is lexicalization. Derivation does not necessarily lead to lexicalization, but it does feed it. MWEs can be considered a special form of lexicalization insofar as they rep-resent the consolidation of formerly conceptually independent meaning units into a single lexical sense. Some MWEs may eventually turn into a single or-thographic or phonological word, as has occurred with nevertheless , and insofar ,although clearly this is more likely to occur with fully substantive and continu-302 8 Dancing with Deer ous MWEs, and not at all likely with schematic MWEs. Still, the term ‘multiword expression’ itself betrays the position held in much of the literature that MWEs are a phenomenon that occurs above the word level, not below. But are MWE phenomena relevant to languages in which the definition of ‘word’ is much less likely to refer to something that aligns with a single se-mantic concept? The absence of polysynthetic languages (and other examples of morphological complexity such as noun incorporation) from so much of the MWE literature would seem to suggest that the most important criterion for MWE-hood is the involvement of multiple ‘words’ in the orthographic (white-space-delineated) or phonological sense. We argue that white-space delineation is not a particularly relevant criterion for MWE-hood in polysynthetic languages (Dixon & Aikhenvald 2003), and that idiomaticity is a far better one. Cxns that bear the hallmarks of lexical idiosyncrasy and (morpho)syntactic creativity are found in polysynthetic languages just as they are found in isolating and fusional languages, and the forces that drive these phenomena appear to be like in kind. Although they only circle the issue, Baldwin & Kim’s definition of MWE does 

make room for inclusion of ‘lexical items’ that comprise a single orthographic or phonological word, as long as they “can be decomposed into multiple lexemes” and “display lexical, syntactic, semantic, pragmatic, and/or statistical idiomatic-ity” (Baldwin & Kim 2010: 269). We follow Borin (2021: 228) in interpreting ‘lex-eme’ and ‘lexical item’ here to be synonymous, and we also propose that these terms are equivalent to our MMUs. Viewing MWEs through a CxG lens makes it possible to include idioms in morphologically complex languages in the conversation. Furthermore, construc-tional templates used for modeling MWEs turn out to be equally useful for sym-bolic computational modeling of morphologically complex predicates, whether idiomatic or not. This serves an important need, as there is an increasing desire for symbolic representations of languages with fewer computational resources, and polysynthetic languages overwhelmingly belong to this category.

Although it was once spoken widely in Colorado, Wyoming, Texas, Oklahoma, New Mexico, Montana, and up into Alberta and Saskatchewan, it is now critically endangered with fewer than 150 speakers re-maining on the Wind River Reservation in Wyoming. Although endangered, the Arapaho Language Project 2 has compiled significant resources over the past 20

Since this and the other noun incorporation Cxns listed in Table 2 are extremely productive and compositional, the verb stems they produce are not considered lexicalized unless further semantic shift occurs, and the elements that fill the slots of these Cxn templates may be considered MMUs. In iiniikohei-, the concrete action final iikohei itself can be analyzed further. It includes a derivational final marking it as an animate intransitive verb (AI), -yei ,which has been applied to the lexically substantive action final iiko ‘go by horse’. Even though iiko is still semantically complex – it encodes both an event concept and a participant concept – the form is fusional and does not appear to be able to be broken down further into distinct morphemes.

So the designation of detached prefixes as particles comes from the perspective that they are syntactic words , although morphose-mantically and constructionally speaking, they are still part of the verb-word. This demonstrates that the detachment Cxn produces noncontinuous verbal MWEs in the canonical orthographic sense (much as verb-particle Cxns are con-sidered MWEs) although these are not MWEs that we expect to become idiomatic in Arapaho. The fact that Arapaho allows meaningful elements to be deincorporated from the verb at all demonstrates that speakers view them as semantically indepen-dent. These elements are specifically elements that fill slots in the detachment Cxn template and participate in its propositional argument structure – and this is the definition of MMU, which we propose as the appropriate unit to use when discussing MWEs in Arapaho and other polysynthetic languages. At this point it is useful to distinguish several concepts. Word-building is the process of constructing the orthographic/phonological words of Arapaho. The 308 8 Dancing with Deer first step of this is filling the slots of word-form Cxns, such as the verb-word Cxn or the obligatory possessed noun Cxn, although the detachment Cxn (another word-building Cxn) should also be applied as part of the process to ensure that phonological rules can be applied correctly. Note that word-building and proposition-building are closely related in Arapaho and other polysynthetic languages, and this is why identifying MWEs has been so difficult. Proposition-building also begins with filling in the slots of the verb-word Cxn in Arapaho. 

Lexicalization is not necessarily tied to word-building in Arapaho. For ex-ample, the output of proposition-building processes should not be considered lexicalized as long as compositionality has been retained. If compositionality is lost and meaning becomes more than the sum of the parts, lexicalization has occurred. 

MWE-formation may occur if a single word-form constructional template re-sults in multiple orthographic forms (like with the output of the verb-word Cxn + detachment Cxn), or if lexicalization occurs across two or more MMUs. This includes cases in which the MMUs lie within the same word-form con-structional template as well as cases where the two MMUs are separate ortho-graphic/phonological words. It should be noted that in cases where a MWE develops within elements of a verb-word, it is not necessarily the case that the entire orthographic word becomes the MWE. For example, if a discourse relation from the first (proclitic) slot in the template lexicalizes with a tense or aspect marker from the third (grammatical preverb), those two elements form a MWE without involving any of the rest of the propositional elements. A caveat here is that the two MMUs should still be identifiable to speakers as having individualized interpretations as well as a combined interpretation. Overall, Arapaho provides evidence that the (orthographic) ‘word’ is not the most salient unit of the language. This aligns with a CxG perspective, which posits that Cxns are the fundamental unit of a language, and that the constructi-con is made up of a taxonomically related set of Cxns that are characterized by differing levels of hierarchical abstraction. As a result, Cxns are often character-ized as existing at the morphological level, the word level and the phrase level, depending upon the form-meaning pairing under analysis. However, it should be noted that this characterization may draw upon an unwarranted assumption – that there is a clear distinction between these levels in the language. Arapaho provides counter-evidence to this problematic assumption. Just as Croft (2022) posits that parts of speech can only be defined according to the Cxns of a lan-guage, we posit that the formal units of a language may not readily align with notions of morpheme and lexeme, and instead should also be defined according 309 Claire Bonial, Julia Bonn & Harish Tayyar Madabushi to the Cxns of the language, with special attention paid to where we see formally identical Cxns instantiated both independently and within higher-order Cxns. 

4.3 Rolesets for Arapaho MWEs 

In this section, we shift again to a real-world use case that benefits from leverag-ing a constructional modeling of MWEs, but this time in Arapaho. Here we focus on the UMR annotation of Arapaho. UMR inherits the PropBank/AMR shared style of representing the lexicon in the form of rolesets, which then guide the as-signment of semantic roles, designated as ‘Arg’ numbers (see Section 3 for details in English). Like AMR, UMR represents sentential meaning as a directed, acyclic graph, but UMR includes flexibility as to what is included in this graph. This flex-ibility facilitates a language-dependent, data-driven representation of meaning in a particular language. Without such flexibility (as is the case with AMR), the meaning representation tends to reflect the idiosyncrasies of the one or two lan-guages that it was originally developed to handle (English and Chinese, in the case of AMR) (Banarescu et al. 2013). When a MWE develops in a verb-word that scopes over the predicate, a new predicate is added to the mental constructicon with a unique argument struc-ture. These are the cases where idiomatic rolesets may be created. Example (10) presents an idiomatic MWE, synonymous with ‘catch a bug’ from (5). (10) nih-3iikon-ceb-eit past-ghost-shoot.with.arrow-4/3

The ‘ghost’ indexes to the subject argument, marked as 4th person with the pronom-inal suffix -eit . Being 4th person (the code used for obviative pronominals in Arapaho transcriptions) makes this entity indefinite, which means their identity may not be known, or they are at least not the primary active entity in discourse. In effect, the focus is actually on the direct object of the verb, the 3rd person, 

getting sick, rather than the act of communicating the disease or the identity of the contagious party. The development of MWE rolesets has been critical to the development of role-sets for polysynthetic languages. The core innovation of MWE rolesets was the inclusion of the token-slot mappings, and these have been used to model token-slot mappings in general cases of morphological complexity even when idiomatic meaning is not present – which as we have seen is the case with the majority of Arapaho verb-words. Since polysynthetic languages tend also to be low-resource languages, speaker communities who wish to participate in development of NLP resources for these languages cannot expect to rely on state-of-the-art AI strategies like LLMs – there is simply nowhere near enough training material to even begin to create such a thing. The Arapaho Conversational Database contains 29,000 sentences, as opposed to the billions upon billions needed to feed an LLM. There is considerable worry that NLP resources for low-resource languages that rely on brute force methods will end up creating faulty representations of the language, causing irreparable harm to documentation of the language and especially to the language communities themselves. Once the bad-NLP horse has left the barn, so to speak, it will be virtually impossible to put it back in. Symbolic meaning representations like PropBank and UMR are well established as highly 312 8 Dancing with Deer successful with smaller training sets, and continue to be increasingly relevant to smaller language communities that wish to participate in NLP research. 

# 5 Critical aspects of MWE research in the era of LLMs 

In the previous sections, we have provided a description of how we can build symbolic resources, grounded in CxG theory, supporting automatic recognition and interpretation of MWEs. However, in English and other resource-rich lan-guages, we recognize that subsymbolic methodologies for a variety of NLP tasks requiring MWE analysis are dominant. Thus, in this section, we turn to how LLMs handle MWEs. LLMs, primarily trained on next-token prediction, have demonstrated an im-pressive range of capabilities. To dismiss them merely as statistical next-word prediction tools would be an underestimation of their potential, as demonstrated by numerous recent studies. However, assuming these models are all-powerful and capable of complex ‘reasoning’ similarly misrepresents their limitations (Lu et al. 2024). The truth likely lies somewhere in between. In this section, we pro-vide a focused, brief overview of what LLMs can reliably achieve, what they are less consistent at accomplishing, and the implications of these boundaries for on-going research into MWEs. Based on this discussion, we design targeted exper-iments to expose specific strengths and weaknesses in LLMs, highlighting the critical areas in MWE and CxG research that remain essential – perhaps even more so – in light of the rise of LLMs. In an attempt to first differentiate the aspects of language that LLMs can han-dle well from those they handle less well we begin by providing some clear defini-tions. Specifically, we adopt and refine the definitions of formal linguistic compe-tence and functional linguistic competence from Mahowald et al. (2024), who de-fine formal linguistic competence as the abilities that typically encompass those required to produce and comprehend language, while functional abilities pertain to using language to achieve specific goals. However, for our purposes, this dis-tinction needs to be further refined to effectively pinpoint the challenges LLMs face with regard to MWEs, and language ‘understanding’ in general. 

5.1 Formal and functional linguistic competence 

We define ‘formal linguistic competence’ as the set of capabilities required to comply with the structural rules and patterns that govern a language. We explic-itly exclude the notion of ‘understanding,’ present in the original definition, and 313 Claire Bonial, Julia Bonn & Harish Tayyar Madabushi our focus is purely on the phonological, morphological, structural and lexical se-mantic aspects of language, which typically are in line with components of the traditional NLP pipeline. Specifically, these include: • Phonological and morphological knowledge: Permissible sound combina-tions and productive morpheme usage. • Syntactic knowledge: Sentence structure and agreement rules. • Lexical knowledge: Ability to associate words with their correct gram-matical and contextual roles. • Constructional sensitivity: Ability to recognize linguistic regularities, ex-ceptions, and idiomatic expressions, including MWEs. A central feature of formal linguistic abilities is their variability across lan-guages and the need for expert training to explicitly label or annotate them. Native speakers, while possibly not being able to annotate or explicitly identify these el-ements, can typically use them fluently and without formal training, relying on implicit knowledge, which we will call ‘tacit linguistic knowledge’ (see Section 5.1.3 below for a contrast to metalinguistic information). For example, consider the sentence: The house key is on the cabinet. Here, the subject ( key ) and the verb ( is ) agree in number. This agreement must remain con-sistent even when the subject and verb are separated by a lengthy relative clause: 

The house key that is brown and was lost last winter only to be found again is on the cabinet. Despite this additional complexity, speakers instinctively ensure subject-verb agreement based on the noun ( key ). This ability of native speakers stems from implicit familiarity with the relevant Cxns, including the intransitive as well as the noun-phrase and relative-clause Cxns. 6 Therefore, while native speakers can track and use these structures effortlessly, they are not likely to be able to complete tasks such as producing parse trees, which require specialized training. There is another important feature of formal linguistic structures: they are theoretical constructs developed by linguists – they do not exist as explicit and tangible entities within a speaker’s mental representation of language. Therefore, they serve as tools to analyze the implicit structural knowledge that underpins
