These tools are post hoc analytical frameworks, and capture aspects of language that have evolved in response to factors such as the phys-ical constraints of speech production and the cognitive limitations of memory. Furthermore, most formal linguistic frameworks are influenced by literacy and based in written language; thus, the postulated structures are those that are re-flected in the patterns of text. It is, therefore, unsurprising that many of these linguistic elements are effec-tively encoded within pre-trained language models trained primarily on next-token prediction or similar learning objectives. Probing classifiers – simple classi-fiers designed to map the internal representations of pretrained language models to labels associated with linguistic information – have demonstrated the ability to extract a wide range of linguistic information, including parts of speech and even parse trees. 

5.1.1 Functional linguistic capabilities 

‘Functional linguistic capabilities’, on the other hand, include skills such as logical reasoning, mathematical reasoning, social understanding, and planning. Notably, these capabilities are largely independent of the specific language a speaker uses. This is not to say that there is no variation: cultural factors play a significant role in shaping how individuals approach these higher-level processes. However, unlike formal linguistic competence, which necessarily varies across languages (with some exceptions), functional linguistic capabilities can remain consistent. For instance, a bilingual individual can apply the same functional linguistic skills when interacting in different languages while adapting to the formal linguistic rules unique to each language. In this sense, functional linguistic capabilities are, to some extent, language-independent. Unlike formal linguistic competence, it is not immediately obvious that an LLM trained on next-word prediction would ever develop functional linguistic capabilities. However, effective next-word prediction often necessitates captur-ing some degree of functional ‘competence’. For example, consider the sentence: 

The [boring/serene] landscape took our breath away. Correctly predicting the word that fits requires some ‘understanding’ – or at least a statistical approx-imation – of what ‘taking one’s breath away’ implies. This suggests that LLMs acquire a limited degree of functional linguistic competence through exposure to vast amounts of text. CxG offers a clear way of distinguishing the functional linguistic competence LLMs might be expected to have or lack. Under the usage-based acquisition of language, frequency plays a role in a speaker’s familiarity with a particular Cxn, 315 Claire Bonial, Julia Bonn & Harish Tayyar Madabushi as well as the entrenchment of certain instantiations of (i.e. words or morphemes realized within) that Cxn, which in turn plays a role in the extension and gen-eralization of that Cxn. For many literate speakers, there are likely a variety of Cxns that have been and continue to be encountered in text. In these cases, the contextual information that is stored with each exemplar experienced may also be largely textual (although we do not discount the cross-modal associations that may arise, for example, when reading in a comfortable chair, accompanied by cof-fee and dark chocolate). To the extent that a literate speaker’s constructicon is made up of such textual Cxns, it may greatly align with an LLM’s constructicon, along with the contextual associations with that Cxn that characterize the stored exemplar. However, where the linguistic information of a speaker will greatly dif-fer from an LLM is in the pre-literate and non-textual encounters with Cxns – language in real-world communicative interactions. As each token of linguistic experience enriches the stored exemplar of a Cxn, an embodied speaker’s con-structicon will be characterized by details that are, of course, inaccessible to an LLM. Consider, for example, Labov’s department store study: speakers demon-strated that they stored socio-economic contextual information with the rhoti-cized lexical Cxn of, for example skirt (Labov 1986). Thus, under a CxG view, LLMs are able to reflect functional linguistic competence insofar as this aligns with a textual context, but are limited in functional linguistic competence that stems from a life-long history of language encounters in an embodied, social context. Therefore, while LLMs excel at formal linguistic capabilities, their robustness in functional linguistic abilities remains limited, even at the largest scales and when trained on extensive datasets like the entire web. Indeed, several works have highlighted this shortcoming, e.g. Bender & Koller (2020). These limitations highlight the possibility that something is missing, making LLMs particularly ill-suited for the task of ‘understanding’, an important element of functional linguistic competence. 

5.1.2 High-level, non-statistically likely functional linguistic capabilities 

Revisiting the example of functional linguistic abilities, it is evident that an LLM would have little difficulty correctly completing the sentence The [bor-ing/serene] landscape took our breath away. This demonstrates the need for a finer-grained classification of functional linguistic capabilities. Therefore, we propose a finer-grained distinction between those elements which typically align with statistical generalizations from text and those that do not. 316 8 Dancing with Deer This distinction is crucial because the pre-training data of LLMs far exceeds their parametric memory. As a result, LLMs can explicitly store only the most frequently occurring patterns, relying on statistical generalizations to handle less frequent information. This type of generalization – drawing inferences from priors in the pre-training data without direct ‘memorization’ – is central to how LLMs address certain functional linguistic tasks. However, the limitations of this approach become apparent when LLMs are tasked with counterfactual reasoning, which requires applying the same underlying rules to scenarios that deviate from standard assumptions. For example, in a counterfactual addition task, the model might need to add numbers in base-9 instead of base-10. For this reason, we should expect LLMs to struggle in scenarios where the statistical generalizations from pre-training data do not align with the require-ments of the task. Conversely, in cases where these generalizations are the norm – such as in word sense disambiguation – they can be highly effective. It is for this reason that our evaluation of MWEs in subsequent sections is divided into cases requiring formal linguistic competence and basic, statistically typical func-tional linguistic abilities, versus those requiring more complex generalizations that cannot be easily derived from pre-training data. 

5.1.3 Metalinguistic vs tacit-linguistic knowledge 

At this point, it is useful to introduce the concepts of metalinguistic informa-tion and tacit-linguistic knowledge . The latter refers to the intuitive, unspoken understanding native speakers have of their language’s Cxns, even if they can-not consciously articulate them. This classification is orthogonal to formal and functional linguistic competence as outlined above, and can apply to either. How-ever, traditionally, metalinguistic information has been more extensively applied in the context of formal linguistic competence. Importantly, testing non-experts on metalinguistic knowledge – such as their ability to identify explicit linguistic Cxns – evaluates only their understanding of formalized concepts, not their tacit knowledge. Assessing tacit linguistic knowledge requires methods that directly examine how these structures are used in natural contexts. This same distinction applies when evaluating LLMs. Testing whether an LLM can annotate metalinguistic information primarily assesses its explicit linguistic knowledge rather than its tacit knowledge of language use. It might be argued that, outside of linguistic use cases, what matters most is tacit linguistic knowl-edge. Therefore, to properly evaluate LLMs, they must be tested in scenarios that reflect real-world language usage. 317 Claire Bonial, Julia Bonn & Harish Tayyar Madabushi 

5.2 Evaluating the extent of MWE generalization in LLMs 

Given this context, we design controlled tests to evaluate the formal and func-tional tacit-linguistic knowledge of LLMs, specifically focusing on their ‘under-standing’ of MWEs. These experiments are designed to allow us to assess these models in areas where they are known to perform well and in areas where they are weaker, without relying on metalinguistic information, which is unlikely to be relevant in real-world scenarios. Additionally, it is critical to account for the extensive data used during model pre-training. Any meaningful evaluation of a model’s high-level abstraction or ‘understanding’ of a MWE must carefully consider the potential influence of pre-training data. Testing whether a model can interpret novel extensions of a MWE in a fashion similar to a human speaker is futile unless we can confirm that those MWEs – and their variations – are absent from the pre-training data. To address this, we conducted tests using novel MWEs that we created, which were therefore, by definition, absent from the pre-training data of LLMs. This ensured that we were evaluating the model’s true generalization abilities, inde-pendent of any confounding factors introduced by pre-training data exposure.

5.2.2 The limits of LLMs: Reasoning with novel MWEs 

Recall our earlier discussion on the varying levels of functional linguistic abilities and how LLMs capture statistically likely functional patterns. This secondary test assessed whether LLMs can generalize independently defined MWE meaning to this level of reasoning over a usage that combines MWEs. The particular lack of robustness to variations in prompts that was more pronounced in these tests highlights this difficulty. While this result is on a particularly small dataset and therefore we cannot say for certain that it is universally generalizable – across annotators, prompts, or LLMs – it provides an indication of what LLMs can do and where they begin to fail. It highlights a gap in LLM capabilities when tasked with rea-soning beyond statistical priors derived from pre-training data. When reasoning over the combination of novel MWEs, people are able to draw upon the immedi-ate definition of the individual MWE, but also compare the novel Cxns against stored exemplars for similarity, arriving at a richer set of associations to draw from when reasoning over the novel combination.

5.2.4 Implications to future research in MWEs and NLP 

Notice that our first set of experiments (Section 5.2.1) observed that LLMs can 

answer fairly complex questions pertaining to novel MWEs correctly, even when these involve novel use of previously unseen MWEs. However, their performance degradation in this new setting, when tested on the very same MWEs, suggests a reliance on single-step inference grounded in pre-training priors, rather than a robust capacity for high-level generalization and reasoning. This distinction is important. The failure to answer the second set of ques-tions, and particularly, the small, but surprising drop in performance of GPT-o1 combined with the lack of robustness to prompt variations of GPT-4o, indicates 326 8 Dancing with Deer that LLMs are using a combination of statistical priors from pre-training and information from the prompt to approximate plausible responses. These priors enable them to perform well in scenarios where the task is in line with familiar patterns (or analogies) from their training data. However, when faced with tasks requiring a higher level of generalization, their limitations become apparent. From a CxG perspective, given the importance of frequency of use, arguably you as a natural language speaker are also using statistical priors from your own experience with language in order to ‘understand’ language. Where this expe-rience is similar for a given Cxn, as in the first experiment, the linguistic abili-ties of people and LLMs are also surprisingly similar. That is, when the level of generalization requires only looking back to one previous token of textual use, people and LLMs can perform comparably. However, the reasoning questions in the second experiment push for generalization of that single attestation to very different contexts, such as counterfactuals (for example, generalizing from the meaning of drown the cables to if the cables were dry... ). Here, speakers tap into a lifetime of experience with embodied concepts such as wet/dry, the effect of wetness on electrical cables, as well as cross-modal contextual and cultural asso-ciations with semantically similar Cxns as metaphors, such as losing the thread 

of a particular topic. These detailed associations allow speakers to consistently reason over the question, while LLMs lack comparable, real-world associations. While it is notable that LLMs successfully solve 70% of our relatively small dataset, it remains unclear how to consistently improve these models, given their opacity and immense scale. Notice that the more powerful GPT-o1 did worse than GPT-4o, and also did not get the same questions right. It is at this juncture that we believe that MWE research has a unique opportunity to contribute. By integrat-ing insights from CxG, MWE research can offer interpretable and explainable datasets and methods. One such method might be the incorporation of AMR or UMR annotation schema into the MWE annotations. These resources can build upon the impressive formal and low-level functional capabilities of LLMs as a foundation, scaffolding toward systems that are more robust and generalizable. We believe this approach represents a more sustainable path forward. 

# 6 Future directions and conclusions 

This research demonstrates the standing value of having linguistic resources like PropBank and UMR for modeling the properties of MWEs. With such resources, we can better understand the patterns of flexibility and productivity. This also facilitates recognition and interpretation of MWEs in low-resource languages, 327 Claire Bonial, Julia Bonn & Harish Tayyar Madabushi where LLMs simply may not ever be feasible. However, such resources are also important in English, as they provide evaluation data with some explanatory power as to what linguistic capabilities LLMs seem to have and which they are lacking. As our experiments have shown here, although an LLM’s ‘knowledge’ of language does seem to have surprising parallels to usage-based acquisition of a constructicon, LLMs remain unable to generalize Cxns in a fashion similar to people, potentially because our extension of Cxns generalizes over a much richer set of cross-modal features than that of a text-based LLM. We have shown that CxG provides a unified way of thinking about MWEs cross-linguistically even when the languages differ greatly with respect to the notion of word-hood. Furthermore, Cxns offer a powerful template for modeling the flexibility of MWEs as well as providing a better understanding of their partial productivity. Developing constructional resources, such as PropBank and UMR, that mark up the fixed and flexible slots of constructions, can also facilitate both theoretical and computational analysis of the range of words that fill certain slots. To the extent that CxG aligns with LLMs as a usage-based theory of language acquisition and grammar, this elucidates why LLMs do seem to have a powerful grasp of language. On the other hand, where CxG highlights the cross-modal na-ture of the information stored for each token of linguistic experience, this also demonstrates the expected demarcation between an LLM’s knowledge of lan-guage in contrast to a person’s. With this awareness, we can begin to bridge the gap between our linguistic abilities and that of our NLP systems’ by pushing forward research into how to encode cross-modal features. While part of the an-swer may come in the form of larger, multi-modal pre-training corpora, we also emphasize the power of symbolic resources in providing explicit form-meaning constructional associations, in order to scaffold the bridge to future functional linguistic competence in our language technologies. Above all, we join others such as Bisk et al. (n.d.) in arguing that in order to process language and arrive at the same interpretation as a person, NLP resources must widen their scope from a focus on text and even images, to aspects of embodied social interaction.

Multiword expressions have long been a challenging research topic for natural lan-guage processing due to their complex syntactic and semantic nature, as well as their structural inflexibility. This research investigates the effectiveness of BERT models for classifying sentences based on whether they contain Greek multiword expressions. The study adopted a two-phase methodology: at first, fine-tuning the GREEK BERT model for masked language modelling using 4,406 MWEs in the Subject-Verb-Object form from lexical resources, and secondly, further fine-tuning and evaluating the model’s performance on Greek sentences originating from web sources containing both text with no idiomatic expressions and text with idiomatic and multiword expressions. Notably, both datasets employ identical verbs but in different contexts and sentence structures. The results demonstrate that the fine-tuned GREEK BERT model achieved higher accuracy in MWE classification com-pared to the non-fine-tuned baseline model, indicating that training BERT mod-els on structured lexical resources can significantly enhance their performance in free text classification tasks. This finding contributes to our understanding of how transformer-based models can be optimized to identify and process complex lin-guistic structures. The source code and data are publicly available.

# 1 Introduction 

Multiword Expressions (MWEs) are linguistic units that exhibit structural rigid-ity and non-compositional meaning, making them challenging for computational processing (Baldwin & Kim 2010, Sag et al. 2002). Their fixedness varies across semantic, lexical, and morphosyntactic levels, influencing their syntactic vari-ability and contextual ambiguity (Constant et al. 2017, Lamiroy 2003). Due to their idiomatic nature, MWEs require specialized identification methods in nat-ural language processing (Ramisch et al. 2018, Savary et al. 2019). Their com-plexity remains a key challenge in automated language analysis, particularly in cross-linguistic studies and NLP applications (Constant & Fotopoulou 2021). Recent advancements in machine learning and natural language processing have significantly impacted MWE processing. Deep learning models, including transformer-based architectures, have shown promising results in MWE identi-fication and processing tasks (Devlin et al. 2019, Brown et al. 2020). However, studies have found that these models capture MWE semantics inconsistently, often relying on surface patterns and memorized information (Ettinger 2020, Sinha et al. n.d.). Challenges remain in developing robust methods for captur-ing the fine-grained semantics of MWEs, as well as addressing issues such as ambiguity between MWE and non-MWE readings (Savary et al. 2019, Schneider et al. 2014). To improve MWE processing, researchers have developed special-ized techniques for identification and representation in lexical resources (Savary & Waszczuk 2020). Despite these advancements, MWEs continue to pose sig-nificant challenges for natural language processing (NLP) applications, necessi-tating ongoing research and development (Constant et al. 2017). Recent studies have also explored cross-lingual settings for MWE identification, leveraging pre-trained multilingual language models to learn knowledge about MWEs that is not language-specific (Ramisch et al. 2018, 2020). The application of masked language modeling prediction tasks to MWEs re-mains a fairly new domain in computational linguistics. This study examines a corpus of MWEs, comprising both frozen idioms with constrained paradigmatic variations and light verb constructions. We implement fine-tuning procedures for the GREEK BERT transformer model (Koutsikakis et al. 2020) to address masked language modeling and classification tasks. The methodological framework en-compasses two distinct phases: initially, we conduct fine-tuning of GREEK BERT in a masked language setting utilizing MWEs from syntactic classifications es-tablished in the PolylexMG resource (Fotopoulou et al. 2024). Subsequently, we further fine-tune the model from the first stage and evaluate its performance in identifying MWEs within Greek language constructions sourced from web-334 9 Fine-tuning BERT for masked language modelling based corpora. This investigation seeks to analyze GREEK BERT’s efficacy in MWE-related classification tasks, thereby contributing to our understanding of computational approaches to complex linguistic phenomena. The rest of the paper is organized as follows: Section 2 presents the related work; Section 3 introduces the background and preliminaries, establishing key concepts; Section 4 describes the PolylexMG dataset and the methodology for processing multiword expressions, detailing the corpus adaptation and prepara-tion procedures for Greek MWEs; Section 5 elaborates on the methodology for masked language modeling and text classification, outlining the fine-tuning pro-cess of GREEK BERT and the specific approaches used for MWE-related tasks; Section 6 details the experimental setup; Section 7 outlines the experimental evaluation; and Section 8 summarizes our main findings and contributions to Greek MWE processing in the broader context of Greek NLP and MWE research through detailed discussion. Finally, Section 9 examines the limitations of our approach and identifies potential areas for future research. 

# 2 Related work 

MWEs are of significant interest in NLP applications, particularly in areas such as machine translation (MT), parsing, and named entity recognition (NER). These expressions, which range from idiomatic phrases to lexical and syntactic con-structs, present challenges for both human and computational processing. The increasing application of deep learning, particularly recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and transformer networks, has led to substantial progress in NLP tasks, highlighting the importance of MWEs in NLP advancements (Vaswani et al. 2017, Yang & Xu 2020). However, the processing of MWEs in computational contexts is complex due to their inherent variability and fixedness, necessitating more standardized and structured approaches for their identification and usage across languages and applications. MWEs have been extensively studied in computational linguistics, focusing on techniques for their lexical detection, extraction, and classification from cor-pora (Parmentier & Waszczuk 2019). These studies, such as those investigating the automatic acquisition of nominal and verbal MWEs (Ramisch et al. 2012), face challenges due to the diverse nature of MWEs and their varying degrees of compositionality. This complexity is further explored through methods such as numerical scoring (McCarthy et al. 2003, Reddy et al. 2011) and categorization schemes (Gurrutxaga & Alegria 2013), which assess idiomaticity, collocability, and compositionality across different languages (Cordeiro 2017, Cordeiro et al. 335 Aggeliki Fotopoulou, Panagiota Kyriazi & Stavros Nousias 2019). Laporte (2018) focuses on improving the classification of MWEs. He em-phasizes the importance of selecting appropriate features, particularly advocat-ing for clear-cut features over fuzzy ones. The paper highlights the value of ex-tensive lexical inventorying in identifying precise classification criteria. Laporte aims to create a cross-linguistically applicable classification system that is useful for computational applications. Regarding limitations, Smădu et al. (n.d.) investigate the performance of sev-eral Large Language Models (LLMs), including Llama 2, Vicuna, and GPT-4, across multilingual and multidomain setups in tasks such as complex word identification, lexical complexity prediction, and MWE processing. Their results indicate that despite the extensive training of LLMs, they often struggle to sur-pass smaller, task-specific models in MWE processing and lexical complexity prediction. Similarly, Miletić & Schulte im Walde (2024) conduct a broad sur-vey on transformer-based models and their handling of MWE semantics. They find that these models rely heavily on memorization and surface-level patterns rather than deep semantic understanding, further questioning their suitability for robust MWE identification. These studies highlight a fundamental limitation of LLMs: while they capture general linguistic patterns, they may not inherently grasp the nuances of MWEs without explicit supervision. Conversely, other works propose novel methods to enhance LLM-driven MWE identification. Tanner & Hoffman (2023) introduce a framework that treats MWE identification as a word sense disambiguation (WSD) task. Their model improves precision by filtering MWE candidates through gloss-based context matching, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines. Meanwhile, Avram et al. (2023) opti-mize multilingual MWE detection by leveraging mBERT with lateral inhibition and domain adaptation techniques. Their approach, applied across 14 languages available in version 1.2 of the PARSEME corpus, enhances language-independent MWE representations and improves performance over prior systems (Avram et al. 2023). These studies suggest that while standard LLMs may struggle with MWE processing, targeted adaptations, such as WSD-inspired architectures or multilingual domain adaptation, can significantly enhance their utility. Among the notable contributions to MWE research, the PARSEME network advanced the modeling and processing of MWEs. This initiative led to the de-velopment of a multilingual corpus annotated for verbal MWEs, covering 26 languages with consistent linguistic guidelines, significantly contributing to the understanding and formal representation of MWEs in NLP (Savary et al. 2023, Ramisch et al. 2018). Anastassiadis-Symeonidis et al. (2020) provide a comprehen-sive overview of research on MWEs in Modern Greek, synthesizing findings from linguistics, psycholinguistics, and NLP. They distinguish between fixed MWEs, 336 9 Fine-tuning BERT for masked language modelling light verb constructions, and both nominal and verbal MWEs, referencing im-portant works in each area. In terms of computational tools for identifying and extracting MWEs in Modern Greek, several studies have contributed to the devel-opment of tools for processing multiword compound nouns and nominal entities (Fotopoulou et al. 2008). These tools not only aid in MWE identification but also in conjugation and provide detailed lexical and syntactic descriptions. Further-more, Markantonatou & Christofidou (2020) have contributed to the growing body of work focused on MWE identification in Modern Greek, emphasizing the importance of such tools in advancing both linguistic and NLP applications. In the field of MWE resources, several significant studies have emerged for Modern Greek. IDION (Markantonatou et al. 2019) is a web resource specifically focused on verb MWEs (VMWEs). It contains 2,000 VMWEs, including 850 fully documented defining sets of synonymous MWEs, which reveal their conceptual organization. PolylexMG (Fotopoulou et al. 2024) represents a more extensive lexicographic database, encompassing 5,635 Modern Greek verbal multiword ex-pressions. Developed using the Lexicon-Grammar theory (Gross 1975) and Har-ris’ Distributional Approach (Harris 1951), the database systematically organizes MWEs into 20 syntactic tables based on their structural and distributional prop-erties. Each entry includes detailed encoding of syntactic features, fixed and non-fixed arguments, and transformational properties. Finally, the PARSEME shared tasks marked an advancement in VMWE re-search, focusing on their automatic identification across 18 languages (Savary et al. 2017, Ramisch et al. 2018, 2020). This initiative established universal annota-tion guidelines and developed a 5-million-word annotated corpus, creating stan-dardized terminology and annotation protocols for VMWEs. The task specifically addressed VMWEs such as “make a decision”, “break one’s heart”, and “turn off,” which present particular challenges due to their syntactic variability and discon-tinuous structures. The evaluation phase included seven participating systems, establishing important benchmarks for VMWE processing systems. 

# 3 Background and preliminaries 

3.1 Methodology on classification of verbal multiword expression data 

The methodological framework adopted for this classification is the Lexicon-Grammar (LG) (Gross 1975, 1986). In this classification, fixedness can be limited to only certain constituents of the sentence; a combination of fixed and non-fixed 337 Aggeliki Fotopoulou, Panagiota Kyriazi & Stavros Nousias constituents in Subject or Object position is permitted. For example, fixedness re-lies on the relation between the verb and the nouns that function as Objects with no paradigmatic variation for any of these components (direct and indirect): (1) VΔίνω NP-acc τόπο PP-acc στην Οργή giving place to anger ‘to swallow one’s pride’ Distributional properties, i.e., types of prepositions, semantic features (i.e., +human, -human) attached to nouns in subject and object positions, and syn-tactic properties such as pronominalization are formally encoded in the so-called Lexicon-Grammar tables. Each table is defined by a set of distinct properties (syn-tactic, distributional, and semantic) and includes all lexical items sharing these properties; entries in one table are therefore considered to form a homogeneous class. A generic syntactic pattern is used to describe each syntactic class in the LG table, as illustrated in Appendix B, in which each class includes abbreviations representing the corresponding syntactic structure. This formal representation indicates that the LG methodological framework provides a systematic and coher-ent way to describe elementary sentences based on their components and encode properties across different languages [ e.g. , N0 (non-fixed subject) V (verb) Prep (preposition) C1 (fixed first complement)]. One of the benefits of LG is its ability to enable comparisons between languages, which can support the development of cross-linguistic resources. The concepts of compositionality/non-compositionality and transparency/ opacity emerged from various studies and research conducted by syntacticians and semanticists. These studies were further enriched by contributions from cognitive linguists and psycholinguists (Gibbs Jr 1987, Levorato & Cacciari 1992, Glucksberg 1993). This diversity stems from the varied nature of MWEs and their varying degrees of compositionality. Regarding the spectrum of idiomaticity and the types of expressions it encompasses, several key studies have contributed to this discussion (Mel’čuk 2014, Nunberg 1978, Moon 1998, Constant & Fotopoulou 2021, Mini 2009). 

3.2 GREEK BERT model 

Koutsikakis et al. (2020) developed and released GREEK BERT, a monolingual transformer-based model for the Greek language, built on the BERT-BASE-UNCASED architecture (Devlin et al. 2019) with 12 layers, 768 hidden units, and 338 9 Fine-tuning BERT for masked language modelling 12 attention heads, totaling approximately 110 million parameters. The model was pre-trained on a 29 GB corpus comprising the Greek Wikipedia, the Greek portion of the European Parliament Proceedings Parallel Corpus (Koehn 2005), and the Greek subset of OSCAR (Suárez et al. 2019), a cleaned version of Common Crawl. To ensure maximum normalization, accents and diacritics were removed, and all text was converted to lowercase. The model employs a custom-designed 35k subword BPE vocabulary optimized for Greek language characteristics. The pre-training process utilized 1M steps with the Adam optimizer, implementing an initial learning rate of 0.0001 on a single Google Cloud TPU v3-8. In perfor-mance evaluation, GREEK BERT achieved an F1 score of 85.7 ± 1.00 in Named Entity Recognition, demonstrating its effectiveness for Greek NLP tasks.

# 5 Methodology for masked language modelling and text classification 

This section describes the methodology for utilizing and fine-tuning pre-trained BERT models for masked language modeling and text classification in the con-text of MWEs. Two distinct architectures operate across two sequential train-ing stages, both employing the Greek-BERT (Koutsikakis et al. 2020) foundation with identical core components: three embedding types (Token, Segment, and Positional) and a 12-layer transformer stack. The architectures differ exclusively in their output mechanisms. 

Stage 1: Masked Language Modeling The first stage executes masked lan-guage modeling on MWEs from the PolylexMG dataset. The architecture em-ploys embedding-to-vocabulary conversion with SoftMax activation for masked token prediction, generating the MWE-pre-fine-tuned-Greek-BERT model. 

Stage 2: Binary Classification The second architecture appropriates the MWE-pre-fine-tuned-Greek-BERT for classification downstream task (Devlin et al. 2019). The architecture has two outputs for Multiword Expression output and Literal Expression output respectively, both processed through dedicated linear layers. Information flows directly from input embeddings through transformer blocks to classification outputs. The second stage fine-tunes the MWE-pre-fine-tuned-Greek-BERT on a classification dataset of 200 annotated text excerpts (binary labels: ”1” for MWE presence, ”0” for absence). Ten-fold cross-validation is used entailing recursive training on 90% of data and testing on 10% holdout sets. The system utilizes the original GREEK BERT tokenizer via Hugging Face’s bert-base-greek-uncased-v1 function. All operations execute on a Google NVIDIA A100 40GB GPU.

# 9 Limitations and future work 

The GreekBERT model is fine-tuned in two stages using derivative datasets con-structed from the PolylexMG corpus. These datasets partially overlap in content due to the limited number of multiword expressions (MWEs) available, but they differ significantly in format and context. Both datasets focus on the same set of verbs but present them in different linguistic environments. The full-expression subdataset contains MWEs in their canonical form – simple present tense, first person singular – designed to rep-resent each expression in a standardized way. In contrast, the classification-task subdataset embeds the same MWEs within real-world language samples, drawn from informal conversations and web content, reflecting varied sentence struc-tures and usage contexts. This two-phase fine-tuning approach enables us to assess the model’s ability to recognize MWEs in naturalistic settings after being trained on their simplified forms. By encountering the expressions first in a clean, consistent format and later within diverse, realistic contexts, we can evaluate GreekBERT’s generaliza-tion capabilities when leveraging structured lexical resources. Future work will involve expanding the dataset with additional MWE types (e.g., nominal or adjectival), incorporating syntactic variability more explicitly, and exploring cross-lingual transfer with multilingual models to improve MWE detection in under-resourced languages such as Greek.

This volume offers a comprehensive overview of current research and emerging per-spectives on lexical resources specifically designed for - or containing - multiword ex-pressions (MWEs), and their use in Natural Language Processing applications. It brings together contributions that address various aspects of MWE modelling, representation, and processing across languages and frameworks, as well as their practical deployment in real-world applications. Particular attention is paid to current developments in the era of large language models.
